In countries where internet retailing is a small share of transactions, retailers tend to tie their online prices to offline prices in order to minimise costs associated with making pricing decisions. In countries where online transactions have a significant market share, online and offline prices are closely related and online prices may lead offline as the demographic of computer-literate, middle-class, cash-rich and time-poor consumers to which online retailers sell are less price-sensitive than the average consumer. As purchasing habits change, these online price series capture prices and changes in product information and can provide real time information on consumer behaviour. records.text: 2 Natasha Kaneva AC (1-212) 834-3175 natasha.kaneva@jpmorgan.com Global Markets Strategy 08 March 2026 J P M O R G A N Much of Iran’s mainland coast along the Persian Gulf is shallow and silty, meaning fully loaded VLCC supertankers, which require 65-82 feet of draft when fully loaded, would have difficulty approaching without very long offshore piers or extensive dredging. Kharg Island sits closer to naturally deeper water, allowing large tankers to berth and load efficiently, while also benefiting from decades of investment in storage tanks, loading terminals, and pipelines built during Iran’s oil expansion in the 1960s-1970s. As a result, the island has evolved into the backbone of Iran’s export system, which handles the vast majority of the country’s crude shipments. It is a cornerstone of Iran’s economy and a major source of revenue for the Iranian Revolutionary Guard. What is the island’s export capacity? records.text: Asia Economic Weekly | 06 March 2026 13 Australia in Focus Nick Stenner, CFA Merrill Lynch (Australia) Johnny Liu, CFA Merrill Lynch (Australia) See report: Australia Watch: Escalation in the Middle East: Oil shock, energy windfall Importing oil, exporting energy Australia is a net importer of oil and refined fuels, but a large net exporter of LNG and other bulk commodities, creating a complex exposure to an oil price shock. Higher oil prices and disrupted trade flows would weigh on external demand, lower export volumes, and push up inflation. But rising energy prices should lift export revenues and national income, although heavy foreign ownership means much of the windfall would flow offshore, limiting the domestic growth tailwind. Oil shock: rapid pass-through to headline inflation We estimate a 10% rise in oil prices increases headline inflation by about 30bps, while underlying inflation rises only marginally. This reflects direct pass-through to retail fuel prices, and broader indirect effects through input costs. If Brent remains around $80/bbl through March, that should increase domestic fuel prices by roughly 10% and add about 0.34ppts to 1Q headline CPI, pushing our forecast up 10bps to 1.1% q/q. records.text: 9 March 2026 Quant Snaps Deutsche Bank AG Page 3 In terms of sentiment indicators, our DBSI index ended the week at 81, marking its entry into risk-off territory. From the news sentiment viewpoint, we are currently at negative states on both non-fundamental and fundamental regimes for the US economy. The geopolitical tensions that started since the military action in Venezuela a few months ago have kept the non-fundamental state low ever since, but the fundamental regime also shifted, a little over a week ago. Even though recent PMI index data pointed to expanding economic activity in the US in February, mixed signals from employment data are keeping the balance towards a negative regime in our sentiment model. Finally, an extra interesting piece of information came from our transient sentiment factor, which has recently added explanatory power particularly when looking at our defensive strategies. Going beyond the topics already discussed, the transient sentiment on Emerging Markets dropped significantly last week, in both Growth and FX dimensions, another indication of a risk-off environment. The S&P 500 and the Nasdaq index fell by 1.9% and 1.2%, respectively, and they were not alone on that. In Europe, the negative effect of high energy prices on inflation and growth affected sentiment, with the STOXX 600 index also falling during the week. Faced with such great uncertainty, we will use this space to summarise what we know and to outline our scenarios for what may lie ahead. Let’s start by taking stock of what we know. Oil prices have risen above 85$/bbl, and TTF prices are up by almost 60% to €50.4MWh. More importantly, our commodity strategists think that even an immediate resolution of the conflict would leave oil and gas prices elevated, as flows are interrupted and take a long time to resume fully. With higher oil and natural gas prices a given for some time, we now expect inflation at 2.2%Y in 2026 (up from 1.9%Y previously) and an unchanged 1.7%Y in 2027 (see here). As a consequence, the ECB is likely to remain on hold throughout 2026 (vs our previous expectations of two rate cuts for this year) - see more here. And we should stress here, this is the mild scenario, which rests on the assumption of a rapid resolution of the conflict. Looking ahead, we see three broad scenarios (see here). A rapid de-escalation (our current baseline), with full flow of traffic in the Strait of Hormuz (SoH)resuming within 1-2 weeks, which would lead to a normalization in oil prices to $65-70/bbl and natural gas falling back to around €30MWh. This could potentially mean more limited fiscal space to address higher oil and gas prices this year, unless any type of support package to households and firms comes with a decline of expenditures elsewhere. 4. records.text: TRADE IDEA T R A D EI D E A STEER : Dislocations widen further; short EURNOK 09/03/2026 1 KEY MESSAGES ▪ Dislocations have broadly widened across G10 and EM as higher oil prices and falling global equities continue to affect fair values while the USD strengthens. Oil prices however still screen as negatively correlated with the USD for most pairs (e.g. AUDUSD, NZDUSD, USDJPY and USDKRW), according to the model, and we again refrain from entering new short USD signals. Last week geopolitical risk dominated market moves following the start of the n Middle East conflict. Implied vols increased across asset classes, led by oil volatility, which reached its highest level since 2020 (Exhibit 1). Equity implied vol also increased, but so far the spill-over from commodity to US equity vol has been modest – the VIX remains below the post ‘Liberation day’ highs so far. Longer-dated Treasury vol remained more anchored too. Equity implied vols have diverged geographically, with implied vol for Japan, Taiwan and especially Korea reaching elevated levels vs. history (Exhibit 2). Geopolitical shocks can pose significant risks to investment portfolios, yet they n tend to be challenging to anticipate or position for as they often eventually de-escalate, but sometimes they can have global and long-lasting effects. Our commodities team see growing upside risks to their oil price forecasts and think it’s likely that oil prices would exceed the 2008 and 2022 peaks, if Strait of Hormuz flows were to remain depressed throughout March. Brent prices opened above $100/bbl today and the market-implied probability that Brent will still be above $100/bbl in c.3 weeks jumped to 50% at the open, but markets are still pricing a lower probability of higher oil prices for longer horizons (Exhibit 3). records.text: M Idea 2 Summary As geopolitical tensions persist, more areas of potential disruption emerge: While the immediate focus of investors when geopolitical tensions first emerged was on the spike in oil prices, that attention is now shifting towards other areas of potential disruption. Watching oil, LNG, fertilisers, propane and transportation costs: In addition to oil, LNG, fertilisers and propane are coming into focus – as the Middle East is either a significant producer of these items or significant levels of trade flow through the Strait of Hormuz. Asia imports about a quarter of its energy needs in the form of crude oil, LNG and propane. The Middle East is also a major producer and trade hub for fertilisers and Asia relies on the Middle East for ~14% of its fertiliser needs. At the same time, with little to no traffic moving through the Strait of Hormuz and with airspace closures over the region, this is leading to a sharp rise in shipping and air freight costs, which is also emerging as an area of investor concern and will affect the transport of energy and non-energy products. records.text: M Global Foundation 6 US Trade and Tariff Monitor US tariffs have been the primary driver of changes in global trade flows this year. To facilitate a detailed assessment of these dynamics, we provide a suite of interactive tools covering three dimensions: economy-level tariffs, product-level tariffs, and economy- by-product exposures. This is accompanied by the corresponding trade data as well. The underlying dataset supports forward-looking analysis of the potential path of tariffs (read more here), assessment of sector- and country-level implications of tariff actions, evaluation of the effects of tariffs on consumer goods (read more here), and comparison of product-level tariff rates across countries. This structure enables a comprehensive view of how trade policy measures are being implemented and where their impact is most concentrated. All tariff data is presented using the NAICS classification system, allowing for direct cross- referencing with US equity market sectors and industries. In parallel, we provide US trade flow data mapped to NAICS codes to support analysis of how tariffs are reshaping trade patterns across geographies and product categories, as well as to assess sensitivity to shifts in global demand, supply-chain disruptions, and further trade policy adjustments. As we wrote last week (“Impact of oil price shocks a ‘frack’- tion of what they once were” ), the emergence of shale production in the US has helped to limit the impact of oil price spikes on the economy. Indeed, within the Fed’s FRB/US model , a $ 20/bbl increase in oil prices only increase s unemployment by about 2bps and has almost no impact on core PCE inflation. However, with downside risk s to the labor market while inflation has run above target for almost five years in a row, the response for the Fed to such a supply shock is not clear. Indeed, looking at the Fed’s prior responses to energy shocks does not yield a regular pattern (see “What does history tell us about the Fed's response to oil price shocks?”). Sometimes, the Fed emphasized the threat to the inflation side of their dual mandate while other times, it sought to protect against any deterioration in the labor market. However, the hit to consumers’ purchasing power at that level of oil prices would likely be substantial, which should weigh against the ultimate inflation response to the initial move in crude oil prices. That is, nonlinearities (which are mostly missing from these models) from historically more extreme price moves might dampen the inflation response, even as they augment the activity responses (as discussed below). The effect on core inflation from an oil supply shock is more muted: most estimates find a negligible impact. Even those studies that suggest a non-zero rise in prices—typically well under a tenth for a 10% oil price shock—tend to report results that are not readily discernible from no net effect at conven- tional levels of statistical significance. For example, the Fed’s FRB/US model finds negligible impacts on core inflation, whereas the above-mentioned DSGE approach estimates a 2bp rise in core inflation on impact, peaking around 6bp with- in a year before decaying fairly quickly back to zero. In a review of the empirical literature, Kilian and Zhou (2023) also find a negligible (and statistically insignificant) impact of oil supply shocks upon core inflation. records.text: M Update 6 Overall, the labor market continues to resemble a “no hire, no fire” environment. Labor market flows indicate that layoffs (transitions from employment to unemployment) remained subdued, while hiring (flows from unemployment to employment) fell to its lowest level since November 2024. The January and February household survey data incorporate updated, lower population estimates. Following standard practice, the BLS did not revise estimates for December 2025 or earlier months. As a result, absolute levels—such as the number of employed or unemployed workers—in January and February 2026 are not directly comparable with 2025 figures. In particular, the sharp decline in employment from December 2025 to January 2026 is purely mechanical and reflects changes in population controls rather than underlying labor market weakness. The updated population controls also altered the demographic weights used to calculate labor market ratios, contributing to the downward revisions in January’s participation rate and employment-to-population ratio. Specifically, the new estimates increased the weight of women aged 65 and over and reduced the weight of prime-age men (25–54), placing downward pressure on those ratios. We have penciled in two 25bp cuts under the next Chair (Kevin Warsh), with low conviction, in June and July for a terminal rate of 3.0-3.25%. records.text: shock. Second, lower-income households are more exposed to oil price shocks, because energy makes up a larger share of their spending. These households are already struggling, so further erosion of their real spending power from surging energy prices could cause another leg up in delinquencies (particularly credit cards and autos). In turn, this could have a lasting impact on their ability to spend, if it constrains their access to credit. Third, higher energy prices could become a bottleneck for AI capex. The hyperscalers – Amazon, Microsoft and Google – have announced massive data center investment plans for this year. Our GDP forecast incorporates a continued tailwind from AI-related investment. Delays in investment because of an energy price shock could be a major headwind for 2026 growth. It is difficult to assess exactly how large and persistent the oil price shock would have to be for these effects to kick in. But in our view, a sustained period of oil prices above $100/bbl (~60% increase) would probably take more than 60bp off GDP growth. And a doubling in oil prices, unlikely as it seems, could cause a recession.

Morgan The economy should not have much trouble weathering a moderate oil price spike, but there is an increasing risk that higher prices could create a more material near-term drag on the economy—particularly if they were to rise well above $100 per barrel and hold there. Even aside from the oil price story, the data flow is sluggish, with private payrolls barely averag- ing any gain over the last few months and uncertainty as to whether the unemployment rate has peaked yet (Figure 2). We haven’t changed our growth forecast, even as we remain attentive to the possibility of an oil-related downgrade. Meanwhile, the soft data that predated the Mideast tensions are still not far from what we’ve been anticipating. After excluding a roughly 1.0% lift from the end of the government shutdown, we're only forecasting 1Q GDP growth of 1.75%. This partly stems from the assumption that households will need to slow consumer spending growth as saving rates have fallen. That is playing out, with adverse January weather also playing a role. In this scenario we would expect markets to continue to price skew to tightening, but would see gradual pressure to reduce the pricing of tightening in reds and greens. As discussed in No rate cuts in 2026, the hurdle for ECB hikes is relatively high, in our view. We think market valuations are broadly in line with this scenario for long end, swap spreads and EGB spreads, but key drivers will depend on the detail around increases in defence spending and/or cost of inflation mitigation policies at euro area and country level. One theme in our recent discussions with clients is the risk around relying on “buy Bund” strategies to hedge geopolitical risks, with uncertainty over usage of the fiscal lever often mentioned as a driver of price action. We think that concerns around fiscal expansion are often exaggerated. For instance, in Still Room for 5x5 to Perform and Enter RX-UB Box Steepener we looked at the impact of the €1tn+ increase in German public expenditure, and we think a similar template can be used here as a starting point. The main difference is that fiscal consolidation can be challenged in countries with a less solid balance sheet than Germany, although we think the impact of a one-notch downgrade should be contained.

To some degree, the decline in measured fertility likely reflects a statistical nuance. Fertility rates are the number of children that a woman would statistically expect to have over her life if the number of children she had at each age were equal to the number of births to women of that age divided by the number of women of that age in a single year. If women gradually shifted over time towards having children later in life— i.e., reducing age-specific fertility rates now, but with the intention of raising older age-specific fertility rates in the future—the natural product would be an interim decline in country-level fertility rates that does not necessarily reflect any intention of having fewer children over one’s life. records.text: In this report, we examine the conditions necessary for the policy mix of n expansionary fiscal policy and rate hikes to produce a desirable outcome for the Japanese economy, namely achieving sustainable growth under price stability, accompanied by a rise in the potential growth rate. The Japanese economy is currently facing supply constraints due to intensifying n labor shortages. Under these circumstances, an increase in government spending to stimulate effective demand could lead to higher inflationary pressure, while having little impact on the real economy. It could also risk crowding out private-sector investment that generates high added value. Therefore, for the government to achieve its goal of raising the potential growth n rate, which is the stated purpose of its expansionary fiscal policy, it needs to focus on improving productivity by promoting investment in intangible assets, such as AI, software, and R&D. Additionally, from a sectoral perspective, it would be desirable for the government to emphasize sectors with relatively large spillover effects. Even if such an expansionary fiscal policy were to be implemented, inflationary n pressure could rise in the short term, because the increase in demand would precede the increase in supply capacity. Over the longer term, the natural rate of interest would also rise in tandem with a rise in the potential growth rate. Defensive equity styles like low volatility, infrastructure and dividend aristocrats have outperformed YTD but less so last week - they might outperform again if the S&P 500 corrects more (Exhibit 4). We shift tactically neutral equities/overweight cash for 3m but recommend hedging the upside tail for equities in the coming weeks. Our global equity strategy team has highlighted risks of an equity correction, but not a bear market - in particular, US equities have been relatively resilient, and the growth repricing has been limited so far. Our updated equity drawdown model incorporating the unwind in equity momentum and sharply rising commodity prices points to a risk of more than 40% (Exhibit 5). We continue to recommend adding more robustness in multi-asset portfolios - as described in our Balanced Bear research, investor should look at a combination of up-in-quality trades in equity/credit/FX, allocations to alternatives, dynamic risk allocation, and option overlays in equities and across assets. Currently we like selective bearish option spreads, calls on V2X and puts on Europe Industrials and German equities. Indeed, even excluding some potential volatility from a new birth/death model, the three-month average appeared to have picked up. But other measures of the labor market hadn’t moved much, and so it wasn’t entirely surprising to see an 86k plunge in February private jobs (-92k total). Likewise, as expected, we got downward revisions to the prior couple of months. Arguably, the best way to approach the recent data is to combine the strong January and weak February reports. Relative refers to the parameter of the underlying asset versus that of the potential hedge. Hedging option type depends on asset classes and correlation signs. For alternative hedging of downside protections, when correlation is positive with the targeting index, option type is put for equity indices and currencies (pay for rates and credits), and vice versa. Hedging Effectively X-Asset: HEXA is a systematic framework to screen for attractive alternative option-based hedging opportunities across equity indices and macro assets. Methodology: Three main factors drive the choice of the optimal proxy hedge. ▪ Strong historical relationship with the hedged asset: We analyse the relationship between spot and volatility markets and select assets that are correlated and co- integrated (spot/spot and spot/vol) with the hedged equity index. ▪ Cost effectiveness: Finding hedges that are cheaper than hedging with puts can be accomplished by comparing current spot price levels and derivative parameters to assess how appealing each looks compared with the hedged asset. ▪ Attractive entry point: We determine this in terms of price and derivative parameters of the cross-asset hedge. Although our US economics team sees the overall slowing in total labor demand last year as predominantly a cyclical response to depressed business confidence, the proliferation of increasingly adept AI tools and their potential impacts on labor markets are important to monitor, even if difficult to predict. records.text: ons. Ahead of last weekend’s events, we had already highlighted increasing risks to our medium-term view on inflation. Notably, in addition to our expectation that tariff pass-through will continue to drive core goods inflation higher in the near term, our baseline outlook for sticky inflation is based on an assumption that a recoupling between job growth and GDP growth will drive a retightening in labor markets over the year, keeping wage inflation sticky. While employment data through January showed early signs that momentum in hiring was picking up, today’s employment report — including downward revisions — suggests that the recent trend can best be described as a stabilization (see What January gives, February takes (jobs) , Abiel Reinhart, 3/6/26). Meanwhile, we recognize that on a rounded basis, core CPI has either come in line or softer than consensus for the last 10 reports (see TIPS Strategy, 2/20/26). Thus, cognizant of the speed of the recent moves and risks around our baseline forecasts, we are hesitant to add bullish inflation exposure, and we remain neutral on breakevens. In real yield space, we closed out of shorts in 10-year TIPS earlier this week and turned neutral (see US Treasury Market Daily, 3/5/26). A moderate price change of the type we have seen so far should be marginally hawkish for monetary policy, though that would not necessitate any change to our call for the Fed to stay on hold this year. We expect the Fed will look through an energy-linked spike in headline inflation that neither boosts core inflation much nor unanchors medium-term infla- tion expectations, consistent with remarks from Governor Waller late this week. Still, this would add to the list of rea- sons to pause, and many FOMC participants would like to see inflation on a sustained downward trend toward the 2% target before they consider cutting rates. Alternatively, a prolonged surge in crude oil prices to $120/bbl or more would result in a much larger drag on growth and could precipitate a dovish turn by the FOMC. That said, the recent experience of above- target inflation could lead the Fed to pivot more gradually toward monetary accommodation. We now see the price cap for Q3 2026 at £1,985, with the cap only returning to its Q2 2026 level by Q2 2028. A policy targeted at holding the price cap at its current level would cost £5.9bn to £6.4bn per year, ceteris paribus. Given the moves in energy prices over the weekend, we revisit our note last week on the fiscal implications of the ongoing energy crisis (see UK Economics – The fiscal implications of energy prices). In it we suggested that there would likely be political pressure for the government to intervene to shield household bills from the spike in energy prices, although there was no urgent pressure to do so. Our view is unchanged: We think that the government has options and pressure to act is growing, but, importantly, they have time to make a decision and wait and see if energy prices normalise before there is a need to intervene. However, the rally over the weekend has meaningfully changed the fiscal maths. In addition to the CTEP, EXIM Bank recently launched the Supply Chain Resilience Initiative (SCRI), a program designed to strengthen US access to critical minerals and other strategic resources. Unlike traditional export finance, SCRI leverages EXIM’s “import authority” to provide financing for international projects that have signed long-term “off-take” contracts with US companies. EXIM’s financing is tied to the value of the off-take contract between the foreign project and the US importer, rather than to US exports. These agreements ensure that EXIM’s support for critical minerals projects directly benefits American companies and workers by securing reliable access to essential inputs for advanced manufacturing and technology. Our analysis suggests that while growth outcomes following similar conflicts have been mixed, the magnitude of growth shocks tend to be correlated with the change in oil price three months after the shock. As such, while we continue to see AI disruption and private credit stress as the key structural drivers of wider spreads into 2026, the risk of sustained higher energy prices increases the probability of a stagflationary environment, particularly in Europe. The stagflationary playbook supports defensives, up-in-quality, and close-to- home positioning Although we believe positioning for a stagflationary environment may be premature, we revisit prior work to identify which segments of credit tend to outperform in such periods. Within IG, our analysis shows that Telecoms (+0.1–0.2% monthly excess return) and Consumer Non-Cyclicals (+0.1% monthly excess return) are the top-performing sectors across both Europe and the US during periods of low growth and high inflation. Within our EU model trade portfolio, we already hold longs in both sectors, supported by their defensive characteristics, attractive carry in Telecoms, and attractive valuations in Consumer Non-Cyclicals. Airfares should decelerate but remain elevated following last month’s strong acceleration, while hotels (lodging away from home) are likely to accelerate. More broadly, we think seasonality will continue to push up other services (excluding medical services, airfares, education, and hotels) in February. 4) Energy CPI accelerates, lifting headline above core. We expect higher gasoline prices and temporarily elevated wholesale natural gas prices in January to push utility prices higher in February. Key questions this print: 1) Will tariff pass-through continue? We think yes. We estimate that tariffs have raised overall prices by about 50bp so far; we expect a total pass-through of roughly 70bp. In other words, there is still room for additional price resetting. That said, the closer we get to the 70bp mark, the higher the likelihood of normalization in core goods inflation. 2) Are there signs of seasonal pressure in February? We expect core services ex-housing to remain sticky, potentially reflecting residual seasonality. 3) Shelter deceleration. We expect shelter inflation to remain around its underlying trend (~0.26% m/m) at least through 3Q this year. Risks are skewed to the downside, and the next few prints will be important in assessing our outlook for the remainder of the year. Mathematically, a reading roundin

In this case, a 6-3 majority is a plausible risk to our base case (as is 5-4 the other way), but we would take little signal from this as it does not require much of a shift in either individual's position. Cautious communication to reduce downward bias in guidance We think the tone of the minutes, and the individual paragraphs of members in the middle of the committee (Bailey, Mann, Ramsden and Breeden) will be particularly cautious. We think in this instance that it is likely that the committee drops the guidance that "on the basis of the current evidence, Bank Rate is likely to be reduced further" and shift the focus instead to the remaining statement that "the extent and timing of further easing in monetary policy will depend on the evolution of the outlook for inflation. " This would allow the committee to retain a downside bias – as not even the more hawkish members of the committee have yet intimated they are discussing a hike (see Bailey at TSC and Chief Economist Pill) and we do not think the current shock would motivate such a discussion – but it would soften the extent of that bias. We think this move was likely even in the absence of recent energy price developments as, assuming a cut to 3.5%, Bank Rate is now in the range we think the median MPC member would interpret as plausibly neutral. Bias by design: AI systems amplify gender biases AI systems can amplify gender biases, portraying women, especially in higher‑status roles, as younger and less experienced and tilting resume screening toward older men at the expense of older women. AI often reinforces gender and age- based stereotypes, depicting women, especially in higher status roles, as younger and less experienced, impacting hiring, evaluation, and promotion of women in the workplace. Research finds that stereotypes about older women are widespread in online images and videos, and that large language models carry and even intensify these biases. By analyzing over 1.4mn images and videos across online platforms, as well as billions of text from the web in 9 language models, researchers found that women are consistently portrayed as younger than men, especially in depictions of higher-status and better-paid occupations. When prompting ChatGPT to generate over 34,500 unique resumes for 54 occupations using typical male or female names, it generated results that portrayed women as younger and less experienced, assigning older male applicants with a higher quality (Figure 33W o m e n a r e r e p r e s e n t e d a s s i g n i f i c a n t l y y o u n g e r t h a n m e n i n b i l l i o n s o f w o r d s s c r a p e d f r o m t h e i n t e r n e t , a s e n c o d e d b y C h a t G P T ). records.text: 6 March 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Page 6 Deutsche Bank AG How we adapted the portfolio The nomination of dovish BoJ members led us to exit the JGB flatteners last week. The combination of cracks in the credit market exposed by AI concerns and increased risk aversion on the back of the latest geopolitical events led us to further reduce risk today and exit bearish rates trades in EUR. In both cases, these changes are not (as yet) reflective of a shift in the structural view but more about risk management in a more volatile environment. For a more fundamental change in view, we would need to see evidence that AI creates enough uncertainty about employment prospects to lead investors and consumers to pull back despite a supportive policy mix. This could be reflected in a tightening of lending standards and weaker consumption. Waiting for evidence of weakness in the labour market will most likely be too late. In Japan, a fundamental change in view would require a demonstrated tolerance from policymakers for a materially weaker currency. Exhibit 5 US: Exploring Monthly Exports at a Product Level (NAICS Classification) Source: AlphaWise Web Intelligence, US Census Bureau, USITC, Haver Analytics, Morgan Stanley Research Methodology We leverage monthly US trade data as reported by the US Census Bureau. The dataset covers imports from, and exports to, the 50 largest US trading partners, with trade flows reported in billions of US dollars. Aggregates for shares by geographic region reflect only these top 50 trading partners. Tariff metrics are derived from US Census data on Calculated Duties. We estimate the share of trade exposed to tariffs as the dutiable value divided by total trade (Customs Value). The average tariff on dutiable goods is calculated as Calculated Duty divided by Dutiable Value. To estimate the effective tariff rate across all trade, including duty-free flows, we divide Calculated Duty by total trade (Customs Value). Trade flows are presented using the NAICS classification system, enabling consistent product- and industry-level analysis and facilitating cross-referencing with US equity market sectors. To start with, both fiscal and monetary policy were in a very different place back then. At the start of the Ukraine conflict, ECB policy was very accommodative, with the deposit facility rate at -0.5%. Right now, the ECB runs a broadly neutral monetary policy at 2%. Fiscal policy was also much more supportive in 2022 than today. The global economy was just coming out of the COVID years, with double digit fiscal deficit stimulus still working its way through the economy, not only in Europe, but also in the US. At the time of the 2022 inflationary shock, European governments were still allowed to exceed spending limits imposed by the fiscal rules, as the European Commission had suspended the Stability and Growth Pact (SGP) due to Covid. Countries delivered large fiscal packages to shield households and firms from rising inflation. At the time, we were estimating the cost of fiscal measures for 2022 and 2023, at a total of 4% of GDP for the euro area (see here). Governments are today much less likely to deliver as much fiscal support as back then. Interest rates on outstanding debt have moved meaningfully higher (from around 1.6% in 2021 to 2.3% in 2024) and should increase by a further 30bp by the end of 2027, based on current market rates. records.text: tee in general more confident that the risk of second-round effects had subsided. Inflation expectations were set to come down as spot inflation fell and the signs were that the recent labour market loosening has been driven more by a cyclical unwinding than problematic structural change. The possibility of a new energy price shock would bring upside risks, particularly around inflation expectations, back onto the agenda for the MPC, and with it, a more cautious tone. ...but not clear how significant that risk is When considering the risk of second-round effects from the energy price shock, there are two interesting state-contingencies relevant for the current juncture. First, BoE staff work suggests that multipliers are larger, and the risk of persistence greater, when the starting level of inflation is higher and if there has been a period of above-target inflation, as it increases the risk of inflation expectations rising. On the other hand, the incidence of second-round effects is less if the labour market is looser, which we and the BoE currently appraise it to be, as workers have less wage bargaining power and firms have less pricing power when faced with weak demand. Key for March's decision will therefore be how the MPC weighs up these two channels. We think that the ambiguity over which channel currently dominates will allow committee members on either end of the range of views space to maintain their positions. Another key observation pertains to the nature of this geopolitical shock, which combines a risk-off with higher Bund yields. Historically, such episodes have tended to significantly harm EGB spreads. To illustrate this, we examine the period from 2015 to today, filtering for days where the weekly change in VIX is above 5 and in SX5E is below -5% (i.e. isolate severe risk-off events). We plot the weekly change in GDPW EGB spread vs Bund on the Y-axis and that of 10yr Bund yield on the X-axis. Unsurprisingly, the scatter plot fit reveals a U-shape, suggesting that extreme Bund rallies can be as detrimental to EGB spreads as extreme Bund sell-offs. In fact, the right-hand-side tail of this U-shape scatter plot contains more data points. This week’s move so far, when assessed vs the 2015-today sample period, demonstrates that EGB spreads are reacting with a much lower beta, evidence of the convergence achieved over the past few years. records.text: re the markers? The most relevant issue will be whether traffic will start to flow via Hormuz and the speed with which US insurance/ escort services are implemented. In addition, the following will also be relevant: Reduced Military Action: A decrease in the frequency, intensity, and scope of strikes; Diplomatic/ Rhetorical Shift: US pivots toward "objectives achieved" or "negotiated settlement"; or Reduced Proxy Involve- ment: Lower activity from Iran-backed proxies (Houthi, Hezbollah, etc.) ~2/3 of positioning has been unwound Positioning was a key driver for FX moves this week; while positioning data is not yet available, we estimate ~2/3 of net USD shorts have been unwound. Prior to the escalation, net longs in EUR/USD stood at roughly 1.5 sigma above average. If this entire long had been unwound, it would have translated to a 4–5% decline in EUR/USD from Friday’s close to 1.1350, and a roughly 2% appreciation in the dollar’s trade-weighted index. Based on the price action this week, we thus estimate that 66% of the positioning in the euro has been unwound. Estimates would be larger if the broad dollar was considered, but the relationship has historically been correlat- ed with the euro and hence we rely on this estimate more. Our scenarios above should be fairly clear: the more persistent the energy price move, the more adverse the economic outcome. But where does all of that leave the ECB? To our mind, the ECB’s sensitivity to energy price shocks of this type is probably higher than normal after the very large and persistent energy price shock from 2022. The central bank probably doesn’t want to be “too late” again (a view we didn’t share into the last hiking cycle) and, as a consequence, could be even less forward looking over the next few months. So even if we expect a non-committal stance in March (the proper preview for that meeting will come next week), and a reiteration of “wait and see”, markets have started to move in the direction of hikes. We are less convinced of hikes per se and even of the timeline the market seems to have in mind. So here are a few points we want to emphasise: 1) In our scenarios 1 and 2 of a normalisation in energy prices by the June meeting, we would expect the central bank to look through the energy price shock. To us this remains the most likely outcome. We would still expect cuts to come in 2027. But while we argued until last week that we could see cuts as early as Sep-26, that risk balance has shifted. We note that the bulk of this week’s repricing higher in monetary policy expectations was concentrated in 1H26 (+5bp in EUR/USD and +15bp in GBP) and 2H26 (+15/20bp on the week), while changes in 2027 pricing have been more contained. Notably, after the attack on Iran last weekend, the ECB OIS curve went from reflecting some probability of cuts to hikes (previ- ously about 10bp of cuts priced in by end-26 vs. around 27bp of hikes currently). Markets have shifted to price only 11bp BoE cuts this year (vs. ~55bp priced in previously) and around 37bp cumulative easing for the Fed (vs. ~43bp before the weekend strikes). Such a hawkish market reaction suggests that rate markets have assigned more weight to the risk of a significant inflation shock that prompts less easing or tighter central bank policy, rather than to the potential growth hit due to supply chain disruptions and overall weaker global business sentiment. records.text: However, overseas contracted projects aggregate many types of “investments”, including financial and non-financial, trade inputs, and services, making it a cloudy definition. While official data are useful to monitor overall investment trends, one key issue is that they underestimate outward direct investment (ODI). We have highlighted this problem with the Latin America FDI case study, and that is explained primarily by the heavy use of offshore financial centers (OFCs) to channel Chinese investments (which hence do not appear as Chinese final investment in recipient economies, but rather as investment coming from a particular OFC). Additionally, while China is the world’s largest official creditor, we lack official disclosure on contracts between Chinese lenders and BRI borrowers. At any rate, official data are useful insofar as they provide a “reality-check” on the aggregate trends we find in our alternative data sources, even if the magnitudes differ. Both datasets point in the same direction. This reaction has been similar in terms of direction to what was seen last year after the outbreak of the 12-day Israel-Iran conflict, although DM curves had remained little changed back in 2025 and the magnitude of the moves was more contained. Instead, this week’s market reaction to the Middle East conflict has been broadly opposite relative to the Russia-Ukraine episode of 2022. In the aftermath of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, DM curves had indeed bull steepened across the board with the front-end rallying 20-25bp in a week, as markets priced in a slower pace of policy tightening from major central banks and resorted to flight-to-quality into govies. If inflation rises above current levels and is stuck above 3% through most of this/next year, it could increase de-anchoring risks and open the door to hikes. Germany: trip notes from Berlin confirm it’s very complicated For once, Germany is the less complicated part of our weekly, but still complicated. We hosted an investor trip to Berlin last week. On return, we felt comfortable with our 1.0% growth this year, and 1.7% next. But energy challenges were left-right-centre in our discussions. The energy price shock from geopolitical escalation possibly poses larger- than-usual downside potential risk to the German outlook this time around. Our discussions reinforced our "sugar rush" view on the effect of fiscal policy: the spending spree has started. Growth effects should show this year before fading again quite quickly in 2027. Complementary structural reform progress is currently focused on faster deployment of fiscal spending, but much more is needed for medium-term growth. The challenges are significant: the energy crisis came with long tails, while demographic ageing is kicking in. A lot needs to be done, but the heavy state election calendar could get in the way. Our analysis suggests that while growth outcomes following similar conflicts have been mixed, the magnitude of growth shocks tend to be correlated with the change in oil price three months after the shock. As such, while we continue to see AI disruption and private credit stress as the key structural drivers of wider spreads into 2026, the risk of sustained higher energy prices increases the probability of a stagflationary environment, particularly in Europe. The stagflationary playbook supports defensives, up-in-quality, and close-to- home positioning Although we believe positioning for a stagflationary environment may be premature, we revisit prior work to identify which segments of credit tend to outperform in such periods. Within IG, our analysis shows that Telecoms (+0.1–0.2% monthly excess return) and Consumer Non-Cyclicals (+0.1% monthly excess return) are the top-performing sectors across both Europe and the US during periods of low growth and high inflation. Within our EU model trade portfolio, we already hold longs in both sectors, supported by their defensive characteristics, attractive carry in Telecoms, and attractive valuations in Consumer Non-Cyclicals. records.text: Global Strategy6 March 2026 ab 2 favor front-end positioning, specifically 1–3yr credit, as well as moving up in quality, with BB-rated credit outperforming CCCs in both regions. Given our expectation for spread widening in 2026 (peak spreads of 350/290bp for US/EU HY, respectively), we also anticipate decompression to materialize in our baseline scenario. Front-end outperformance during stagflation also aligns with key takeaways from our carry model, where we prefer the front end over the back end of the credit curve. How have other sectors performed during prior conflicts? Outside of stagflation, we also look across prior episodes of conflict-driven supply-side energy shocks and identify several recurring patterns in sectoral performance. In the US, Pharma, REITs, and Media spreads tend to widen the most as energy prices rise across both IG and HY, while Utilities, Energy, and Technology have generally tightened on a relative basis. Europe presents a more nuanced picture: unlike the US, Utilities have typically underperformed, reflecting structural challenges in the natural gas subsector and limited ability to pass higher input costs through to end consumers. However, similar to the US, EU IG Media and Pharma have experienced the largest relative widening, while Technology has seen the most net-tightening. Despite Tech performing well in both regions during prior conflicts, we remain less constructive on the sector given the context of AI disruption and hyperscaler issuance

records.text: 3 Insights Information Classification: General About State Street PriceStats PriceStats is a source of high frequency inflation information drawn from prices of over five million items sold by online retailers. The items include food, beverages, electronics, apparel, furniture, household products, prescription drugs and over-the-counter medicines. The prices are collated for all the countries we monitor to produce individual Country Inflation Series. Country Inflation Series detect changes in inflation trends with real-time data. We publish the indices with a lag of three business days; they are direct reflections of prices of real products on sale at online retailers in each country. Country Inflation Series are not seasonally adjusted and are not designed to match official data. Across the board, realized fertility rates were lower than forecast, particularly so in South Korea and China. Relative to the UN forecasts made in 1990, 2000 and 2010 for this set of countries, fertility in 2023 surprised to the downside in all but one singular case—fertility in Germany in 2023 was 0.04-points above the level that was forecast by the UN in 2000.5 5. To some degree, the decline in measured fertility likely reflects a statistical nuance. Fertility rates are the number of children that a woman would statistically expect to have over her life if the number of children she had at each age were equal to the number of births to women of that age divided by the number of women of that age in a single year. If women gradually shifted over time towards having children later in life— i.e., reducing age-specific fertility rates now, but with the intention of raising older age-specific fertility rates in the future—the natural product would be an interim decline in country-level fertility rates that does not necessarily reflect any intention of having fewer children over one’s life. records.text: M Global Foundation 10 Global Trade Profiles These interactives provides a detailed snapshot of the trade profile of any given country across time. The data can be portrayed multiple ways, either by country/ sector over time or growth trend. The level and trend can both be consequential in mapping how supply chains are reacting. The data underlying these interactives is critical for us in understanding the structure of global trade, and allows us to examine potential for, and impediments to supply chain restructuring, as discussed in Multipolar World: Supply Chain Strain. Data on imports can allow Macro portfolio managers to identify where growth or inflation risk to domestic demand might manifest based on trade barriers and/or shifting supply chains. Fundamental portfolio managers can see dependence of imports across countries and sectors as well as potential gains from nearshoring. Data on exports can assist macro portfolio managers can use the data to see how any individual sector affects the broader economy — whether an exporter can absorb disruption in a single sector or whether there is market concentration risk. The disaggregation can help differentiate "beta" versus "alpha" opportunities. Fundamental portfolio managers can trace the evolution of export relationships between two countries to benchmark comparisons either by country or over time if the level of trade shifts.

As one of the major buyers of crude oil from the Middle East, China is exposed to risks ranging from higher energy costs to supply disruptions of petrochemical products. Morgan Securities plc Global Markets Strategy Global Fixed Income Markets Weekly (Advance version) 06 March 2026 J P M O R G A N • DM rate markets have repriced significantly following last weekend’s strikes on Iran: yield curves bear flattened 10-20bp over the past week with a 25-50bp sell-off in 1Yx1Y rates, with European rates’ underperformance driven by the energy price spike and liquidations of crowded positions. Relative to previous similar events, the response of DM rate markets to this week's Middle East tensions differs substantially from previous comparable events such as the outbreak of the Russia- Ukriane conflict in 2022. The magnitude of this week’s market moves and anecdot- al evidence suggest that unwinds of crowded positions has played an important role in exacerbating market moves, particularly in Europe. We think that the situation in the Middle East remains fluid, with the duration and scale of the oil and gas supply disruptions remaining key to determining the impact on inflation and growth over the coming months. We therefore remain cautious on outright fading the move in the Euro area duration but enter OW 5Y Germany vs. US as low-beta way to fade the cheapening and enter bullish proxies via options. In the UK, we have a bullish bias on 1Yx1Y SONIA vs. SOFR and receive Dec26 MPC OIS. DM

FDI: A new instrument of competition The US remains the clear leader in both FDI inflows and outflows, but China has rapidly narrowed the gap, particularly as a major investor in developing economies. The US continues to dominate FDI in advanced markets and knowledge-intensive sectors, leveraging its strong alliances and technological edge. In contrast, China’s FDI is heavily concentrated in resource extraction, infrastructure, and manufacturing, primarily through its Belt and Road Initiative (BRI), which has established extensive investment networks across Africa, Asia, and Latin America. This divergence reflects each country’s strategic priorities: the US focuses on innovation and market integration, while China prioritizes resource security and supply chain control. In recent years, both countries have adjusted their approaches. records.text: Europe • Main versus cash: Main has underperformed the IEAC ETF in recent sessions and is currently trading trading 7.5bp wide to the IEAC ETF on a five-year regression basis, a divergence at the 86th percentile (Figure 2). Should US-Iran tensions persist or escalate, we would expect Main to continue drifting wider versus cash, reflecting its higher sensitivity to macro volatility and limited supply in cash markets. We do not consider the risk of retail outflows in IG to be a potential material headwind to cash. • Main versus equities: Main has outperformed SX5E through the volatility, breaking a multi- week streak of underperformance, but continues to screen noticeably wide versus equities (Figure 3). With equity valuations still looking rich and long-risk positioning in Main extremely light versus history, we see scope for continued Main outperformance should market sentiment deteriorate further. • Xover versus Main: The Xover–5x Main basis initially compressed sharply during the volatility spike but partially retraced that move over the past two sessions (Figure 4). With the basis stretched and Xover trading tight versus cash, Xover could underperform Main once short-risk positioning in the index is eventually flushed out, particularly in a bearish macro scenario. • Main versus CDX.IG: Main has underperformed CDX.IG, with the basis now at 2.5bp, representing a 3.2bp widening since Friday. These downside surprises have not occurred in a vacuum—to the contrary, they have been realized in many cases in spite of concerted policy action intended to raise fertility rates out of policymaker concern about the inevitable economic and fiscal consequences of low fertility. For instance, in recent years, China scrapped its longstanding one-child policy, exhorted people to have more children, offered payments to families with young children, broadened and extended maternity benefits and entitlements, and levied taxes on birth control, amongst other actions. However, long- term empirical evidence has shown that pro-family polices have at most only marginally raised fertility rates.6 And indeed, fertility rates have fallen sharply in China in recent years as noted below. From a long-term macro perspective, we believe one should be quite circumspect about the prospect pro-family policies will lead to meaningfully higher fertility rates. Instead, the weight of the evidence suggests to us that fertility rate forecasts are more likely to turn out to be too high than too low in the final estimation. Korea’s sharp equity decline should be viewed in the context of its prior gains Conflict in the Mideast has prompted Asian equity markets to sell off, with none hit harder than Korea. In the first few trading days following the start of the conflict, KOSPI has fallen a cumulative 20% from its closing high on Feb 26, including a record 12.06% decline on Mar 4, sparking commentary about a ‘crash‘ or a ‘bear market‘. While the peak-trough move meets the widely accepted definition of a bear market, we think it is more appropriate to view the decline in the context of the exceptionally strong gains seen in Korean equities during the past year. From the Liberation Day low on 9 April 2025, KOSPI rose 176% to its late February 2026 high, and from the low on 21 November after a 3-week modest correction, KOSPI gained 65%. The decline since end February is equivalent to half the recent gain and less than a third (30%) of the full move since last April. With the ensuing 10% rebound on 5 Mar, the index is back above its 30-day moving average and has not broken its longer uptrend. This fact pattern indicates the recent decline should be viewed as an overdue correction rather than the start of a bear market. Further analysis supports our constructive Korea equity view. First, the index has tended to recover well in the 3, 6, and 12 months following prior deep single day KOSPI declines. OIS pricing was stable, implying a 65% probability of a 25bp hike by the April MPM. State of Women in the Workforce: More jobs, fragmented hours, stagnant pay Women’s workforce participation globally has remained stable at 49% compared to 73% for men in 2025, according to the International Labour Organization. However, there has been little progress in closing the gender pay gap, which remains stuck at 19.1% and 11.1%, respectively, in the US and Europe, with women still underrepresented in the highest paying fields. Job gains have been concentrated in lower-paying, service-centric industries like Healthcare and Care (58.5%) and Education (52.9%). AI adoption will accelerate structural shifts in global labor markets, raising concerns that women could potentially be more adversely impacted as there is a sizeable gender gap in AI adoption. We examine key employment and wage trends for women in the US, Europe, Japan, China and emerging markets. Recent analysis from the Institute for Women’s Policy Research (IWPR) shows that the gender pay gap in the US worsened in the latest data. In 2024, women working full-time year-round earned 80.9 cents for every dollar earned by men— implying a 19.1% pay gap and marking the lowest earnings ratio since 2016. records.text: hough . The large and ongoing rise in oil prices, and the lack of clarity on how long th is will persist, means that inflation could run hot and for a prolonged period. While the textbook policy response to energy shocks is to look through the inflation as “transitory” and focus on their negative cyclical effects, after more than five years of elevated “transitory” inflation, it is unclear how confident Fed policymakers would be in executing this textbook maneuver (see Global macro: Crude reality (4), dated 4 March). The tail risk remains an unexpected hawkish shift to guard against a loss of credibility. In 2007-2008, the Fed was faced with high, energy -fueled inflation, weak labor data, and emerging financial stability risks. In this environment, it did cut rates but with hesitancy due to concerns for its inflation -fighting credibility and with occasional large hawkish surprises, such as a very hawkish speech by Chair Bernanke in June 2008. To be clear, we think the growth outlook is strong a nd the parallel to this period is limited. But it underscores that the Fed takes its inflation credentials seriously in disorderly environments and that it may feel the need to somehow communicate that it will do what is necessary to achieve durable macroeconomic stabilization. We also raise our Apr/May JKM forecast, to $29/$25/mmBtu (from $20/$15), at a positive premium to TTF to help Asia attract enough Atlantic basin cargoes to replace Qatari supply. We expect our revised TTF and JKM forecasts to potentially trigger incremental industrial demand destruction beyond the G2O switching we embed in our balances, although the fact that a significant portion of energy-intensive industry in NW Europe has not recovered since suggests this process might take even higher TTF prices in particular. Most vulnerable to supply lines disruptions are Iraq, Bahrain, Kuwait, and Qatar, although the latter two are more insulated due to their accumulated foreign assets. UAE has partial export ability (c50% of production) outside the Hormuz Strait, with a 1.5mn bpd nameplate capacity for the Habshan–Fujairah crude oil pipeline. Saudi Aramco’s East-West pipeline provides it export flexibility, and has capacity of 5- 6.5mn bpd, unless the Houthis resume disruptions in the Red Sea (10% of exports now). The Yanbu oil terminal on the Red Sea (West Coast) has seen its average handling and export capacity increase in 2018 by 3mn bpd to over 4mn bpd. Egypt is vulnerable due to crowded positioning and oil exposure but Gulf support could provide a buffer. The external financing picture remains tight but approval of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) fifth and sixth reviews provide near-term buffers. The currency could weaken with outflows on a risk-off scenario, but real rates are likely to remain high. Claudia Goldin, the 2023 Nobel laureate in economics, Professor of Economics at Harvard University and Co-Director of the Gender in the Economy group at the National Bureau of Economic Research, identifies greater female autonomy as producing lower birth rates. She notes that over the past 50 years, birth rates have declined in virtually every country. One of the great demographic surprises of the modern era is a negative relationship between per capita income levels and fertility. Higher-income households have fewer children than their lower-income counterparts. The greater agency that women have gained as they obtain more education and pursue a career has led to lower birth rates. Her modeling shows that the faster the per capita economic growth, the more the level of births desired by men relative to the level desired by women will diverge. The Fed’s FRB/US model implies that a $10 rise in oil prices yields around a 35bp rise in headline PCE inflation that dissipates fairly quickly. That was akin to about a 15% jump in oil prices when published by the Fed, so a 50% shock would be consistent with around a 1.2%-pt initial rise. The FRB/US model is a large-scale macro model; Presno and Prestipino (2024) investigate this question using a more parsi- monious and micro-founded DSGE modeling approach. They conclude that a 10% foreign real oil shock boosts headline US inflation by 12bp on impact, but unlike the FRB/US model they find a more persistent effect that lasts several quarters. (This finding may reflect a more slowly decaying oil shock than in the FRB/US results.) Rescaling to a 50% jump in crude oil prices suggests a 60bp increase in headline inflation. These models imply that a sustained supply shock that dou- bled the price of oil, to around $120/bbl, would mechanically deliver a jump of 1 to 2%-pts in headline inflation. records.text: Considering the Policy Mix of Expansionary Fiscal Policy and Rate Hikes Under its expansionary fiscal policy, the Takaichi administration aims to realize a “strong economy” by making bold “strategic investments that enhance resilience against potential crises” and “investments that promote growth”. Based on this policy, the government selected 17 strategic sectors1 at the Council for Japan’s Growth Strategy at the end of last year and plans to decide on concrete measures for its growth strategy by this summer. Meanwhile, the BOJ has been proceeding with the normalization of monetary policy, but the future pace of rate hikes and the terminal rate could be affected, depending on the content and impact of the expansionary fiscal policy. In this report, we examine the conditions necessary for the policy mix of expansionary fiscal policy and rate hikes to produce a desirable outcome for the Japanese economy, namely achieving sustainable growth under price stability, accompanied by a rise in the potential growth rate. As a starting point for this discussion, we will first hypothetically consider two types of fiscal policy (effective demand stimulus measures and productivity improvement measures) and examine their potential impact on the Japanese economy, which is facing labor shortages, and on monetary policy. So, any headwind to consumers from higher energy prices should be partially offset by a windfall for energy producers. Three risks from a large and persistent energy price shock Our base case on the impact of the conflict is very much in line with consensus. The more interesting question for investors is: what could go wrong, and how? WTI is up around 26% since the build-up to the conflict started (Jan 28). A key risk to our sanguine base case is that non-linear effects could set in if the shock to oil prices is large and sustained. This could happen, for example, if the Strait of Hormuz remains closed for several weeks. There are at least three channels through which non-linear effects might play out. First, a big spike in oil prices – and the sort of conflict that would cause such a shock – would likely lead to meaningful tightening in financial conditions. And the economy is probably more sensitive than usual to markets. That’s because spending growth is being driven by higher-income households, who have benefited from a near-doubling in stocks over the last three years. An enduring equity downturn could weigh substantially on higher-income spending, exacerbating the shock. records.text: Michael Metcalfe 9 March 2026 1 Insights Classification: Premium Material Firm Feb inflation and seven days of fuel prices in March A week ago we explored what higher energy prices might mean for the inflation outlook here, through the lens of Alberto Cavallo’s papers on pass through and State Street PriceStat’s fuel indices. In this chart heavy piece, we test that analysis with a week’s worth of hard data (see Figures 5-10 overleaf). We also take a look at our point forecasts for US February CPI. Given the potentially dramatic change in the inflation outlook seen so far in March, February data already looks a little stale but noting the firmness in the data going into the energy shock suggests it is not without importance. Firm February first. Prices typically rise in February, but the 41bp (nsa) increase in the US price level captured by PriceStats was the largest monthly gain in 23 months and exceeded February 2025. As a result, annual inflation is moving back toward three‑year highs. Headline inflation is broadly in line with expectations, with Bloomberg consensus at 44bp m/m (nsa). Geopolitics may be hitting Germany in a particularly weak spot. • Structural reforms are probably getting delayed by politics. Bandwidth for any EU related matters is very limited. In summary: One day, six meetings, and bad weather We hosted an investor trip to Berlin last week– one day, six meetings with politicians, representatives of ministries, industry chambers and pollsters. Our discussions reinforced our “sugar rush” view on the effect of fiscal policy: the spending spree has started. Growth effects should show this year before fading again quite quickly in 2027. Complementary structural reform progress is currently focused on faster deployment of fiscal spending, but much more is needed for medium term growth. The challenges are very big: the energy crisis came with long tails, demographic ageing is kicking in. A lot needs to be done, but the heavy state election calendar could come in the way. China’s BRI What is BRI? The Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) is China’s ambitious international development strategy, initially proposed by President Xi during his visit to Central and South-East Asia in 2013. Its main goals are to improve regional cooperation and connectivity on a trans-continental scale. The proposal of the BRI program came at a time when China’s potential growth had slowed notably since the GFC, and the economy was starting to deal with domestic overcapacity and growing global protectionism and trade tensions—issues that have only grown acute in time. With these goals in mind, the major focus of BRI has been on infrastructure development, which would better connect economies involved, foster tighter trade and investment links, and improve financial integration, policy coordination and people-to-people connectivity, hence boosting regional economic co-operation. Intensifying regional cooperation and improving connectivity among BRI economies, coupled with the fact that many of them are well-endowed with energy and natural resources, aimed at expanding China’s export markets and securing natural resources. records.text: US Economics 06 March 2026 Citi Research 2 January core CPI was stronger than in previous months, which were partly affected by measurement issues due to the government shutdown. But residual start-of- year strength has come to be expected, and details still showed this January slowing compared to previous years. We expect further slowing in inflation in February with a 0.23%MoM increase in core CPI. Many components of strong services prices in January should slow in February, including in transportation prices like airfares and personal services. We also continue to see downside risks for shelter inflation in any given month, although goods prices may remain a bit sticky from start-of-year price increases. Currently, our expectations for CPI and PPI imply a 0.26% increase in core PCE inflation in February, much softer than last year. In our base case, stickiness in core inflation led mostly by goods prices affected by tariffs starts to fade in coming months while services prices continue to slow (with shelter even abnormally soft). But even if February data seem somewhat more favorable for slowing inflation, upside risks to goods prices have increased in recent months and have become particularly pronounced with a spike in energy prices. Markets may be hesitant to price back in more Fed cuts from muted February inflation data as new upside risks for data after February have arisen. This reaction has been similar in terms of direction to what was seen last year after the outbreak of the 12-day Israel-Iran conflict, although DM curves had remained little changed back in 2025 and the magnitude of the moves was more contained. Instead, this week’s market reaction to the Middle East conflict has been broadly opposite relative to the Russia-Ukraine episode of 2022. In the aftermath of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, DM curves had indeed bull steepened across the board with the front-end rallying 20-25bp in a week, as markets priced in a slower pace of policy tightening from major central banks and resorted to flight-to-quality into govies. records.text: 2 Asia Economic Weekly | 06 March 2026 This Week in Focus The US–Israel military operation in Iran since Feb 28 has drawn significant market attention. In our view, impact on Asia will be transmitted mainly through disruptions to oil supply and trade channels, with heterogeneous effects across countries. Country- wise, China’s NPC set the 2026 GDP growth target at 4.5%–5.0%, lower than last year’s “around 5%”. Feb NBS manufacturing PMI softened, partly due to Lunar New Year distortions. In India, strong manufacturing activity led to an upward revision of the FY26 growth estimate to 7.6% (from 7.4% previously). In Japan, core CPI inflation (excluding fresh food) fell below 2% for the first time since Oct 2024, driven by lower energy prices. China: March NPC lowers 2026 growth target; Geopolitical risks in focus Policymakers released the 2026 economic targets at the annual National People’s Congress on Mar 5, setting a lower GDP growth target of “4.5%–5.0%”, compared with last year’s “around 5%”. Fiscal and monetary stances remain broadly unchanged, with emphasis on channeling fiscal resources toward investment and flexibility on RRR and rate cuts. Consumption remains a priority, supported by continued subsidies and a new coordination fund. As one of the major buyers of crude oil from the Middle East, China is exposed to risks from higher energy costs. records.text: M Global Foundation 14 Margin Drivers Across the Value Chain by Country and Industry While the previous illustrations focus on the trade of finished goods, this interactive attempts to trace the value add contributions across the supply chain by country and/or industry. Taking standardized national accounts data, we see how attribution is made across the P&L from a top-down perspective. For a sector or fundamental analyst, this data can trace the input costs across the supply chain to determine where risks lie on the supply chain continuum. For example, tariffs may raise the cost of goods, but FX moves can offset that increase by lowering relative labor costs. These differences are not always obvious, so the data can be used to decipher the balance of cost shifts in a supply chain shock scenario. The blue section of this exhibit enables a granular analysis of the inputs each industry consumes (Industry View), where those inputs originate (Country View) or both (Country and Industry View). In green, we examine the value addition aspect of each industry: Gross Operating Surplus (profits), Employee Compensation, and Taxes less Subsidies. In yellow, we examine the consumers of each industry's outputs: again, either at a country level, industry level, or both. This interactive allows easy visualization of sector-wise interdependences and geographical exposures. The charts will help show production chains and how supply chains feed into value add. Given our expectation for spread widening in 2026 (peak spreads of 350/290bp for US/EU HY, respectively), we also anticipate decompression to materialize in our baseline scenario. Front-end outperformance during stagflation also aligns with key takeaways from our carry model, where we prefer the front end over the back end of the credit curve. How have other sectors performed during prior conflicts? Outside of stagflation, we also look across prior episodes of conflict-driven supply-side energy shocks and identify several recurring patterns in sectoral performance. In the US, Pharma, REITs, and Media spreads tend to widen the most as energy prices rise across both IG and HY, while Utilities, Energy, and Technology have generally tightened on a relative basis. Europe presents a more nuanced picture: unlike the US, Utilities have typically underperformed, reflecting structural challenges in the natural gas subsector and limited ability to pass higher input costs through to end consumers. However, similar to the US, EU IG Media and Pharma have experienced the largest relative widening, while Technology has seen the most net-tightening. AUD banks’ HQLA demand is supported by a boomy housing market, as banks tend to run a fairly stable share of securities to total assets. But as above, the upside for mortgage credit growth now is less clear. Other things equal, this is a positive for semi spreads to ACGB, in that if swap spreads were to narrow back, semi-ACGB spreads typically move in the same direction, with a beta of about +0.4. In the latter half of the month, following the Bank of Japan's policy board member nominations announced on the 25th, the perception of a stronger "reflationist" stance accelerated short-term overseas futures buying. The Nikkei 225 temporarily surpassed 59,000 yen, hitting record highs on consecutive days. Uncertainty over the Trump administration's tariff policies and heightened tensions in Iran at month-end weighed on the market, but sentiment remains strong toward policy expectations for Sanaenomics under political stability. Small- and mid-cap stocks (SMids) outperformed large caps, partially reflecting the higher risk profile of those names as well as policy expectations. • Growth potential under a long administration provides upside for Japanese equities; SMid risk profile to improve: The LDP's historic landslide victory ended the opposition party-led fiscal expansion that had continued under a minority ruling party since October 2024, leading to a shift toward self-directed fiscal management by the administration. The materialization of political stability and stabilization of interest rates and the yen have improved the risk-reward profile for Japanese equities, especially SMids, which were exposed to key risks such as a rapid rise in long-term JGB yields and increased domestic inflation. Current events mean downside… the question is how much and for how long The Russia/Ukraine war and Israel/Gaza conflict seem to have raised the risk tolerance of investors around the world. Since Feb 27th, when the bombing of Iran started, the MSCI ACWI Large and Small indices are each down close to 3%… that is equivalent to a bad day of trading in our view, but not to the reaction we would expect to the situation we are currently facing. While it is hard to predict how it will all end, our analysis indicates that it could take close to six months for energy prices to come down to pre-conflict levels. Should this happen, real GDP growth would most likely slow YoY in 2026 (somewhere around 30-40 bps depending on the region), which would add even more downside to what we have been noting were already rich consensus expectations of growth. So how to position through this time of uncertainty? First, recent trading supports our preference for SMid-Caps so remain OW SMid vs Large. Second, this is perhaps the time to rethink your regional and sector allocation – as we show in this report, the market is clearly going against the consensus views that were in place at the start of the year (US / UK, Energy, Utilities and Real Estate are all winners since Feb 27th). records.text: 6 March 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Deutsche Bank AG Page 5 Taking a step back Over the past two weeks, we have reduced risk in the macro portfolio and are down to only three trades: (1) short UST10y, (2) long Dec-26 ESTR, and (3) long UST5Y spreads. We exited bullish-leaning trades in Japan last week and bearish-leaning trades in Europe today. Given the recent adjustments to the portfolio, we take a step back to (1) summarise the rationale behind the core views, (2) explain how it was supported (or tested) by events, and (3) outline the motivations for the recent changes. Underlying rationale The mild bearish bias was predicated on three elements: (1) the shift in policy mix (with, in particular, more fiscal support) leading to cyclical tailwinds and a recovery of the ex-AI economy (aka the lower branch of the K); (2) a shift in the global supply/ demand of savings supporting a higher neutral rate; and (3) tail risks from AI (bubble or substitute to labour). The first two elements supported the bearish bias. The third one led us to low-ball the assumptions, effectively aiming for 4.25-4.50% rather than 4.75-5.00%. Given Japan's strong external position and the resilience of wage growth, we attributed the excessive steepness of the JGB curve to the BoJ being behind the curve and market segmentation, rather than genuine sovereign risk. Refer to important disclosures on page 26 to 27. 12944590 Global Economic Weekly Only persistent oil spikes really matter Global Letter: Only persistent oil spikes really matter Since the US-Israel operation in Iran started, oil price volatility reignited inflation concerns. But how worried should we be about an increase in global inflation? While market and survey-based inflation expectations can be sensitive to oil at high frequency, history suggests only marked and persistent spikes in the price of crude trigger persistent inflationary cycles. If the status quo persists, with oil prices around $15 higher than the pre-war level, we would fade (oil induced) inflation concerns. But an escalation driving oil prices persistently above $100 would become more concerning. US: Iran-limited risk for now, but effects can be amplified History suggests the Iran conflict is likely to have little impact on the US economy. But what are the risks? Iran war implications for Japan US/Israel enter war with Iran, oil prices rise, JPY depreciates On 28 February, the US and Israel jointly launched large-scale attacks focused on military facilities across Iran. By that point, US forces had already amassed their largest air power deployment in the Middle East since the 2003 Iraq war. With the attack on Iran, the key focus of impact on the Japanese economy is oil supply and prices. Due to US sanctions on Iran, Japan has suspended crude oil imports from Iran since May 2019. However, Iranian crude accounts for around 4% of global production, meaning any impact on Iranian output would be expected to push crude oil prices higher. On the morning of 2 March, the first business day after the outbreak of war, Brent crude prices rose by around 13% to briefly reach USD80/bbl ( Figure 1). While subsequently retracing into the 70s later that day, they have climbed back into the 80s since the 3rd.
