The growth shock in the UK is slightly smaller than in the eurozone and is driven primarily by private consumption rather than industrial production. While the inflation shock is lagged, it does peak around similar levels to the eurozone. The first scenario would knock-off around 0.2% from the level of GDP in 2026 and 0.3% by 2027 cumulatively (Figure 11). This would lower our 2026 GDP forecast by 0.2pp to 0.8% y/y but keep growth steady in 2027 (1.3%). Accounting for both direct and indirect effects, we estimate that inflation would be around 0.5pp higher by the end of this year, taking our annual average forecast to around 2.7% from the current 2.2% (Figure 13). This impact is broadly consistent with recent analysis from the Bank of England (Figure 7). The second scenario, which embeds escalation, would shave off 0.7% from the level of GDP by end-2026 and add 1.5pp to average Q4 y/y headline inflation in 2026. Policy hands are tied: Beyond the magnitude of the shock, duration will be critical to determine the policy response. The call for policy adjustments will grow. HMT will feel pressure to support households and cut inflation. And the Bank of England will grow more nervous the longer the energy shock lasts. In Scenario 1, we would expect our baseline of two rate cuts to come, with the next rate cut likely to come in April/June, followed by a (late) summer rate cut (in either July/Sep). Fiscal policy, we expect, will remain on the sidelines, given the speed in which the shock dissipates. In Scenario 2, we still think two rate cuts may be likely. But rate cuts are likely to be spaced further apart, with one likely in summer and another just around the turn of the year. Fiscal policy will most likely be deployed to shield households - particularly in the form of easing fuel duty increases (which is scheduled to rise from August). In Scenario 3, where the energy crisis persists, we expect a two-pronged approach by Government. One, not only would the chances of a fuel duty free extension rise inexorably, but we think the Chancellor may begin to entertain the idea of temporary cut to fuel duty. Any asymmetries for USD are likely conditional on the backdrop. In other words, if geopolitical tensions are increasing with spiking oil prices and a higher USD, then a weak CPI will not do much to impact dollar strength while a strong CPI could accelerate dollar buying . If, on the other hand, geopolitical tensions are easing and the USD is selling off, then a strong CPI is unlikely to have material affect while a weak CPI could see the USD sell-off accelerate. Bigger picture, we do see two implications. First, as we have been flagging, USD/SPX correlations are normalizing (back to negative; Figure 4). A structural headwind for the USD is that uncertainty around the USD “safe haven” status could lead foreign equity investors to increase their FX hedge ratios (sell USD); however, quantitatively, the correlation breakdown appeared to be temporary rather than a structural shift . While this relationship continues to normalize, it could weaken the case for an increase in FX hedge ratio adjustments. Second, this overall situation is a reminder that Europe remains vulnerable given its external reliance on energy and underinvestment in defense. records.text: 10 US Economic Weekly | 06 March 2026 Core views Growth: a dose of optimism • Our 2026 average US GDP growth forecast of 2.8% is well above consensus (2.1%). The key drivers are easier fiscal and monetary policy, and our expectation of more growth-friendly trade policy. We now project that consumer stimulus from the OBBBA will be more front-loaded into tax season. This prompts us to tweak our forecasts: we modestly raise 1H 2026 growth and lower 2H. Risks to our projections are tilted to the upside. A 3-handle on 2026 growth wouldn’t be a big surprise. Inflation: to remain stuck above the Fed’s target through 2027 • We continue to expect inflation to remain above the Fed's target throughout our forecast horizon. In the near term, supply-driven inflation due to tariffs should push inflation towards 3% y/y as businesses continue to slowly shift costs to consumers. Inflationary pressures from tariffs should fade towards the end of 2026; however, core PCE inflation should end 2026 at an elevated 2.8% y/y and only decline to 2.4% by year end 2027. We continue to believe underlying inflation is above 2%, and our growth and monetary policy outlook should generate more demand-driven inflation causing a delay in inflation’s return to the Fed’s 2% target. UK consumer: Moderate outlook with downside risks Complete report: UK Viewpoint: UK consumer: Moderate outlook with downside risks 05 March 2026 Moderate consumption growth in 2026 In this note we examine the outlook for household consumption in 2026. In 2025, we finally saw a fall in savings rate, driven by a drop in real interest rates. Having said that the fall was likely tempered by a rise in precautionary savings. Clearing of Budget uncertainty should allow for a rebound in consumption in early 2026, but the key question is if the strength is sustained, which we don't expect. We expect moderate consumption growth of 1.2% in 2026, amid a small fall in savings rates (from 10.1% in 2025 to 9.5% in 2026) and slowing real income growth (from 1.1% to 0.6%). This is before accounting for the recent rise in energy prices. Slowing real income growth and small fall in savings Monetary easing and falls in interest rates can continue to reduce the motivation to pay down debt, hold savings and make it cheaper to borrow, causing a small decline in savings rate in 2026. While the decline in inflation and rate cuts should act as tailwinds, real income growth is likely to slow amid softening wage growth and looser labour market. Calculated Duty: Calculated duty represents an estimate of duties associated with dutiable imports and does not necessarily reflect duties actually paid. These estimates may be affected by offsetting distortions. For example, US-origin goods returned after processing abroad may be partially eligible for duty-free treatment, potentially leading to overstatement in duty estimates. Conversely, in cases where goods are subject to special or variable tariff rates, dutiable value may be reported without a corresponding calculated duty, leading to understatement. Accordingly, calculated duty should be interpreted as an analytical proxy for tariff exposure rather than a precise measure of realized tariff collections.

In East Asia and the Pacific, private investment leads, with FDI exceeding US$480 billion, half of which is concentrated in Indonesia, Malaysia, and Vietnam and spread across manufacturing, automotive, and communications, signaling deeper supply chain integration with China. In Africa, state-owned enterprises dominate, focusing on infrastructure, energy, and mining, with loans (US$180 billion) outpacing FDI (US$170 billion, excluding Egypt). Europe and Central Asia show a balanced mix, with US$270 billion in FDI and US$240 billion in loans, mainly in Russia, Kazakhstan, Türkiye, Italy, and Hungary, spanning energy, industry, infrastructure, and renewables. In the Middle East and North Africa, investment is modest outside Egypt, UAE, and Saudi Arabia, and mostly targets Iran, Iraq, Oman, and Qatar. Latin America mirrors Africa, with loans (US$125 billion) exceeding FDI (US $100 billion), both focused on mining, infrastructure, and energy, and largely driven by state-owned firms. Notably, Brazil and Mexico, which together account for US$130 billion in Chinese FDI and where private sector involvement is more prominent, are not part of the BRI. If the Strait were closed, the impact on the Chinese economy would be severe. Given its strong economic dependence on China, Iran would likely not find it easy to sustain a long-term closure. In addition, Japan holds oil stockpiles totaling 254 days when combining public and private reserves (as of end-December 2025: 146 days of national reserves, 101 days of private reserves and 7 days of joint stockpiles with oil-producing countries). Unless the closure were to become extremely prolonged, domestic oil supply would not be cut off. LNG reserves, on the other hand are rather limited at just three weeks. Some (such as Waller) have stressed looking at market measures, such as the 5y5y-forward breakeven inflation from the TIPS market or 5y5y-forward inflation swaps, rather than surveys. Broadly stable inflation expectations over the medium and longer term would be another reason for the Fed to look past an oil-in- duced spike in headline inflation—even one that might look to be spilling over into core inflation initially. With anchored inflation expectations, the hit to demand will weigh on core inflation before long. Unfortunately, market measures of forward inflation expecta- tions are often remarkably sensitive to spot moves in oil pric- es (Figure 7). This empirical attribute makes it harder to appeal to them as supportive anchors for inflation expecta- tions, and a rise in breakevens (or inflation swaps, which behave similarly) on the back of a surge in oil prices would certainly complicate the Fed’s messaging. However, there are recent signs of some decoupling in this relationship, and the likelihood is that once oil prices start to come back down, so too will these measures of inflation expectations. In the mean- time, some backup of market measures of medium-term infla- tion expectations could reinforce a somewhat more gradual embrace of easing by Fed officials than otherwise, but we would still expect rate cuts to follow a particularly large shock to activity from a supply-driven surge in oil prices. 1.0 1.5 2.0 2.5 3.0 3.5 -16 23 61 99 137 175 99 04 09 14 19

records.text: US Rates Weekly 06 March 2026 Citi Research 12 Inflation: Impact from energy prices We examine the inflationary impact that is currently being priced from recent moves in energy prices and analyze risks for higher inflation expectations in the near term. What is currently priced? Most of the impact from oil is still mostly confined to near term inflation expectations. The move higher in energy prices this week had very limited impact on longer term breakevens for the most part in both US and Europe. We are starting to see some move higher beyond the 1y point on Friday. 1y inflation expectations on the other hand have increased from 2.49% on last Thursday to 2.89% at the time of writing. While the magnitude of move was higher in Europe, that should not be a surprise given the higher dependency on Middle eastern energy. European natural gas prices have increased significantly compared to US natural gas (Henry Hub) prices which have stayed relatively unchanged over the last week. Figure 18. US headline inflation expectations beyond the 1y point have not moved much over the last week. Figure 19. records.text: ab 6 March 2026 Global Research Global Strategy Stagflation vs. Disruption: is it time to revisit the stagflationary playbook in credit? Exec Summary: In the wake of recent escalations in Iran, client discussions have highlighted renewed concerns around the risk of a stagflationary shock, particularly if energy prices rise further due to additional damage to infrastructure or prolonged shipping and logistics disruptions through the Strait of Hormuz. While a swift resolution remains plausible and a stagflationary outcome could be avoided, elevated geopolitical risk in recent months has increased the likelihood of higher energy risk premia and the risk of stagflation, even if the US–Iran conflict is ultimately resolved. Revisiting our prior work on sectoral leadership during stagflationary periods, we find that IG Consumer Non-Cyclicals and Telecoms tend to ourperform and that previous periods have favored moving up in quality and front-end positioning in HY. Although we believe that positioning for stagflation would be premature, the potential for Telecom and Consumer Non-Cyclical outperformance in such a scenario reinforces our existing longs in these sectors in Europe. We also identify some irregularities in sectoral leadership following this conflict relative to other supply-side energy shocks, most notably that EU IG Healthcare and US IG Energy have seen net-widening vs. the index rather than the net-tightening that other historical precedents would suggest. Child care responsibilities are holding an estimated 708mn women worldwide back from the labor force, according to the ILO, and represent the main barrier to women entering and staying in the labor force. The Child Penalty Atlas builds a world atlas of child penalties in employment based on microdata from 134 countries. Most countries display clear and sizable child penalties (Figure 27H e a t m a p o f c h i l d p e n a l t i e s ). Their atlas shows that men and women follow parallel trends before parenthood, but diverge sharply and persistently after parenthood. records.text: ab 6 March 2026 Global Research Japan Macro Watch Wage momentum looks solid—but can oil prices spoil the recovery? Shunto wage talks likely to deliver another strong outcome based on demand data As we had anticipated, this fiscal year’s spring wage negotiations (Shunto) are likely to deliver another strong outcome, following last year’s results. Rengo, Japan’s largest labor union federation, yesterday released its aggregate results of wage hike demands covering 2,508 labour unions. As in the previous year, wage demands remain robust. Including regular wage increases, total wage hikes are running at 5.94% year on year, marginally below last year’s 6.09%, but still indicative of strong underlying momentum (Figure 1). Base pay increases (base-up), which are more closely linked to monthly wage statistics and therefore carry greater macroeconomic implications, came in at 4.37%, down modestly from 4.51% last year. Based on this bottom-up aggregation of wage demands, which has historically been a highly accurate predictor of Rengo’s first-round results to be released on 19 March, base-up increases for FY2026 will come in at 3.7% in our estimate, slightly lower than last year (first round: 3.84%, final: 3.70%, Figure 2). This outcome would be close to UBS’s forecast (first round: 3.6%, final: 3.5%), further increasing confidence that wage momentum will be sustained. records.text: 6 March 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Page 42 Deutsche Bank AG Correlation breakdown in funding term structure Following up on our note last week on how banking regulators could bring down bank demand for reserves, today’s chart explores the pricing of expected funding conditions. Specifically, we show how the correlation between the 1Y SOFR/FF and 2Y SOFR/FF bases, typically close to 1, can break down significantly during periods of key developments in funding markets. Over the last four years, two episodes of correlation breakdown were notable: 1) the increase in coupon supply announced at the Q3 2023 QRA, and 2) the sharp rise in repo rates in fall 2025. In the first episode, the term structure of SOFR/FF flattened significantly (2Y basis became more negative than 1Y basis), indicating concerns of future funding stress. In the second episode, the term structure steepened, reflecting expectations of acute but temporary funding stress. Notably, in both instances, policymakers (Treasury in 2023 and the Fed in 2025) stepped in to help reverse the situation. Over the last few weeks, the correlation has dropped yet again. The timing of this change aligns with Warsh’s nomination as Fed Chair and his expressed desire to reduce the size of the Fed’s balance sheet. As in the previous correlation shifts, we believe this one also presents a trading opportunity in the term structure of funding conditions. The Center for Strategic International Studies estimates that costs of the operation have totaled $3.7bn so far, and Congress is already reportedly discussing a $50bn supplemental defense bill after appropriating $150bn to defense in the One Big Beautiful bill. $50bn is ultimately a small drop in the bucket for the $30.9tn publicly traded Treasury market, and it would add just 0.15pp to our deficit-to-GDP forecast of 5.8% in FY 26. That said, the costs would likely increase materially if the conflict lasts longer than expected and/or if it involves troops being deployed. Around 95% of Japan’s crude oil imports come from Middle Eastern countries (2024; Figure 3), and roughly 80% of tankers bound for Japan pass through the Strait. As a result, if the Strait were closed completely, Japan’s crude oil imports would be expected to temporarily undergo a sharp drop. On 28 February, Iran’s Revolutionary Guard declared the “closure of the Strait of Hormuz, ” and reinsurance companies suspended underwriting, effectively creating a state of closure at present. On the other hand, Iran’s FM Araghchi subsequently announced that Iran does not currently intend to officially close the Strait of Hormuz or disrupt navigation, leaving the situation fluid. Source: Citi Research, Bloomberg There has been some tacit acknowledge that there may be a need to intervene, with the Prime Minister stating a need to manage economic fallout (Bloomberg, 9 March). No further detail has been offered or suggested, however. We think the most credible path for intervention would be directly via the policy costs embedded in the household energy bills (much like the Chancellor announced at the Autumn budget). This solution carries its own problems (which we outline here: UK Economics and Rates – 2025 Budget Review: On Fiscal Credibility) but may be the easiest to implement. Such a policy could then be targeted both in terms of size of relief and scope of application to mitigate costs as necessary and have the benefit of mechanically reducing CPI as well as supporting households. However, an intervention would raise fiscal questions. We think the OBR’s forecast last week—and by extension the framework in which the Treasury makes economic decisions—overestimated the headroom against the fiscal rules given the condition assumptions used. Headroom, while still robust relative to recent levels, is likely lower than the OBR implies. BOX: Monetary Policy Under Rising Inflationary Pressure and a Higher Natural Rate of Interest In this BOX, we use the conceptual diagram presented by Bullard (2010)5 to highlight the impact on monetary policy when (1) inflationary pressure rises and (2) the natural rate of interest rises due to an increase in potential growth. Bullard (2010) uses two elements: Fischer equation (the nominal interest rate is the sum of the real interest rate and inflation rate), and the policy reaction function (the central bank sets the policy rate in response to the deviation between the target inflation rate (2%) and the actual inflation rate). The intersection of these indicates the equilibrium, and we assume that the initial equilibrium point is shown as state ‘a’ in both cases. (1) Rising Inflationary Pressure When inflationary pressure rises, the central bank follows a path of initially raising the policy rate to a level corresponding to ‘b’, and then lowering the rate to the equilibrium point ‘a’ as inflationary pressure subsides. Investors questioned the impact of the conflict on consumer health, particularly against the backdrop of a K-shape recovery. Our consumer credit ABS performance outlook for the year ahead remains unchanged, for prime and nonprime, as the impact on economic data remains to be seen and likely to remain uncertain and volatile on geopolitical headlines. Should there be real economic stress, we would be equally concerned about the performance of both prime and nonprime collateral but much more concerned for lower tier sponsors with higher default risks. Floating oil storage outside Middle East: Being located mostly outside the Middle East and already loaded on ships, these floating cargoes are a relatively quick fix. Kpler data suggests about 100mn bbl of floating storage, of which about 40% is locked in ports dependent on Hormuz transit (mainly Kharg Island and Ras Tanura). This leaves about 60mn bbl of floating storage available (this is 2mbd, or 13% of the shortfall, if it all unloads in one month, which is an aggressive assumption). About 65% is sanctioned; we don’t expect the latter will be a large constraint for the time being, though. Further price upside is likely if Hormuz flows don’t resume: Even if we push all circuit breakers to their theoretical limit, we would be able to displace 12.5mbd, leaving the market still 2.5mbd short. This would in our view imply a price of about USD85/bbl, which is around the level we started with today (Friday, March 6). Under realistic assumptions, therefore, we expect further Brent upside and believe USD100/bbl is well within reach in March if Hormuz flows remain scuppered. 06/03/2026 Lack of barrels implies more Brent upside unless Hormuz flows resume

records.text: For the time being, developments in Iran and trends in the oil market will remain the key focus. On 2 March, US President Trump spoke about the US and Israeli attacks on Iran, saying “we initially expected it to last four to five weeks, but we have the capability to continue for longer, ” while US Defense Secretary Hegseth said on 4 March that it could last “up to eight weeks” (Bloomberg, 5 March). Japan relies on the Middle East for about 90% of its crude oil imports, and if transport disruptions were to be prolonged, there is a possibility that oil reserves – said to meet 254 days of demand – could be released to ensure the stability of domestic supplies. However, if the conflict were to be prolonged and oil prices were to rise further, there is also a risk that selling pressure on the JPY could intensify, as seen in 2022. Key economic indicators in the week ahead include, on the domestic side, January Maikin wage data (9 March) and revised Q4 GDP (10th). Overseas, the main releases are China’s February inflation data (9th) and the US February CPI (11th), January personal consumption/PCE deflator, Q4 real GDP and January JOL TS job openings (13th). records.text: Asia Economic Weekly | 06 March 2026 11 India in Focus Rahul Bajoria BofAS India Smriti Mehra BofAS India See report: India Watch: India’s exposure to West Asia in the spotlight West Asia conflict puts a shadow on near term sentiment In light of developments in West Asia over the weekend, we have been getting questions on India’s exposure to the wider region. The region is heavily intertwined with India in terms of having mutually high dependencies, and India’s economic exposure to West Asia has grown significantly in the last decade. For instance, UAE is India’s second largest exporting destination for India and foreign workers, while Saudi Arabia is a very large destination for Indian workers in West Asia. Whether it is GCC economies or non- GCC economies, the economic linkages primary flow through three channels for India. Linkage 1: People and remittances According to ministry of external affairs data, India has an estimated 9.7mn people working and living in West Asia, with the largest population of Indians living overseas in UAE, estimated at just below 4mn. Put together, India gets at least 35% of its remittances (~USD132bn annual) from West Asia according to RBI, with the number likely to be north of 40% given small economy exposures. This would India’s estimated exposure in remittances to be between UD45bn – USD55bn. Scandies and CHF The NOK's hawkish exuberance; Middle East tensions add to CHF appeal The NOK's gains from the Middle East conflict have been limited so far, in line with our estimates for modest and largely temporary appreciation in instances of negative energy supply shocks. Accordingly, expectations of an RBA-style hawkish pivot by the Norges Bank in the upcoming March meeting continue to underpin the krone's elevated valuations, with market pricing now implying an 80% probability for a 25bp hike by Q4. In our view, such expectations are likely excessive in light of Norges' dovish reaction function and revealed preference for leaning against (or avoiding altogether) demand weakness. What is more, unlike Australia, Norway does not benefit from a positive demand-driven terms of trade (ToT) shock or significant hedging flows, which could afford sustained support to its currency. In consequence, we are less constructive than the market, absent tangible evidence of a shift in the Norges Bank's reaction function. That said, there is still some time until the March meeting and another upside surprise in Tuesday's CPI release could sustain the market's optimism for a sharp hawkish pivot for longer. The spike in energy prices and a global fixed income sell-off have eliminated expectations of interest rate cuts, with the Riksbank now priced for a 25bp hike by Q1 next year. records.text: 6 March 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Deutsche Bank AG Page 39 Assessing EGB spreads' reaction both locally & historically Over the past 15 years, the pass through of major geopolitical shocks to the broader EUR rates universe, or the Eurozone economy in general, was affected (and in most cases amplified) by the reaction in EGB spreads vs Bund, especially those of peripheral countries. At this juncture though, with the average EGB spread vs Bund back to levels last seen more than 15 years ago and the theme of convergence setting the tone for some time now, it’s interesting to assess the reaction function of EGB spreads to the broader risk-off in markets. To do that, we’ll revisit the PCA framework we explained in our recent note FICOTD: EGB spreads start 2026 with last year’s momentum. Indeed, EGB spreads began 2026 by outperforming vs other risky assets relative to their 2025 beta. Notably, the AI-driven risk-off move, which led to wider credit spreads, failed to impact EGB spreads, hence leading to further outperformance up until last Friday’s close. This week however, EGB spreads pared back almost half of their YTD outperformance vs other risky assets, with the residual of the average 10yr EGB spreads vs Bund rising by 3bp from -6bp to -3bp. BTPs, OATs and OLOs underperformed the most relative to their last year’s beta. Fuzesi, 4 March, if energy prices persist at current spot levels, the total inflation impact in the Euro area is roughly around +0.4%-pt over coming months, so headline running around 2.3% oya over coming year. If energy prices stay relatively close to current levels, we would still see the ECB as quite firmly on hold, especially because the supply shock on energy also implies some hit to growth. The duration and depth of the energy price shock therefore will deter- mine the inflation and growth/sentiment impact on the Euro area which in turn will drive the ECB reaction. We, therefore, believe a further material increase in energy prices is required for the ECB to start tightening and even they will be calibrating the response based on growth/sentiment impact and also fiscal/policy responses. We find recent ECB tightening expectations repricing excessive, however given geopoliti- cal headline uncertainty will linger for a while, at least, and position/liquidity technicals will further add to market volatility, we do not find risk reward attractive in outright dura- tion exposures near-term and prefer to fade via conditional structures (see European Derivatives section) or low-beta cross-market structures (see below). records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 3 that we had forecast has materialized - see Exhibit 1 . Our GDP forecast for Italy was based on a 2.2pp drag over 2024-26 from the post-Superbonus correction. As we show in Exhibit 2 the actual correction shown in the revised numbers this week was even larger than that - shaving off 2.9pp from GDP in 2024 and 2025 alone. How can we explain the fact that GDP was still stronger than we anticipated? The answer lies in the redistribution of growth away from dwellings and into other buildings and structures. Non residential construction has seen a substantial upward revision this week. The latest data show that investment in this segment rose by almost 85% from 1Q21 to its peak in 1Q25 (see Exhibit 3 ), far outpacing other major euro area economies - see Exhibit 4 . What may have driven such a sharp, and idiosyncratic increase? We do not have a complete answer at this stage. The first and easiest answer is the implementation of the Recovery Fund. As per latest OpenPolis data, Italy has spent around €86bn of the RRF funds received, worth around 3.8% of GDP. Yet Spain has deployed a comparable amount with a much more muted response in non residential construction (see here). While the RRF clearly supported activity, particularly as the unwinding of the Superbonus freed up capacity elsewhere, the scale of the increase suggests that additional factors are likely at play. All in all, the magnitude of this week’s market moves and anecdotal evidence suggest that unwinds of crowded positions has played an important role in exacerbating the market reaction to the energy price shock. For instance, carry trades in intra-EMU spreads and vol space had been widely subscribed in recent month. We had previously highlighted that the slim carry levels would not be enough to cushion against potential risk-off moves and our cautious stance has been vindicated this week. At the peak of this week’s widening, carry trades in intra-EMU spreads have cost, on average, 5-10 months worth of carry if implemented vs. Germany and 3-5 months for trades implemented vs. €STR (Figure 6T h i s w e e k ’ s p e a k s p r e a d w i d e n i n g i n i n t r a - E M U s p r e a d s h a s c o s t 3 - 1 0 m o n t h s ' w o r t h o f c a r r y ). That would transmit shocks into global electronics supply chains. A supply shortage is harder to address than a price spike Policy makers would seek remedies in the event of a sustained gas shortage, but the constraints are tighter when physical supply- not just prices- is the problem. When LNG price surged in 2022 as a result of the Ukraine crisis, the playbook was clear: freeze most residential power tariffs and target increases at heavy users, allow limited gas price rises for the power sector, and let CPC/Taipower absorb much of the shock— later cushioning losses with fiscal support and phased tariff adjustments. This time, the risk includes physical availability through a single chokepoint. Taiwan’s imports from Russia were already minimal after a contract expired in Mar 2022, but exposure to Qatar has grown via new long‑term contracts—tying a significant share of supply to Hormuz transits. We therefore expect elements of the 2022 playbook to reappear, while acknowledging there is no perfect way to plug a sustained shortfall: • Importing more LNG from alternative sources, yet such supplies are usually locked in long-term contracts and constrained by infrastructure. The US pledges to provide insurance backstops and naval escorts for commercial shipping through the Strait of Hormuz are unlikely on their own to restore tanker flows in the region, as Iran’s extensive disruption capabilities must first be neutralized. Thus, our commodities strate- gists highlight that the oil market faces a clear asymmetry in price outcomes: prices may decline by $10 on reassuring headlines, but they could rise by $30 to above $120/bbl once Gulf production shut-ins begin to materialize and ripple through the market (see Oil Flash Note: Ten down, thirty up , Natasha Kaneva, 3/6/26). This latter scenario would justify another 10+bp of widening in 5-year breakevens. Concepts such as a broader catastrophe fund diluting the utilities in the wildfire liability process, a durable fund (ie, with an auto-replenishment mechanism), broader funding for wildfire mitigation beyond just three large IOUs (to prevent urban fires as in 2025), and discussion of limits on non-economic and punitive damages would all be material improvements to the status quo. Ratings upside ('A' category for FMBs; IG for holdco): We think PCG will continue to see positive rating momentum, with the agencies likely to continue compressing PCG's ratings towards EIX. We think S&P could upgrade PCG (on positive outlook) by one notch (FMBs to BBB+) even before a legislative fix this year given successful progress on wildfire mitigation in its territory, which could trigger compression to EIX levels. We think Moody's (Baa1 Pos) and Fitch (BBB+ Stbl) could eventually upgrade without a stronger fix to match EIX opco's 'A' category ratings, but a strong legislative fix in 2026 could accelerate that process into this year. China’s pivot toward FDI is, in part, a reaction to the negative consequences of its lending practices, which have sparked debt crises in countries like Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Zambia, Ethiopia, and Kenya. Many of these nations took on significant debt for projects with uncertain profitability, and the pandemic exposed their commercial weaknesses. Debt restructuring has been complicated by China’s insistence on equal treatment for its loans and those from multilateral lenders, resulting in delays and political backlash. While banks have been allowed to use the discount window as a way to mone- tize their highly liquid assets, they have been unable to rely on liquidity from their pre-posi- tioned collateral. Allowing this is likely to unlock some liquidity and enable banks to hold less cash; however, the benefit is likely to be much less than the current collateral value as banks will likely assume additional haircuts over and above reserve bank haircuts for their stress testing and as it will take time for banks to become comfortable with fully relying on the discount window in their internal stress tests. At best, we would expect such liquidity changes could unlock ~$500bn of liquidity, allowing reserves to stabilize around ~$2.4-2.5tn. Even if banks are encouraged to hold a smaller liquidity buffer as part of liquid- ity reform, it is unlikely that this would result in a fundamental shift in how banks operate, and they will likely continue to manage to a buffer they deem prudent (see Pane manage- ment: potential changes to liquidity regulation, Ipek Ozil, 3/5/26). This change would allow banks to deploy more into repo and other assets. For banks with room to spare on their risk capital metrics, that could mean expansion into loans and non- HQLA securities; for banks that are more capital constrained, that might mean a shift from cash into USTs/MBS. We note that the bulk of this week’s repricing higher in monetary policy expectations was concentrated in 1H26 (+5bp in EUR/USD and +15bp in GBP) and 2H26 (+15/20bp on the week), while changes in 2027 pricing have been more contained. Notably, after the attack on Iran last weekend, the ECB OIS curve went from reflecting some probability of cuts to hikes (previ- ously about 10bp of cuts priced in by end-26 vs. around 27bp of hikes currently). Markets have shifted to price only 11bp BoE cuts this year (vs. ~55bp priced in previously) and around 37bp cumulative easing for the Fed (vs. ~43bp before the weekend strikes). Such a hawkish market reaction suggests that rate markets have assigned more weight to the risk of a significant inflation shock that prompts less easing or tighter central bank policy, rather than to the potential growth hit due to supply chain disruptions and overall weaker global business sentiment. US FDI is highly diversified, spanning sectors such as consumer products, food and beverage, tourism, business software and IT, financial services, oil and gas, communications (notably data and hosting centers), automotive, and semiconductors. Since 2005, the US has invested at least US$100 billion in greenfield projects in each of these sectors, with investments reaching up to US$680 billion in communications, US $390 billion in oil and gas, and US$330 billion in software and IT services. Historically, US FDI has supported the development of integrated supply chains and established a strong corporate presence across key sectors in host countries. Notable examples include major investments in the automotive industries of Mexico, Germany, and Canada, making North America a highly integrated automotive hub. The US has also invested heavily in electronics and manufacturing in Asia, as well as in financial and IT services, where it maintains a dominant position. Most of these industries are knowledge-intensive, with oil and gas being a significant exception. While these patterns highlight the US role in GVC expansion, recent trends in greenfield FDI are particularly revealing. Since the pandemic, US greenfield investment has become more concentrated. Europe appears uniquely exposed to the compounding nature of shocks that are hitting. The US can absorb an energy price shock better due to its domestic oil production, which benefits from a rise in oil prices. China has large strategic reserves and bilateral agreements that shield it from disruption somewhat. Europe has neither, and it is decoupling its energy supply from Russia while also absorbing a tariff shock to the export sector and deploying what fiscal headroom it has (in Germany mainly) to increase defence spending. Assessing the impact: We consider the following factors when assessing the macroeconomic consequences of geopolitical developments for Europe. ▪ Net energy importer: The energy trade deficit is around 2% of GDP for the eurozone and around 1% for the UK. As such, rising energy prices represent a negative terms-of-trade shock that squeezes incomes. Their weakening currencies exacerbate the impact on the cost of typically USD-priced energy inputs. ▪ Low gas storage: We see gas as more vulnerable to disruptions than oil. Global equities will focus on solid macro and look through the temporary supply loss, and view higher headline inflation as 'transitory'. That term may stir up some difficult memories for those who remember how long 'transitory' turned out to be in terms of elevated inflation post-pandemic. But given how in this scenario there's one observed source of supply shock, markets will be liable to believe central banks wouldn't turn hawkish. The preference for equities over fixed income stands; while this backdrop may mean markets don't price in hikes, the timing of cuts – if they come at all? – becomes more uncertain, and rates vol stays elevated relative to equity vol. Credit will still face AI-related issuance pressures, but rates staying higher for longer means absolute yields on corporate bonds remain compelling, attracting strong inflows; allocation to cash is high for similar reasons. In fact, this scenario is not dissimilar to 2022-2023 – probably not what rates investors or anyone involved in portfolio construction would like to hear… Allocation in this scenario: OW equities, UW government bonds, EW corporate credit, OW cash.

Because the denominator excludes duty-free trade, this measure does not account for the share of imports entering without tariffs. To address this limitation, we also estimate the effective tariff rate on total trade by dividing calculated duty by total trade (Customs value). This captures the aggregate tariff burden across the full import basket, incorporating both dutiable and duty-free flows. Variable definitions follow the US Census Bureau’s International Trade Definitions. Customs Value: Customs value represents the value of imports as appraised by US Customs and Border Protection under the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended. It is generally defined as the price actually paid or payable for merchandise sold for export to the United States, excluding US import duties, freight, insurance and other international transportation-related charges. The term “price actually paid or payable” refers to the total direct or indirect payment made by the buyer to, or for the benefit of, the seller. In transactions between related parties, the relationship must not influence the declared value. If assistance (“assists”) is provided to a foreign manufacturer for use in producing goods exported to the United States, the value of that assistance must be included in the Customs value. At the risk of oversimplifying, the US exports economic shocks, but it doesn’t import them. Will this time be different? Focus on oil prices To the extent that geopolitical events (particularly those in the Middle East) do affect the US economy, the biggest concern would be oil prices. Energy goods and services account for less than 4% of US consumer spending. About half of that is gasoline. Accounting for the pass-through from crude oil to energy and other inflation components, we estimate that a 10% increase in crude oil prices would raise PCE inflation by nearly 10bp in the near term. This effect would fade over the course of a year, as higher oil prices would weigh on demand for other goods and services. We estimate that the headwind to consumer spending would be like the upside to inflation: about 10bp. What about other components of GDP? Input-output data suggest that petroleum and coal products make up about 1% of total value added across industries. Putting everything together, we estimate that a 10% increase in energy prices would weigh on US GDP by no more than 10bp. Subsidized childcare is generally seen to have raised female employment, particularly in countries with higher baseline childcare costs, while extended maternity leave probably reduces female employment and earnings (see Balancing the scales: Childcare and female labor force participation rate, Joyce Chang et al., 11 Mar 2025). Child care responsibilities are holding an estimated 708mn women worldwide back from the labor force, according to the ILO, and represent the main barrier to women entering and staying in the labor force. The Child Penalty Atlas builds a world atlas of child penalties in employment based on microdata from 134 countries. Most countries display clear and sizable child penalties (Figure 27H e a t m a p o f c h i l d p e n a l t i e s ). Their atlas shows that men and women follow parallel trends before parenthood, but diverge sharply and persistently after parenthood. The map divides countries into deciles of the child penalty, with darker colors representing larger penalties. Countries with a penalty less than or equal to zero fall in the “No Penalty” category. records.text: e progress in closing gender pay gap The female working-age population (ages 15-64) labor force participation rate in Japan has been rising steadily, reaching over 77% in 2025—a high level even by international standards (Figure 5J a p a n ’ s f e m a l e l a b o r p a r t i c i p a t i o n r a t i o a n d g e n d e r p a y ). However, progress in closing the wage gap has stalled in recent years. While rising inflation and a tight labor market since 2022 have led to significant increases in nominal wages, companies have not used this opportunity to close the gender pay gap. The gender pay gap remained largely unchanged from 2022 to 2024, with women earning only 75.8% of men’s wages in 2024. In 2025, the ratio of female executives at listed companies rose by 1.5%-pts to 14%. To address these issues, the government made it mandatory in July 2022 for companies with more than 301 employees to disclose gender pay gaps. Furthermore, from April 2026, this requirement will be expanded to companies with more than 101 employees. Going forward, a key question will be whether mandatory disclosure of pay gaps and action plans will drive corporate change through market pressure. In contrast to the volatility in macro markets, funding conditions remained stable—a sharp departure from the early days of the Russia–Ukraine conflict—with liquidity at the front end not a near‑term concern. Bank CP/CD spreads were mostly unchanged as issuance activity remained near historical averages and, following coupon settlements earlier in the week, repo rates retraced lower towards pre-month-end levels ( Figure 3B a n k C P / C D s p r e a d s a r e o n l y m a r g i n a l l y h i g h e r t h i s w e e k , u n l i k e t h e 2 0 - 2 5 b p s p i k e d u r i n g t h e o n s e t o f t h e R u s s i a - U k r a i n e c o n f l i c t ). We expect CP/CD spreads and repo rates to remain relatively stable in the weeks ahead, though we could see some modest firming into quarter-end. Indeed, technicals at the front-end remain strong, as MMF AUMs have already grown by more than $150bn YTD, outpacing recent seasonality, to roughly $8.1tn. This has come alongside the continued growth in corporate liquidity portfolios and the buildup in cash has coincided with a sharp rise in long-term debt issuance among the hyperscalers. To the extent that corporations continue to raise debt with proceeds that are not immediately deployed, it is possible that a portion of those funds could be temporarily placed in a taxable MMF. Market commentary Over the weekend, the US and Israel launched a strike on Iran, resulting in the death of Iran’s Supreme Leader. Notably, Japanese equities have largely retraced their post-election gains. Meanwhile, JPY rates bearishly steepened this week, outperforming global peers, which generally experienced bearish flattening. This move appears to be driven primarily by positioning and views on the BoJ’s potential reaction function should geopolitical risks intensify further (Figure 2J P Y r a t e s b e a r i s h l y s t e e p e n e d t h i s w e e k , b u t o u t p e r f o r m e d g l o b a l p e e r s ). That said, a broad range of investors appear to have remained on the sidelines in the JPY rates space for the most part, reflecting elevated uncertainty and a lack of consensus and conviction on the implications. records.text: 6 March 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Deutsche Bank AG Page 7 Reducing risk The latest geopolitical events in the Middle East are most immediately market relevant via the potential disruptions to the Strait of Hormuz and oil production capacity, and the associated impact on oil prices. So far, Iran has not declared the Strait of Hormuz closed, and US air superiority would suggest that Iran's ability to conduct large-scale attacks should diminish over time. However, the risk premium in oil prices is likely to persist given (1) some evidence that the decision-making process in Iran has been decentralised, and (2) creating disturbances (as opposed to full closure) in the Strait of Hormuz is relatively low-tech. Also, one should monitor the tail risk from unrest in neighbouring countries in general, and Pakistan in particular (e.g., the events around the US consulate in Karachi yesterday), given its geopolitical relevance. The impact on the rates market can occur via three channels. Firstly, risk aversion and deleveraging should be bullish for rates. Secondly, a negative supply shock to oil prices should be bearish for rates on a standalone basis, but could trigger more risk aversion and deleveraging (more on that below). Thirdly, the impact on deficits and fiscal policy is also bearish, but is unlikely to be relevant in the short term. But five state elections could get in the way of that story, too. The upcoming Baden Wuerttemberg and Rhineland Palatinate elections matter for federal dynamics: The CDU coming first in both could reduce SPD appetite for compromise in the federal ruling coalition. The September elections in Saxony Anhalt, Berlin and Mecklenburg Vorpommern could show the far right AfD gaining the largest vote share – possibly even an absolute majority – in one or perhaps two states, which could derail political capital for the ruling coalition at federal level even further. Opinion polls show that voter priorities have shifted in recent years. Climate-related concerns have lessened since Covid. Recent measures to curb migration seem to have reduced those concerns, too. The economy remains the major concern now. A sense that the current government may have “overpromised” on economic improvements after the elections may weigh on voting intentions. That is symptomatic of the “catch-22” situation much of Europe has been stuck in for years. Positioning is less extended than some investors may think The sharp drop in Korean equities has prompted investor worries about overextended positioning and potential further forced selling. There are several areas of concern in this regard, including high hedge fund net exposure (which was recently at 5-year highs according to our Prime Services data), increased retail investor margin borrowing, and signs of non-dedicated foreign investors following price momentum (often called “tourist capital”). However, a closer look at positioning and flow data suggests a more balanced picture and therefore less unwind risk. First, foreign investors have been net sellers ytd of $15bn. This has been concentrated in the heavyweight semiconductor stocks and reflects a) profit taking after exceptionally strong performance (Hynix +70% and Samsung Electronics +85% ytd to their recent highs), and b) some forced passive selling from rebalancing in the EWY iShares MSCI South Korea ETF. Despite this selling, foreign ownership of Korean equities is 34.5%, equivalent to +0.7 s.d vs. the range since 2000. In aggregate, foreign positioning looks full, but not stretched. Second, retail investors have been net sellers of Korean equities in 2025 and in the early part of 2026 until they reversed to net buying in February. Numerous recipient countries entered IMF programs requiring significant debt restructuring, a process complicated by China’s opaque approach. Consequently, Chinese loan issuance dropped sharply, fueling speculation that the BRI was losing steam. However, China has continued to advance its global agenda. The nature of BRI investments has shifted significantly. As lending slowed, FDI accelerated and now exceeds loans as the main investment channel. Of the US$2 trillion invested, FDI makes up US$1.2 trillion, while loans account for US$800 billion. Chinese greenfield FDI to BRI countries surpassed US$800 billion by 2024, with annual greenfield investment rising from US$16 billion before the BRI to over US$50 billion after its launch. Loans, once the preferred vehicle, averaged US$117 billion per year between 2013 and 2019 but have tapered off since then. The post-pandemic period saw a rebound in overseas contracted projects, hinting at some recovery in loan activity, but FDI remains the dominant channel, underscoring China’s growing willingness to take on greater equity risk as its interests deepen in recipient economies (Figure 6C h i n a ' s t o p 2 5 B R I l o a n s a n d F D I d e s t i n a t i o n s ). Three risks from a large and persistent energy price shock Our base case on the impact of the conflict is very much in line with consensus. The more interesting question for investors is: what could go wrong, and how? WTI is up around 26% since the build-up to the conflict started (Jan 28). A key risk to our sanguine base case is that non-linear effects could set in if the shock to oil prices is large and sustained. This could happen, for example, if the Strait of Hormuz remains closed for several weeks. There are at least three channels through which non-linear effects might play out. First, a big spike in oil prices – and the sort of conflict that would cause such a shock – would likely lead to meaningful tightening in financial conditions. And the economy is probably more sensitive than usual to markets. That’s because spending growth is being driven by higher-income households, who have benefited from a near-doubling in stocks over the last three years. An enduring equity downturn could weigh substantially on higher-income spending, exacerbating the shock. Second, lower-income households are more exposed to oil price shocks, because energy makes up a larger share of their spending. Morgan Securities LLC Steven Palacio(1-212) 834-5031 steven.palacio@jpmorgan.com Armstrong Mbi(212) 622-5896 armstrong.mbi@jpmchase.com Industry & Policy Thematics FDI: Shifting from outsourcing to securing supply chains 06 March 2026 J P M O R G A N Introduction A perfect storm A series of self-reinforcing structural shifts in the 1990s paved the way for a decades- long boom in FDI. On the technology front, the internet revolution and container shipping dramatically lowered communication and transport costs. On the global trade front, the 1994 Uruguay Round of GATT, which created the WTO in 1995, expanded global trade rules to cover services, intellectual property, and investment, while deepening tariff cuts and strengthening regulations on subsidies, agriculture, textiles, and dispute settlement. The round also integrated more developing countries into the system, giving them a stronger voice and clearer rules. This shift paved the way for more open, rules-based trade, as developing nations lowered barriers and liberalized investment. China’s WTO entry in 2001 added vast low-cost manufacturing capacity to the global supply chain. Multinational companies quickly capitalized on these changes by relocating supply chains to China and other developing countries, fueling a surge in FDI (Figure 1G l o b a l g o o d s t r a d e a n d F D I ). Indeed, our base case is that the Iran conflict will not affect the trajectory of Fed policy, though it will probably strengthen the consensus around staying on hold at the next two meetings. At the time of this writing, markets have almost perfectly priced this outcome. A large and longer-lasting shock would be stagflationary. This would mean renewed tension between the Fed’s two mandates. In the near term, substantially higher oil prices would make it harder for the Fed to cut. With inflation already above target, we think most of the FOMC would prefer to err on the side of caution by staying on hold. Some policymakers might even call for hikes if inflation expectations, which are typically sensitive to oil prices, were to move up meaningfully. But we think the bar to raise rates will be high under Warsh. In the medium term, however, the Fed might get concerned about demand destruction from the energy supply shock. The saving rate is already low by historical standards, so consumers don’t have much buffer against a spike in energy prices. A spending slowdown would weigh on both job growth and inflation (once oil prices stabilize), pushing the Fed in a more dovish direction. records.text: , realized losses are broadly in line with our prior framework at roughly 3.3 mbd of crude (or 3.6 mbd including products). Reported cuts now total at least 3.5 mbd (Figure 4): • Iraq 3.2 mb/d (south 3.0; north 0.2); • Kuwait up to 0.3 mbd; • the UAE is just beginning to reduce. By the end of next week, as storage fills and bottlenecks persist, we project regional shut‑ins of more than 4 mbd. A disruption at Kharg Island would add a further 1.0 to 1.5 mbd, lifting total losses to at least 5 mbd and more than 8 mbd when refined products are included. Iran, previously expected to be among the last to shut in, could move ahead of Kuwait and the UAE. For now, consuming markets have not fully felt the shortage because pre‑escalation cargoes are still arriving: roughly 10 days to India, 21 to China, and 10 to Northwest Europe— temporarily masking disruptions as the buffer shrinks. Within a week, as pre‑conflict cargoes are absorbed and new loadings stall, visible shortages could begin to emerge. The global export 10‑day moving average fell to 31 mb/d this week, excluding cargoes loaded within the Strait of Hormuz that later became stuck (Figure 3). While the magnitudes vary depending on how fundamentally negative the circumstances surrounding the sharp daily drop were, the historical record of the equity market recovering from price shocks is encouraging. Second, the pattern of returns during spikes in the global geopolitical risk index shows a drop concurrent with heightened geopolitical risk but gains in the following 3, 6, and 12 months. Third, Korea also tends to recover after 10% corrections in global equities, especially if there is no ensuing US recession. As we recently noted in Assessing regional geopolitical sensitivity in light of Mideast conflict, the duration and magnitude of the oil price shock will determine the fundamental impact on regional earnings and economic growth. As of now, we have made no changes to our forecasts, and therefore we view the equity market pullback as a correction that will likely be followed by a recovery to new highs after a period of consolidation. In addition to selling to adjust positions at the end of the fiscal year, this could also be seen as correcting the outperformance against the 10y sector in February. Rebalancing accompanying equity weakness would also weigh on 15y. If the decision is made to change maturity categories for liquidity tap auctions, it would provide support to this sector, but it would be negative for 11y to maturity. We also expect an increase in the interest rate applied to whole-life lump-sum life insurance policies, which would likely contribute to increased surrender rates for policies in force. While carry relative to shorter maturities remains highly attractive, we expect interest rates overall to rise in April- June, so we cannot recommend actively buying as delta. In OIS, the 10y softening trend continues for the 5s10s20s butterfly. It seems risk premium pricing has continued in the 10y sector. However, it is also possible to see this as range-bound since February, and we think scope for further weakening is narrowing from an historical point of view both for the 5s10s and 10s20s. The decline in FDI flows despite the rapid expansion in global trade since 2022 (see Figure 1) highlights both the maturing of existing and the reappraisal of where and in what sectors to build new supply chains. This disconnect also reflects rising lending rates. Data issues: a small but necessary digression Official data on FDI are readily available, but suffer from two notable shortcomings. First, according to international standards, only equity holdings that grant at least 10% of voting power are classified as FDI; smaller stakes are categorized as portfolio investments, even if they provide effective control through other means. For instance, subsidiaries may use local or parent-company loans to finance acquisitions, but these transactions are recorded as loans rather than FDI. Official statistics often do not update when such loans are later converted into equity, which can obscure the true extent of effective control. Second, is that investors commonly route capital through offshore financial centers (OFCs) for tax, regulatory, and confidentiality considerations; however official data in destination-countries attribute the origin of the inflow to the last transfer jurisdiction rather than the ultimate investor, which creates implausible aggregates and obscures true source countries. Morgan, Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac On the regulatory front, Vice-Chair Bowman gave a speech on Tuesday outlining her thoughts on liquidity regulation reform. Treasury Undersecretary McKernan also delivered remarks prepared by Treasury Secretary Bessent on a similar topic. Both sets of remarks expressed concern that the liquidity framework introduced in the wake of the GFC has caused banks to hoard reserves and HQLA, potentially to the detriment of their ability to extend credit. They point out that reluctance to use HQLA at the discount window during periods of stress means that banks tend to hold buffers in excess of what they might be required to by LCR, and a reluctance, in stressed periods, to drop HQLA below 100% of the amount required by LCR means that HQLA goes unused while banks try to monetize less liquid assets.

If declined or not exercised, the home must be widely advertised and, if no individual buyer purchases or even makes an offer within 60 days, the operator is deemed compliant with the disposal requirement. An active lease that begins no later than six months before the disposal date can delay disposal until the lease expires, and the tenant may be offered renewals for up to 36 consecutive months. REITs are exempt from the disposal requirement if the transaction incurs a 100% tax rate under the REIT rules. records.text: 5 06 March 2026 Five Ws defining the state of gender balance: Work, wages, wealth, waning fertility and readiness for an AI-wired world In this year’s edition of our report on the state of gender balance, we focus on what we reference as the five Ws defining and impacting gender parity—Work, Wages, Wealth, Waning fertility and readiness for an AI-Wired World—and future trends to watch. In an era where gender equity remains a global challenge, our 9th annual State of Global Gender Equity Report tracks the progress and ongoing hurdles faced by women worldwide. Our report includes a comprehensive review and analysis of metrics and key dimensions related to women’s careers and lives, such as labor force participation, leadership representation, the gender pay gap, the wealth accumulation gap at retirement, home ownership and political empowerment. We find that more women than ever are working based on female labor force participation rates (LFPR), but the representation for women at the C-suite and board levels has stalled. The gender pay gap remains little changed, and women lag in wealth accumulation as a result. Progress may have plateaued given future challenges that include a decline in fertility rates and births, which is negatively impacting the working age population. At the same time, greater adoption of AI could be more disruptive to women in the workforce as the gender gap in adoption is wide and AI systems can amplify gender biases. The Cross-Border Equity Flow Indicator (xbEFI) measures the purchases and sales of equities by institutional investors, and is produced on a daily basis with a two day publication lag. The Cross -Border EFI focuses on trades by investors with base currencies that differ from a stock’s settlement currency. The indicator also includes transactions where the investor’s base currency is the same as the currency in which the trade is settled, and the settlement currency is different from that of the stock’s country of incorporation. An example of such a trade would be the purchase of a Dutch company’s American Depositary Receipts by a U.S. dollar-based fund. The Sovereign Bond Flow Indicator (SBFI) measures the purchases and sales of domestic and foreign sovereign bonds by institutional investors across countries and in regional aggregates and is available in unweighted and duration -weighted forms. We use unweighted flows in this document to capture the most relevant variable for a currency view. The SBFI is updated daily with a two-day publication lag. We use cross-border sovereign bond flows where available and total sovereign bond flows for all other countries.

Fading downward impact from sample replacement However, we need to take the upside surprise with a grain of salt. A downward bias in YoY wage growth caused by the sample replacement implemented in January 2025 has finally dropped out in this survey. Because the sample replacement had lowered total cash earnings in January 2025 by 0.9ppt, if we assume this downward impact lasted through December, then much of the January 2026 wage growth, from in December 2025, can be explained by the fading the distortion in the statistics (see Technical factors heighten uncertainty around the macro wage outlook, 8 April 2025). Sample replacement will again be key focus in 2026 Today's preliminary figure for January is based on the 2025 sample. The 2026 new sample will be applied starting with the revised January data to be released on 8 April. As with last year, the sample replacement could again distort the data. Therefore, when assessing the (statistically measured) nominal wage growth outlook for 2026, the impact of this sample replacement will hold a key. Unfortunately, the next comprehensive NZ labour force survey is not due until early May. This lack of a trigger links to a common topic in client discussions: the difficult carry set-up to play NZ policy normalization. NZD 1s/2s is steep, and the RBNZ is likely to normalize, but doesn’t show urgency to start. The relative underreaction of NZ assets to the survey and growth data is then partially justified in the sense that excess capacity buys the RBNZ time, pushing policy normalization into the forwards, which are now close to fair value (Figure 8N Z D 1 Y x 1 Y i s a b o u t f a i r i n o u t r i g h t t e r m s g i v e n m a c r o i n p u t s a s t h e y s t a n d ). The precise timing of the coming unemployment rate decline in a sense summarizes the carry headwind, as an imminent tightening of the labour market would overcome negative carry concerns. In our models, every 1%-pt lower on unemployment flattens 2s/10s swap by 40bp, and 6m forward 2s/10s is about 15bp below spot. A roughly 0.3-0.4%-pt fall in unemployment in the next six months is then needed to beat the forwards. If current curve shape is preserved, we look to re-enter NZD flattening trades closer to the 1Q labour data. State of Women in the Workforce: More jobs, fragmented hours, stagnant pay Women’s workforce participation globally has remained stable at 49% compared to 73% for men in 2025, according to the International Labour Organization. However, there has been little progress in closing the gender pay gap, which remains stuck at 19.1% and 11.1%, respectively, in the US and Europe, with women still underrepresented in the highest paying fields. Job gains have been concentrated in lower-paying, service-centric industries like Healthcare and Care (58.5%) and Education (52.9%). AI adoption will accelerate structural shifts in global labor markets, raising concerns that women could potentially be more adversely impacted as there is a sizeable gender gap in AI adoption. We examine key employment and wage trends for women in the US, Europe, Japan, China and emerging markets. Recent analysis from the Institute for Women’s Policy Research (IWPR) shows that the gender pay gap in the US worsened in the latest data. In 2024, women working full-time year-round earned 80.9 cents for every dollar earned by men— implying a 19.1% pay gap and marking the lowest earnings ratio since 2016. In the Senate, the left (Pacto Historico) increased its seat share to 25% (from 20% before), while that of the right and center-right parties decreased to 46% (from 49%). The center-left’s share decreased to 29% (from 31%) (see Figure 10 in Appendix for number of seats by party). Primary elections: The primary election for the right parties surprised analysts on two counts: the high turnout (5.8 million) and the high number of votes for Paloma Valencia (3.2 million, Figure 2). The strong support for Valencia makes her a formidable competitor against Abelardo de la Espriella in the first round of Colombia’s presidential election. Even though De la Espriella polls better than Valencia in run-off simulations against Ivan Cepeda, Valencia could better absorb centrist votes, making her highly competitive in the race. The primary for the left parties was a non-event as Roy Barreras (center left) did not get enough votes to challenge Ivan Cepeda’s candidacy (see Figure 6 in the Appendix). A moderate politician with traction in the center of the political spectrum, Barreras was the only candidate who could have redefined the presidential race for the left. Finally, we note the low turnout for the center primary (0.6 million, see Figure 7 in the Appendix). This reaction has been similar in terms of direction to what was seen last year after the outbreak of the 12-day Israel-Iran conflict, although DM curves had remained little changed back in 2025 and the magnitude of the moves was more contained. Instead, this week’s market reaction to the Middle East conflict has been broadly opposite relative to the Russia-Ukraine episode of 2022. In the aftermath of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, DM curves had indeed bull steepened across the board with the front-end rallying 20-25bp in a week, as markets priced in a slower pace of policy tightening from major central banks and resorted to flight-to-quality into govies. Swap spreads widened on risk-off sentiment, while intra-EMU spreads tightened 5-15bp on the week given the ECB's implicit commitment to prevent fragmentation, the symmetric nature of the price shock and the announcement of fiscal responses across the whole Euro area. records.text: E M – L O C A L E YE S FO R A G L O B A L V IE W 0.1 1.8 1.3 0.4 0.1 0.1 0 0.5 1 1.5 2 2021 2022 2023 2024 2025 2026 Eurozone discretionary fiscal measures in response to high energy prices and inflation (% of EA GDP) 306/03/2026 Fiscal space constraints: In the event of a material escalation in the conflict and more significant spike in energy prices, we do not think eurozone and UK governments would be able to provide the degree of support that they did after the energy shock of 2022. The estimated discretionary fiscal measures (including subsidies and tax measures) in response to high energy and inflation following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine amounted to some 1.8% of eurozone GDP in 2022 and around 1.3% in 2023 (Figure 3). In the UK, energy support measures cost around an estimated GBP50bn, 2% of GDP (OBR; see Figure 16). But we now see little scope for significant cushioning stimulus, with eurozone aggregate government debt to GDP elevated and government bond yields materially higher than when Russia invaded Ukraine, and what remaining fiscal space there is (for example in Germany) being directed towards higher defence and infrastructure spending – the former clearly of strategic importance in a fragmented and war-torn global environment. Meanwhile, the UK has maintained a strong emphasis on fiscal prudence, keeping policy on a tightening trajectory to alleviate market concerns about debt sustainability. We run a few scenarios for energy prices, impact on inflation and BoE’s reaction function Scenario 1: If gas and oil prices are sustained at current levels (£60/barrel and 140pence/therm) Energy is ~6% of the UK’s CPI basket. Oil prices at ~£60/barrel are around ~25% higher in sterling terms. If this move is sustained and doesn’t reverse, it can add ~20-25bps to inflation in 2026. Petrol prices usually reflect the moves in oil prices fairly quickly. In terms of gas, while the Ofgem price cap has already been set for April and is set to see a ~7% drop, a sustained rise in gas prices can affect price caps in H2 (July and October). If we assume British natural gas prices of around 140pence/therm, that is an an increase of more than ~70% from an average of 77 pence/therm. We estimate this could raise the energy price cap by ~11-12% in July assuming this is sustained. In the near term, inflation could be 20-25bps higher from March- June and be around ~55-60bps higher in H2 2026 (vs. 1.9% in our current forecasts), with December inflation likely at 2.5%. Overall inflation could be ~35bps higher in 2026 (vs. 2.2% in our current forecasts) and 20bps higher in 2027 (vs. 2.0% in our forecasts). Crowded positioning, unfavorable technicals and a sizable discount between spot and the fix prompted us to tac- tically neutralize our CNH longs. While this was never meant to be a risk management play against Middle East risk, it has proved to be a timely move with USD/CNH retracing higher this week following a broad-based de-risking move and short covering in the dollar. External uncertainties and global risks are likely to remain in the driver's seat for the near-term out- look for CNY FX, with risk biased for further consolidation. Our global FX team noted that a complete neutralization of dollar shorts could be worth a 1.5-2% rise in the USD TWI, which would be consistent with USD/CNH settling into a range of 6.89-6.93 based off the historical beta. Our medium- term bias leaves us on the look-out to re-engage with CNH longs once external uncertainty subsides. While upside risk to USD/CNH lingers, with much of that dependent on the trajectory of the conflict, CNY FX has proved to be more resilient than its non-USD peers with the CFETS TWI tracking DXY higher This is not uncommon during non-China centric risk-off events, with stable PBoC fixings, a managed FX vol and corporate dollar selling serv- ing as organic stabilizers and a source of support for CNY’s passive appreciation against non-USD pairs.

records.text: Global Economic Weekly | 06 March 2026 15 Asia Helen Qiao Merrill Lynch (Hong Kong) Asia: Assessing the Iran conflict impact through oil and trade shocks Complete report: Asia Economic Weekly: Assessing the Iran conflict impact on Asia through oil and trade shocks 06 March 2026 Asia to feel the brunt from Iran conflict We expect the US-Israel military operation in Iran to leave a meaningful and long-lasting impact on global geopolitics. In our view, the impact on Asia will be mostly felt through the disruptions of oil and trade channels with heterogenous impact across different countries, in addition to risks from financial condition tightening and remittance declines. The trauma could potentially become even greater, if the conflicts last longer with widespread supply disruptions, in our view. Magnitude and duration of the oil shock holds the key Depending on the state of the Hormuz Strait, regional energy infrastructure, and Iranian oil production and export, oil prices could potentially see a much greater jump ranging between $40-100/bbl without an immediate normalization. If the oil shock turns out to be more than a transitory change, with oil prices plateauing at a much higher level for longer, most Asian economies will likely witness downward pressure on growth through terms of trade losses, along with higher inflation. In reality, subsidiaries often finance acquisitions by borrowing locally or from their parent companies. These transactions are recorded as loans, not FDI, and official statistics rarely update the classification when loans are later converted into equity. As a result, strategic control exercised through stakes below the 10% mark is often obscured in the data. OFC routing and origin misattribution (the “last-mile” problem) As discussed previously, investors often channel funds through OFCs to take advantage of favorable tax regimes, regulatory environments, and confidentiality. Recipient countries typically record the source of investment as the last jurisdiction the funds passed through, rather than the actual origin. This practice leads to distorted statistics and masks the true source of foreign investment. For example, while the combined GDP of the Netherlands, Hong Kong, the Cayman Islands, and Luxembourg is just US$1.6 trillion, these jurisdictions together are reported as the source of US$9.1 trillion in global FDI stock, an implausible figure that highlights the extent of capital routing through OFCs. It also means that the true FDI by countries such as the US and China is likely to be much higher than shown in Table 1. A prolonged conflict with elevated energy prices could be a drag on eco- nomic growth and consumer spending, which would be negative for CRE in general (see CMBS). Cautious sentiment has carried over into the non-agency residential credit space, with non- QM AAAs in the ~130bp context, at least 30bp wider than their January tights. Furthermore, the inflation fears driving Treasury yields higher is likely pushing mortgage rates back above 6%. Risks of delays to cuts in March/ June if moves don’t reverse quickly The BoE has become increasingly sensitive to energy price moves, especially as second round effects to inflation and wage expectations from energy price moves have become more prominent in last few years. Our current holding base case is for the BoE to cut rates in March and June, driven by weaker labour market and current expected leg down in inflation. However, if these energy moves don’t reverse quickly, risks would rise that the BoE delays and slows down cuts. In that scenario the BoE is likely to worry more about second round effects, especially as wage expectations are still elevated. A March cut would be in doubt if the energy price moves don’t reverse by then (unless the labour market report released on 19 March is fairly weak), increasing risks of a delay of the next cut potentially to sometime in Q2 and the second cut to H2. We don’t change forecasts yet and will reevaluate our March cut call next week. Overall, if the energy price moves reverse quickly say within the next couple of weeks, then the BoE can likely resume its cutting cycle as per our base case of March and June. It is worth noting that UK consumer energy prices are regulated via the quarterly Ofgem price cap (and are now fixed for April) which is based on NPB forward curve rather than wholesale prices. We currently estimate a mechanical 0.3% impact on headline CPI from the move in the forward curve and taking into account second round effects we currently estimate the recent energy shock might increase headline CPI by around 0.6% by July to 2.7%. We acknowledge that increased gas prices limits the ability for the BoE to ease in the near term but assuming the conflict does not extend beyond several months into the summer, we think BoE easing later this year is still a possibility against a backdrop of an ongoing easing in the labour market. In addition, global downside growth risks likely increase if oil were to persistently rise above 100$/bbl. Given this, we recommend recveiving Dec26 MPC OIS with a few bp of easing priced. records.text: 2 Europe Economic Weekly | 06 March 2026 Weekly view The value of waiting, for now We have heard many times from central banks that, when uncertainty spikes, there is option value in waiting. That could become very relevant soon given developments in the Middle East and uncertainty on the size and persistence of the energy price shock the global economy will endure. Not surprisingly, beyond the increase in energy prices, we are already seeing a significant uptick in our measure of economic policy uncertainty (Exhibit 1). In our baseline scenario, we don't expect a protracted conflict, limiting potential upside to oil to not much more than what we have seen so far and the shock fading in the next few weeks. In that scenario, our current forecasts and calls for central banks would be broadly ok. We would not expect much of a reaction from the ECB and our call for cuts in 1H27 would still be very valid. More immediately, the Bank of England (BoE) would still cut in March. But things could change if we are still facing the current shock by the March meeting. In the case of the ECB, the value of waiting would not change things much – at the end of the day nobody expects anything from them in two weeks. But the general message is likely to be one of wait-and-see, in line with ECB speak this week.
