records.text: r fertility rates than forecast Our Long-term Strategy team has long argued that working-age depopulation is a substantial headwind to growth, generally feeding one-for-one into economic growth. The working-age population of DM began to shrink in 2024 and will accelerate in years to come. They find that relative to the 2000-2024 period, working-age population growth in the next decade will be slower—or contraction faster – in almost every DM country and some of the largest EM countries. Working-age population growth should be reduced by 0.5%-pts pa in the US, 0.8%-pts pa in the Euro Area, 0.1%-pts pa in Japan, 0.2%-pts in the UK, 1.3%-pts in China, and 1.8%-pts in South Korea (see The Long-term Strategist: Working-age depopulation has arrived, Alexander Wise, 16 Jan 2025). After a Baby Boom in the aftermath of World War 2, fertility rates have declined substantially in many countries, meaningfully below the so-called “replacement level” of 2.1 children per woman. From 1995 to 2024, 63 countries saw their total fertility rate fall below the replacement rate of 2.1 birth per woman, as according to the UN. The ultimate consequence of this steady fall in fertility rates has been rapidly aging populations, shrinking working-age populations in many countries, and outright shrinking populations in some countries. Structural trends in China show similar sentiment and a sharp rise in China’s singletons. A quarter of all households in China were made up of just one person as of 2020, up from just 8% twenty years prior. The rise in solo living has been most stark amongst 25-29 year olds and those over 65. Falling marriage rates and the growing average age of first marriages is in part responsible for the rise of single-person households and implies a gap in terms of intimate relationship formation. Aside from dating apps, our China analysts highlight the growth in otome, or romance narrative- driven games, as a window into how services aimed at this demographic may evolve (see Trend Tapestry: Alone but not lonely: Serving China’ s singletons, Hannah L Lee, 17 Jul 2025). Family size in China is shrinking despite a shift in the one-child policy in 2016. One and two-person households are now the most common type, compared to three and four- member households just two decades ago. records.text: 20 Global Economic Weekly | 06 March 2026 Terms of trade resemble positive productivity shock The rise of the terms of trade (ratio of export to import prices) – 19.1% in 2025 – has obvious positive implications through the demand channel by increasing the disposable income of the economy (more money for consumption and investment). But it also shares characteristics of a positive productivity shock. It’s like technological progress in the sense Peru is producing more value added with the same amounts of inputs. Impact of US Section 122 tariffs on Peru seems moderate Peru is somewhat worse off after SCOTUS ruling and Section 122 tariffs The Supreme Court of the US struck down the IEEPA tariffs, including reciprocal measures (10% for Peru). In response, President Trump imposed a global Section 122 tariff of 15%. Peru is worse off because its US tariff increased (to 15% from 10%) and some competitors gained cost-advantages. We expect some trade diversion, away from Peru, to happen. For example, US imports of textiles & garments from Asia and Central America may grow at the expense of Peru. But the overall effect seems moderate. Textiles & garments exports negatively impacted, but small in big picture On the textiles & garments sector, we note Asian competitors have seen big declines in their US tariffs (to 15% from ~31.5%-66.5%) while the Trump administration decided to exempt textiles & garment imports from Central America and the Dominican Republic (DR-CAFTA). In our view, the best indicator of whether or not investors can expect any rerating upside is “Excess Yields” and that metric today suggests there is no rerating upside outside of parts of Europe, Japan, Singapore, Thailand, and Peru. The tables below show the trailing earnings yield of SMid-Caps (and Large-Caps) in each region measured on an equal-weighted average ex-outliers basis, and how it compares to the local central bank risk-free rate. This “excess yield” has historically been 1.6% for the S&P 500. Our equal-weighted average ex-outliers analysis should demand higher “excess yields” given that such math lowers the exposure to the supposedly steadier, lower-risk mega caps. Moreover, the excess yields should be even higher for EMs and SMid-Caps, both of which should incorporate a higher risk premium. As we see in the tables below, most regions don’t offer any rerating upside potential, as the excess yields of their SMid and Large-Caps over the risk-free rate are not far from the 1.6% S&P 500 historical mark, and are even negative in some instances. records.text: Economic data took a backseat to geopolitical developments, but the February employment report came in weaker than expected, showing a 92K drop in nonfarm payrolls, with a downward revision to prior months, and a tick up in the unemployment rate to 4.4%, although AHE rose 0.4%, a touch stronger than expected. In understanding what the Iran conflict means for the fair value of breakevens, we first con- sider the expected pass-through of the energy price move into headline CPI. Energy CPI has tended to exhibit about a 25% beta to Brent oil prices, and energy has a 6.4% relative impor- tance in CPI, so every 10%-pt increase in Brent should push headline CPI up by about 16bp on the margin. Thus, the 30% rise in Brent prices since last Friday should contribute to roughly a 0.5%-pt boost in headline CPI, justifying roughly 11bp of widening in 5-year breakevens. Meanwhile, our economists have shown that models which try to measure the effects of oil prices on core inflation tend to have weak explanatory power and large standard errors, generally implying a negligible impact of oil on core inflation (see US: Oil and the economy, Abiel Reinhart & Michael Hanson, 3/6/26). Despite this, spreads now trade only modestly wider in Europe and flat to tighter in the US versus last Thursday’s close, suggesting investors are hesitant to materially shift positioning in response to the conflict. Rates markets have been somewhat more decisive: while higher swap rates have largely been driven by inflation components, moves have been concentrated in the front end, with longer-term inflation expectations remaining relatively anchored, particularly in the US. This phenomenon is material because elevated jump risk is not healthy for the provision of liquidity (as can be seen in the sharp decline in market depth), and thus liquidity conditions seem destined to remain poor for a while longer. In addition, elevated jump risk can bias implied normal basis point volatility consider- ably higher because of the nonlinear gains to long gamma positions from large jumps. This also makes carry-seeking short gamma strategies unattractive, as a single day of “jump” can erode multiple days of carry (Interest Rate Derivatives, US Fixed Income Mar- kets Weekly, 2/6/2026). To illustrate this in stylized fashion, we may imagine that each day, the market realizes either a “jump” of 8bp or a “regular sized” move of some magnitude. Figure 6 shows the magni- tude of the “regular sized” move required to break even on long gamma positions versus the assumed frequency of jumps. This figure tells us, for instance, that a 2-sigma jump probabil- ity of ~7% requires non-jump-day volatility of only 4.5 bp/day for an option trading at 5bp/ day. records.text: M Update Morgan Stanley Research 3 In short, both fiscal and monetary policy will provide much less support to domestic demand than they did in 2022. And economic activity is no longer benefiting from pent-up demand seen in the immediate aftermath of COVID, when reopening effects and the normalization of saving rates gave a significant boost to private consumption. The just released details of 4Q25 GDP point to strong consumption as a key driver of euro area growth at the moment. The current shock is likely to dampen that dynamic significantly. Finally, the supply side of the global economy seems in better shape than in 2022. Post-COVID pent-up demand was happening just after a prolonged closure of entire ports in China, causing major backlogs in global supply chains. While the current situation poses some risks to prices beyond energy (~30% of fertilizers originate via the SoH, and this could put pressure on food inflation, see here), there is no evidence of broader supply chain disruptions so far. A-priori, all these factors point to a more limited inflationary push than the one seen in 2022. Monetary policy will tread carefully, for now. 2026 is not 2022. But things could get worse before they get better, and close monitoring is key. We are curious to see which scenarios the ECB will publish along with its projections on 19 March.

Banks' securities portfolios declined $3bn over the week to February 25, driven by a $6bn drop in MBS holdings across bank categories. This was offset to some extent by a $5bn increase in UST holdings, mostly at large banks, though a small part of the increase likely reflects valuation effect as rates drifted lower over the week. Overall, banks' UST holdings are $70bn higher year- to-date, extending the banking sector's solid demand for securities observed in 2025. According to ISTAT, GDP grew by a total of 0.5%Y in 2025 (NSA, annual national accounts). A strong contribution came from 4Q25, when GDP rose by 0.26%Q, stronger than we had anticipated. Overall, the Italian economy grew by 0.48% in 2H25, resulting in a carry over of 0.3% for 2026. Investment saw strong growth at the end of the year, while private consumption growth was positive but weak, at 0.08%Q, suggesting that the saving rate remained elevated at the end of the year, after the 1.4pp increase to 14.1% in 3Q25. Net exports brought a large negative contribution in the quarter (-0.7pp) - a combination of strong import growth (+1.0%Q) and weak exports (-1.2%Q). Overall, GDP would have fallen by 0.38% in 4Q25, if it had not been for a very strong inventory build-up, which contributed 0.6pp to activity at the end of the year. Credit market reaction has been benign so far, but stagflation risks loom Since the end of last week, volatility across risk assets has increased, with US IG/HY cash spreads peaking at +3/+10bp versus pre-conflict levels and European IG/HY spreads peaking at +7/+20bp. Despite this, spreads now trade only modestly wider in Europe and flat to tighter in the US versus last Thursday’s close, suggesting investors are hesitant to materially shift positioning in response to the conflict. Rates markets have been somewhat more decisive: while higher swap rates have largely been driven by inflation components, moves have been concentrated in the front end, with longer-term inflation expectations remaining relatively anchored, particularly in the US. By contrast, European and UK inflation swap rates have repriced more sharply, reflecting their sensitivity to regional natural gas prices (TTF +55% over one week), which have been affected by the Qatari LNG production halt, low regional storage levels (30% versus 40% a year ago), and limited supply alternatives. Rising inflation expectations have also been accompanied by concerns around a growth shock, given the historical link between supply-side energy shocks and demand destruction. records.text: M Idea 2 February CPI - 1Q strength continues We expect core CPI to rise 0.27% m/m, a mild deceleration relative to January but still a pace that is not consistent with 2% inflation. We anticipate that core services inflation will soften relative to January, mainly because airfares and health services—both of which posted strong readings in the prior print—are likely to decelerate. Core goods inflation should remain close to 0%, reflecting continued softness in used vehicle prices, although tariff pass-through is still evident in other goods categories. Our forecast is slightly above consensus, which currently stands at 0.25% (average). We view an unrounded print of 0.3% as more likely than 0.2%, given signs of greater seasonal acceleration in February, even if it is less pronounced than last month. Any January price resets should show up in February for cities surveyed on a bimonthly basis, where prices are effectively compared between February and December. In addition, recent changes to seasonal factors suggest a potential upward bias of around 2bp in February. Finally, looking at post-COVID data, both January and February tend to record m/m core CPI readings above the annual monthly average. We believe a 10% rise in oil prices would lead to a 0.5-1.0% rise in the USD. Among the G10 currencies, while the AUD is likely to benefit from improved terms of trade, oil-importer currencies such as the EUR, GBP and JPY are likely to remain vulnerable (see Looking beyond Middle East uncertainties, 4 March, for details). While the pace of JPY depreciation may slow in the short term due to concerns about FX intervention, the longer-term outlook will depend on BoJ policy. records.text: In focus Leonardo Crimella, Barclays, UK | Sheryl Dong, Barclays, UK | Erick Martinez, BCI, US | Audrey Ong, Barclays Bank, Singapore | Lhamsuren Sharavdemberel, BSJL, Japan | Lemon Zhang, Barclays Bank, Singapore USD Elevated energy prices a tailwind for the dollar The escalation in the Middle East has benefited the dollar via higher energy prices, in line with our estimates for a 0.5-1.0% boost for every 10% increase in oil, and elevated risk aversion. This, in our view, is likely to remain the dominant factor for price action in the weeks to come, pending the emergence of a path towards a more-stable geopolitical equilibrium. US data developments are playing second fiddle in this environment and this applies to last week's weak NFP report too. It also bears noting that the details of the report appear somewhat inconsistent with the totality of recent and broadly resilient US data, thereby casting doubt on its signaling value. In any event, the lesson from the Ukraine war episode is that competitiveness considerations dominate relative shifts in variables such as rate differentials in the context of a global energy shock, which ends up benefiting exporters versus importers. This entails a more-resilient near-term outlook for the dollar for as long as oil and gas prices remain elevated. Notably, after the attack on Iran last weekend, the ECB OIS curve went from reflecting some probability of cuts to hikes (previ- ously about 10bp of cuts priced in by end-26 vs. around 27bp of hikes currently). Markets have shifted to price only 11bp BoE cuts this year (vs. ~55bp priced in previously) and around 37bp cumulative easing for the Fed (vs. ~43bp before the weekend strikes). Such a hawkish market reaction suggests that rate markets have assigned more weight to the risk of a significant inflation shock that prompts less easing or tighter central bank policy, rather than to the potential growth hit due to supply chain disruptions and overall weaker global business sentiment. Although our US economics team sees the overall slowing in total labor demand last year as predominantly a cyclical response to depressed business confidence, the proliferation of increasingly adept AI tools and their potential impacts on labor markets are important to monitor, even if difficult to predict. An IMF study suggests US women are relatively more exposed to AI than men—given their higher reliance on AI-exposed office and other service work over manual labor occupations—creating greater opportunities for complementarity but also displacement, particularly in clerical jobs. A study from Brookings similarly found that women make up a greater share of workers who have limited capacity to adapt if AI displacement occurs, again primarily concentrated in clerical and administrative roles. In fact, SMid stands to benefit from AI… perhaps more than Large-Caps from here on. It is true that Large-Cap tech has beaten Small-Cap tech since 1995 through the e-commerce and now the AI era (we take 1995 as the start given that is when eBay and Amazon IPOed), but: A) Even then, the S&P 400 beat the S&P 500 over the same timeframe, with the S&P 600 matching its perf; B) US Large-Caps have already rallied strongly on the back of AI, which means the yearly CAGR of the index should decelerate from here if only because of the rule of numbers; C) AI should be able to reduce labour intensity in many industries, thus having a larger impact on the P&L of SMids which are far more labour intensive; and D) all of it while large-caps have benefited from strong structural tailwinds over the last 25 yrs that might not be there going forward: i) globalization, ii) the birth of China as a new mkt and an affordable manufacturing hub, iii) the birth and grw of big tech to be 33% of the S&P 500, and iv) a structural decline in interest rates that benefited the more leveraged balance sheets of Large-Caps. But a March cut would be in doubt, if energy price moves don’t reverse by then. • If these moves reverse within a few months, we would still expect two cuts this year, even if there is a delay. If moves are sustained for longer or become larger, it can add to doubts on whether BoE can cut twice this year but may mean deeper cuts next year. • The bar for a hike is still likely to be high. If we see a scenario where inflation rises above current levels and is stuck above 3% through this/next year, this can increase de-anchoring risks and open the door to hikes. These historical sensitives aside, we believe there are four fundamental dissimilarities for the EM inflation cycle compared with 2022 (which, as discussed above, appears the most apt comparison to the potential supply shock at hand today) that we would anticipate resulting in lower pass-through in this environment. These include (1) Central banks are no longer emerging from an ultra-low interest rate environment. (2) Goods price pressures appear more muted, with China no longer under lockdown. (3) pandemic-related pent up demand that exacerbated inflationary pressures in 2022 appear much less relevant today; in other words, demand-destruction could kick in faster than in 2022 (4) The 2022 Russia supply disruption likely had stronger pass-through to consumers owing to its persistence - our analysts do not expect that to be the case this time as seen in UBS' oil forecasts. A more transitory supply shock may disincentivise governments from passing on costs. As such, we believe the current supply disruptions, if sustained, may be better thought off as a growth shock than a purely inflation shock. Wait, what's oil got to do with correlations? As we've pointed out over the past few years, the 'classic' negative correlation between stock and bond returns is underpinned by the 'traditional' relationship of growth and inflation travelling in the same direction: stocks offset losses in bonds as growth rises alongside inflation, and vice versa. records.text: CLP: Inflation eased further in February, helped by lower electricity tariffs and continued disinflation in non-tradables following the appreciation of the CLP in past months. However, the print is backward-looking, with markets now focused on the recent rise in oil prices. Chile is particularly exposed to this shock: it is one of the largest net oil importers in EM, energy carries a relatively high weight in the CPI basket (Figure 6), and pass-through to inflation tends to be faster than in peers. The hit to terms of trade would also warrant some reversal of the recent CLP strength. This combination helps explain the spike in breakevens and argues for a more- cautious stance from the BCCh. We expect the CLP to underperform if the oil price shock becomes persistent. PEN: Peru is facing a severe natural gas disruption, following a leak in a key pipeline that has halted shipments in the southern Cusco region, which effectively supplies the bulk of the country’s natural gas. The shock comes on top of other factors set to push inflation higher in March, including rising global oil prices (Peru is a net energy importer, Figure 6) and the impact of El Niño. Together, these factors are likely to push the March CPI higher and place upward pressure on Soberanos’ yields. In addition, the approaching election could further weigh on rates, as our analysis suggests. Against this backdrop, the BCRP is likely to strike a more- cautious tone at its decision on Thursday. records.text: Asia Economic Weekly | 06 March 2026 3 Asia in Focus Helen Qiao Merrill Lynch (Hong Kong) Ting Him Ho, CFA Merrill Lynch (Hong Kong) Kai Wei Ang Merrill Lynch (Singapore) See report: Asia Viewpoint: Assessing the Iran conflict impact on Asia through oil and trade shocks Asia to feel the brunt from Iran conflict We expect the US-Israel military operation in Iran to leave a meaningful and long-lasting impact on global geopolitics. In our view, the impact on Asia will be mostly felt through the disruptions of oil and trade channels with heterogenous impact across different countries, in addition to risks from financial condition tightening and remittance declines. The trauma could potentially become even greater, if the conflicts last longer with widespread supply disruptions, in our view. Magnitude and duration of the oil shock holds the key Depending on the state of the Hormuz Strait, regional energy infrastructure, and Iranian oil production and export, oil prices could potentially see a much greater jump ranging between $40-100/bbl without an immediate normalization. If the oil shock turns out to be more than a transitory change, with oil prices plateauing at a much higher level for longer, most Asian economies will likely witness downward pressure on growth through terms of trade losses, along with higher inflation. records.text: India may only hold 5-6 days of LNG inventory. LNG importers have already started to cut supply to industrial customers in anticipation of shortages. Japan's Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry (METI) has stated that LNG inventory is equal to around 12 days of domestic use for the week that ended on March 1. In Korea, the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Resources noted that Korea maintains strategic reserves equivalent to 208 days of crude oil demand and 52 days of LNG demand, with inventories exceeding mandatory stockpiling requirements. In Taiwan, the Ministry of Economic Affairs announced that Taiwan has at least 11 days of LNG supply, and has secured sufficient natural gas supplies for March (including supplies already on the way). If the situation prolongs through April, policymakers would: (1) Increase purchases from non-Middle Eastern sources, such as the US and Australia; (2) Buy from other Asian importers, such as Japan and Korea; (3) Utilize coal-fired power generation as a last resort. In Thailand, policy makers are already trying to diversify their purchases in the spot LNG market and are looking to procure supplies from the US and Malaysia and are adjusting their procurement plans, though they have also warned of potential intensifying competition for LNG outside of the Middle East, which may result in price spikes and potential shortages.

records.text: 6 March 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Deutsche Bank AG Page 41 Swap spreads and geopolitics Today’s FICOTD examines the impact of geopolitical shocks on German swap spreads. We utilise the geopolitical risk index which has moved significantly in recent days. The chart shows daily changes in the index versus daily changes in swap spreads – using 10Y spline yields vs 6s swaps to obtain a longer history (the results are similar for 10Y or 2Y spreads versus €STR since 2007). While the Russian invasion of Ukraine and 9/11 are associated with wider swap spreads (bond outperformance), more broadly, there is no clear impact on spreads during major shocks. Assessing spread performance two days around the event leads to a similar conclusion. This suggests there isn’t a typical knee-jerk response spread widening to headlines as widely perceived. The sample of events associated with (immediate) energy shocks is fairly limited; viewed through this lens, the spread move this time appears more contained, though this reflects broader conditions as well. Using our framework of assessing DU-€STR spreads versus a risk metric (credit or the ECB’s composite stress indicator) and funding conditions suggests spreads should have widened a couple of bps, versus being largely unchanged at the time of writing. records.text: 6 Insights Information Classification: General Appendix Note on Percentiles We use percentiles to gauge the significance of a flow or positioning metric over a variety of time periods and countries. Th e percentiles have the advantage of making no assumptions about the shape of the distribution of the indicators, such as normality. Our use is aimed at being a simple way of ranking flow and positioning indicators relative to their own history. For all of the flow indicators within the Investment Climate, we calculate the percentiles based on the distribution of flows over the last five years using the daily aggregate time periods shown in the tables. Before calculating the percentiles, we constrain the 50 th percentile as equivalent to neutral. Flows above the 50 th percentile, therefore, are all positive and those below the 50th all represent selling of the market in question. A 100th percentile reading represents the strongest buying in five years; and a zero percentile equals the strongest selling. A reading in the 50th percentile would signal that net flows in the asset over the period are at zero. We use a simple colour coding scheme to highlight strong (top 20 th percentile) and weak (bottom 20th percentile) flows. We percentile our FX Holdings indicators in the same, conditional fashion, using the same five-year look-back period, as FX flows. The Stanford Social Innovation Review (SSRI) reports that a sizable AI adoption gender gap has opened: about 50% of men vs. 37% of women reported using generative AI in the prior 12 months. A similar gap appears among weekly users, implying unequal access to productivity gains. The gap is not explained by income, education, age, or race. Self-assessed knowledge explains most of it (~75%), while privacy/trust concerns and perceived job risks reflect “fierce ambivalence” and account for much of the remainder. A Harvard Business School meta-analysis of 18 separate studies covering 143,008 individuals across 25 countries found women had 22% lower odds of using generative AI than men. A Deloitte study found that AI adoption declines with age, and the gender gap is most pronounced in the 45+ group. Recent Pew research shows that women predict AI will do more harm across personal, professional, and public life than benefits. Unequal AI adoption risks widening existing gaps (e.g., men’s research productivity rose 6.4% more than women’s after ChatGPT’s release). records.text: Second part of report title FOCUS F O CU S 1 Oil disruptions: Further upside unless Hormuz flows resume Circuit breakers in oil markets: While disruptions last, much attention will be paid to how much oil there is to replace the 15 million barrels per day (mbd) of disrupted crude in the Strait of Hormuz. We don’t see much of a buffer for LNG, and no diversion options for Qatari LNG flows, which is why we see more breakout potential in gas markets. As we wrote in Crude reality (4) on 4 March, we see several circuit breakers that could help moderate aggressive price spikes. The price-dampening impact of those depends critically on how much of an offset we can expect from each and by when. Given ongoing retaliatory attacks, we also gauge the disruption risk of each. We identify five circuit breakers in oil markets: strategic petroleum reserves; diversion pipeline in Saudi Arabia and the UAE; OPEC+ supply increases; Chinese crude stocks; and floating oil cargoes outside the Middle East. Figure 1 on page 3 summarizes our assessment. Strategic petroleum reserves: We anticipate the largest potential impact from SPRs around the world. Compared with the 15mbd shortfall from a closed Hormuz, member countries of the International Energy Agency hold about 1.1bn bbl of strategic stocks. The US is a member and holds about 370mn bbl. In IG, cyclicals were a slight outperformer, while quality underperformed, which was atypical of a spread-widening environment. HY performance was the opposite, with cyclicals underperforming and quality outperforming significantly, while carry also underperformed (Figure 2). The performance of the HY factors was largely consistent with what we would expect when spreads are moving wider. While spread performance over the first few days of March has been more constructive, we see reasons to be cautious. Markets have seemingly shrugged off concerns about the Iran conflict, but the length and eventual resolution remain highly uncertain. BDCs have also rallied off the wides, but we think concerns about private credit performance and the potential effect on other segments of the market with exposure are likely to persist. At the same time, valuations, despite the recent widening, remain compressed for most parts of credit (Figure 3), which we think makes positioning defensively prudent in the near term. In a historical context, March has been one of the weaker months for investment grade excess returns, with a median return of -0.1% since 2000 (ex-2020) (Figure 4) and positive returns only 46% of the time. Slowing real income growth and small fall in savings Monetary easing and falls in interest rates can continue to reduce the motivation to pay down debt, hold savings and make it cheaper to borrow, causing a small decline in savings rate in 2026. While the decline in inflation and rate cuts should act as tailwinds, real income growth is likely to slow amid softening wage growth and looser labour market. At the same time, the recent rise in energy prices, if sustained, may slow the path of disinflation and rate cuts. Moreover, the number of fixed rate households potentially facing higher mortgage payments is expected to rise again and mortgage interest payments as a share of income is likely to rise marginally, providing a marginal drag to consumption. Four downside risks to consumption But risks to consumption are tilted to the downside. We highlight four key downside risks to consumption 1) The recent rise in energy prices, if sustained, can slow the path of disinflation and rate cuts and weigh on real incomes and consumption 2) The pickup in number of households facing higher mortgage rates can cause savings rate to rise again 3) Bigger weakness in the labour market or higher uncertainty can weigh on real incomes and keep precautionary savings elevated. Our scenarios above should be fairly clear: the more persistent the energy price move, the more adverse the economic outcome. But where does all of that leave the ECB? To our mind, the ECB’s sensitivity to energy price shocks of this type is probably higher than normal after the very large and persistent energy price shock from 2022. The central bank probably doesn’t want to be “too late” again (a view we didn’t share into the last hiking cycle) and, as a consequence, could be even less forward looking over the next few months. So even if we expect a non-committal stance in March (the proper preview for that meeting will come next week), and a reiteration of “wait and see”, markets have started to move in the direction of hikes. We are less convinced of hikes per se and even of the timeline the market seems to have in mind. So here are a few points we want to emphasise: 1) In our scenarios 1 and 2 of a normalisation in energy prices by the June meeting, we would expect the central bank to look through the energy price shock. To us this remains the most likely outcome. We would still expect cuts to come in 2027. But while we argued until last week that we could see cuts as early as Sep-26, that risk balance has shifted. Morgan Securities LLC Steven Palacio(1-212) 834-5031 steven.palacio@jpmorgan.com Armstrong Mbi(212) 622-5896 armstrong.mbi@jpmchase.com Industry & Policy Thematics FDI: Shifting from outsourcing to securing supply chains 06 March 2026 J P M O R G A N Africa - Resisting China’s dominance Over the past 20 years, both the US and China have been highly active in Africa, but their strategies are increasingly converging. China, which initially prioritized large-scale loans for infrastructure and energy projects under the BRI, is now shifting toward direct FDI in response to criticism over “predatory loans” and mounting debt problems in recipient countries. Meanwhile, the US is moving away from its traditional focus on humanitarian aid, having provided US$326 billion in assistance from 2010 to 2024, and is adopting a more strategic investment approach. This new US strategy emphasizes trade, investment, and security cooperation, with a focus on fast-growing sectors such as communications, renewable energy, and critical minerals, as demonstrated by initiatives like the Minerals Security Partnership and the Lobito Corridor. Despite these changes, the US still trails China in Africa, particularly in terms of FDI. It prompted us to launch coverage of European SMid-Caps with an UW rating in July of 2007, upgrading to a Neutral stance in Nov of 2008 and again to OW in Feb of 2009, a rating we maintained through to the start of 2016 when we went back to Neutral, arguing that 2016 would be a range-bound year for SMid-Caps, with clear pockets of opportunity (oil, Brazil, Russia). We turned bullish again in 2017, as we saw upside risk for investors with clear pockets of alpha (Periphery being one). But our bullishness was short-lived and it gave way to the more cautious stance we maintained from the start of 2018 and until Mar 17th, 2020. During this time, our SMid strategy framework showed upside being limited for the remainder of the cycle, with no shortage of downside risk and volatility, in what were clearly the late stages of a bull market. This contrarian cautious stance played out, as SMid indices stayed flattish during 2018-2019 (with 2/3rds of SMids actually falling during that time), before COVID-19 took the broad market down 40% in Feb-Mar of 2020. A sustained $10/bbl increase in oil prices would reduce GDP by around 15bp and lift inflation by 40bp. A sustained €10/MWh shock to gas prices would be additive to the oil shock, take GDP down by a further 10bp and increase inflation by an extra 30bp. Around half of this impact would come already within 2 months from the shock through higher energy prices, the remaining effects would be spread over several quarters through both direct energy prices and indirect cost pass through (see here for the detailed inflation profiles flowing out of each scenario). What matters for inflation and growth is not only how high commodity prices can go but also for how long they stay at these levels. A quick de-escalation would have a very limited impact on growth. One or two months of impaired traffic could mechanically reduce growth by as much as 70bp. In the most extreme scenario, the euro area economy could be flirting with recession in 2026. One might wonder whether expecting such a big hit to growth could be too pessimistic. After all, the shock in gas and oil prices of 2022 was much larger than now, and yet the euro area economy did not fall into recession, with the lowest growth rate recorded in 2023 at 0.22%Y. records.text: ab 6 March 2026 Global Research Global Strategy Stagflation vs. Disruption: is it time to revisit the stagflationary playbook in credit? Exec Summary: In the wake of recent escalations in Iran, client discussions have highlighted renewed concerns around the risk of a stagflationary shock, particularly if energy prices rise further due to additional damage to infrastructure or prolonged shipping and logistics disruptions through the Strait of Hormuz. While a swift resolution remains plausible and a stagflationary outcome could be avoided, elevated geopolitical risk in recent months has increased the likelihood of higher energy risk premia and the risk of stagflation, even if the US–Iran conflict is ultimately resolved. Revisiting our prior work on sectoral leadership during stagflationary periods, we find that IG Consumer Non-Cyclicals and Telecoms tend to ourperform and that previous periods have favored moving up in quality and front-end positioning in HY. Although we believe that positioning for stagflation would be premature, the potential for Telecom and Consumer Non-Cyclical outperformance in such a scenario reinforces our existing longs in these sectors in Europe. We also identify some irregularities in sectoral leadership following this conflict relative to other supply-side energy shocks, most notably that EU IG Healthcare and US IG Energy have seen net-widening vs. the index rather than the net-tightening that other historical precedents would suggest. If energy prices stay relatively close to current levels, we would still see the ECB as quite firmly on hold, especially because the supply shock on energy also implies some hit to growth. The duration and depth of the energy price shock therefore will deter- mine the inflation and growth/sentiment impact on the Euro area which in turn will drive the ECB reaction. Our conviction in rate cuts below 2% in 2027 due to an inflation undershoot remains unbroken, however. The economy is not in great shape, and even a short-lived energy price shock risks leaving some scars on GDP levels. Though not our base case, the cumulation of shocks also starts to increase our concerns around non-linear effects, something the ECB dubbed “latent risk of rolling recessions”. The risk balance to our current base case of cuts in Mar/Jun-27 has moved from earlier to tentatively later cuts below 2%. But even if the ECB hikes in the summer, our conviction in the policy rate being at most at current levels, and more likely below 2%, by end-27 remains unbroken. Three scenarios to show persistence may matter more than magnitude As a reminder, our current base has growth at 1.2% this year and 1.3% next, with headline inflation at 1.7% in both, and ECB cuts in March and June 2027 (25bp each) on a permanent inflation undershoot. This base case was built on oil prices at c USD 70/barrel in February and March and close to USD 65 for the rest of the forecast horizon. Morgan Under the OBBBA, we expect a modest year-over-year increase in filers subject to the AMT and an eventual uptick in supply. This section provides an in-depth analysis of the implications of the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act” (OBBBA) for Alternative Minimum Tax (AMT) filers and AMT bonds within the municipal bond market. Our assessment indicates that the total number of AMT filers is expected to increase only marginally compared to levels observed under the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA). Consequently, the primary investor base for AMT bonds is likely to remain concentrated within the fund community, suggesting that spreads will continue to be driven predominantly by fund flows. Additionally, we highlight the potential for a significant increase in AMT bond issuance related to spaceport projects in the coming years. Much of the expected supply will be high-yield private-public sector partnership bonds. Recall, the OBBBA authorized tax- exempt PABs for ‘spaceport’ projects, similarly to the airport sector. Importantly, unlike other PABs, spaceport bonds are not subject to a statutory limit, encouraging large-scale private investment. Additionally, the bill allows these bonds to finance manufacturing and maintenance of facilities for spacecraft and components, which is typically not allowed in other public infrastructure projects. records.text: Japan Rates Weekly 06 March 2026 Citi Research 3 No decline in yen interest rates despite risk-off sentiment Sentiment is now risk-off due to the Middle East situation, but upside remains hard to come by for the bond market. Interest rates have risen across maturities compared with the end of last week, and this could be seen as being more impacted by the index extension at the end of last month. That the rise in crude prices means the environment is not purely risk-off is also having an effect. The key will be how long the turmoil lasts, and the market is probably not simply waiting for the end of the conflict. The keys will be the normalization of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and the stabilization of energy prices. Normally, the impact on the market of geopolitical risks ends after a short period, although near-term volatility is possible. In this environment, eurozone markets are pricing in rate hikes while the pricing of rate cuts has receded in the US markets are clearly conscious of inflation risk, even if it derives from cost-push factors. Yield curves are flattening. There has been steepening at times in the JGB curve, but it has flattened at longer than 5y to maturity. We think the impact of overseas markets has been larger than that of domestic factors. On the JGB curve the 15y sector is weak. In addition to selling to adjust positions at the end of the fiscal year, this could also be seen as correcting the outperformance against the 10y sector in February.

We had been raising stops meaningfully into positive territory in recent weeks to short-circuit any blow-ups, and we have accordingly been tactically neutralized on CAD positions. If the Iran conflict cools and oil risk premium recedes, we’ll likely turn short-CAD again. If the conflict persists, USD remains bid and oil encroaches $100, CAD can con- tinue outperforming. Investors turned to Gold and the US dollar, as government bonds, typically a haven in uncertain markets, weakened as markets baked in additional inflation risk premia into front end rates. Yields on bunds and gilts rose 0.08 and 0.11 percentage points respectively as bonds failed to provide protection against risk off events. Reduced probability of interest rate cuts seen in swap markets show that 50bps of BoE cuts are no longer priced by the end of 2026 , following European gas prices surging more than 30%. Volume: Elevated volatility last week drove a rally in DM and EM FX volumes. On aggregate, EM volumes are at the highest weekly levels in the past year, with DM activity lifting into the top decile. Volume data from July 2020 onwards represents the combined total traded volume across EBS and Reuters sources. To estimate average trade size prior to July 2020 we use all future data for total trading volume and trade count. We then apply a 20-day moving average and rank the current value over the prior one-year lookback window**. Bias by design: AI systems amplify gender biases AI systems can amplify gender biases, portraying women, especially in higher‑status roles, as younger and less experienced and tilting resume screening toward older men at the expense of older women. AI often reinforces gender and age- based stereotypes, depicting women, especially in higher status roles, as younger and less experienced, impacting hiring, evaluation, and promotion of women in the workplace. Research finds that stereotypes about older women are widespread in online images and videos, and that large language models carry and even intensify these biases. By analyzing over 1.4mn images and videos across online platforms, as well as billions of text from the web in 9 language models, researchers found that women are consistently portrayed as younger than men, especially in depictions of higher-status and better-paid occupations. When prompting ChatGPT to generate over 34,500 unique resumes for 54 occupations using typical male or female names, it generated results that portrayed women as younger and less experienced, assigning older male applicants with a higher quality (Figure 33W o m e n a r e r e p r e s e n t e d a s s i g n i f i c a n t l y y o u n g e r t h a n m e n i n b i l l i o n s o f w o r d s s c r a p e d f r o m t h e i n t e r n e t , a s e n c o d e d b y C h a t G P T ). The Hormuz Conundrum As we write this, Brent has exceeded $90/barrel, up some 35% from the average over the last year and nearly 50% from the lows at the start of the year. As we discussed in a note this week, each 10% increase in oil prices relative to recent averages should add about 15bp to headline CPI and could take off 15-20bp from growth, were the price increase to be sus- tained for some time. Given the state of the energy futures curve, we have only added a tenth of a percent to Q4/Q4 CPI, relative to our forecast on Friday, as futures markets do not see the price spike continuing for very long. The risk remains for a much larger and more sustained increase in oil prices should disrup- tions to supply persist. In that case, while the economic impact would appear stagflationary, we would expect the Fed to focus on the hit to activity. Most estimates find little spillover of higher energy prices into core inflation, whereas a sharp reduction in aggregate demand as consumers’ purchasing power plunged would likely impart downward pressure on core prices. 24 06 March 2026 Incentives like cash payments and tax breaks can bring births forward by a year or two, but they rarely lead to increases in family size. New research by Cevat Giray Aksoy at the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development shows that remote work would positively boost fertility. In many high-income countries, roughly one- quarter of paid workdays are now completed at home, up from around 3-5% before 2020. In the 38-country sample, estimated lifetime fertility when both partners work from home at least one day a week is about 0.32 children higher (roughly 14%) than for couples where neither does. In the US, the corresponding gap is 0.45 children, or about 18%. Their estimates imply that current work-from-home arrangements account for just over 8% of US births (around 291,000 babies per year). They also suggest that fertility rates in countries such as Japan, South Korea, France, Germany, and Italy could rise by 2-5% if their remote-work levels were on par with those in the US, the United Kingdom, and Canada.12 Turning to policies that are most effective at supporting women in the workplace, the heavier burden from unpaid family care work, especially childcare, is one globally common factor holding females back from active labor participation (see J.P . records.text: Outlook for the economy and prices (last updated 20 February) Real GDP growth rebounded in Q4 after a Q3 contraction driven by temporary factors, but sharply undershot market expectations. That said, the drag came largely from volatile components such as inventories and public investment; excluding these, growth would have been slightly more than 1%. Moreover, recent data such as real exports and machinery orders have been notably strong, so we are not particularly concerned. Looking ahead, we expect growth of around 1% on average due primarily to firm capital investment on the back of structural factors such as labor-saving expenditures and stable consumption stemming from a recovery in the real income environment under slowing inflation. Although the economic measures decided by the Takaichi administration are limited in terms of their growth-boosting effect relative to scale, they are likely to provide a certain degree of support to the economy. On the price front, we expect CPI inflation excluding perishables (core) to ease as a trend, albeit with fluctuations, in the near term due mainly to declines (y/y base effects) in goods, especially food. However, inflation is increasingly sticky, suggesting any deceleration will be more moderate than we previously expected. Furthermore, services inflation has become increasingly robust as the dynamic synergy between wages and prices strengthens on the back of irreversible structural changes in the labor market. records.text: M Global Foundation 18 At the product level, goods are defined within the context of the producing industry. For example, motor vehicle parts are classified within the motor vehicle manufacturing industry grouping, even if similar components may be traded under multiple HS headings depending on material composition or use. The key distinction relative to HS is methodological: • HS classifies goods by what they are (material composition and physical attributes). • NAICS product classification groups goods by who produces them (production process and industry of origin). For equity and macro analysts, mapping HS codes to NAICS industries enables translation of product-level trade exposure into industry-level revenue, margin, and value-added sensitivities. Structure of Tariff-Related Data Tariff Exposure Metrics Across the tables in this interactive, tariff exposure is calculated using value-based US import data. First, the share of goods exposed to tariffs is estimated as the dutiable value of imports divided by total trade (measured using Customs value) with a given country. This indicates the proportion of bilateral imports that are subject to duty. Second, the average tariff on dutiable goods is calculated as calculated duty divided by dutiable value. This reflects the average statutory tariff rate applied only to goods that are subject to duty. Because the denominator excludes duty-free trade, this measure does not account for the share of imports entering without tariffs.

Agreement between State Street’s Foreign Exchange Holding Indicator (FXHI) and Foreign Exchange Hedge Ratio Indicator (FXHRI) enhances a positioning-driven view for developed market currencies. Because the impact of flows on future returns also depends on the positions of institutions in that currency, the FXHRI is, with the FXHI, designed to quantify and measure empirically this aspect of investor behaviour. The indicator is updated on a daily basis with a two -day publication lag. We publish foreign currency hedge ratios against multi-asset portfolios and are able to disaggregate this multi -asset hedge ratio into hedges against equity assets and fixed income assets. FX Behavioural Factor Flows and Factor Holdings measure real-money demand for and positioning in FX factors. At a high level, the indicators reveal whether real -money investors are leaning into or leaning out of a given FX factor (e.g. carry, value, momentum). The indicators aggregate single currency indicators, including the Foreign Exchange Flow Indicator (FXFI) and Foreign Exchange Holdings Indicator (FXHI), into broader factor aggregates. The indicators cover seven regions: Global, Global ex-pegs, Global ex-USD, G10, G10 ex- USD, Emerging Markets, and Emerging Markets ex-pegs. records.text: asing The moves – if sustained – could have implications for our outlook for the US economy and monetary policy in 2026. We find that a 10% increase in oil prices coming from a negative supply shock adds 35bp to headline CPI for 3 months, but just 3bp to core CPI (for our prior work on the subject, see here and here). Movements in oil prices translate quickly into higher prices at the pump for US consumers; they also downstream quickly into diesel and other refined products. Higher energy prices must be sustained for some time to have a greater, more durable effect on core prices. Oil has transitory effects on US headline inflation, allowing the Fed to "look through"... On the one hand, a supply-side driven energy price move that pushes headline inflation higher while leaving underlying core inflation unchanged is good news for the Fed since, like tariffs, it means a one-off increase in oil prices does not put permanent upward pressure on inflation. Unlike tariffs, the speed of transmission to headline inflation is fast, with the peak effect on mont-on-month rates of inflation reached about three months after the initial spike in oil prices. In contrast, we anticipate tariff pass-through to end about a year after tariffs were implemented. records.text: US Rates Weekly 06 March 2026 Citi Research 8 Short-end: Still like April SOFR/FF This week, the SOFR/FF strip has cheapened as a geopolitics-driven VaR shock has rippled through markets. In Figure 12, we show how the April SOFR/FF contract has broadly followed the tightening in 5y swap spreads driven by the VaR shock over the past week. Despite the move, we still like our long April SOFR/FF as a ‘cheap’ option in case liquidity moves into abundance in the first half of April (-3.5bp as of 2:00pm on 3/6/26, see US Rates Weekly - Renewed appeal as risk-off hedge). In other words, we see an asymmetric risk/reward in SERFFJ6 as the market is, in our view, underappreciating the risk of reserves moving higher in the first two weeks of April. The redemption of funds supplied under lending support operations is one reason for the decline in NSFRs. The weighting for inclusion in ASF is 100% for 1y and longer, 50% for less than 1y, and 0% for less than 6m. However, borrowings by the big banks were ¥13.8trn as of December last year, so they represented a modest part of the ¥53.5trn total. We think the breakdown by maturity is on the long side, and operation usage since the term became 1y has been limited. A look at factors driving quarterly change in NSFRs indicates that the impact of growth in RSF has been large, so the issue is on the asset side. ASF changes have in fact been contributing to an increase in NSFRs. This is despite the repayment of funding raised via lending support operations, and we think that banks may have increased liability raising. Yen weakness is also negative for NSFRs, because most deposits are denominated in yen. In the future, RSF is likely to grow because of the $550bn US investment scheme. The risk weighting will be lower if government guarantees are provided via NEXI, but even if the assets are unencumbered, 65% will add to growth in RSF. It is well known that Smaller-Caps are more domestic than Large-Caps when it comes to their revenue exposure and, thus, should be better shielded from any disruption in global trade. However, since most companies don’t disclose the regional source of their purchases, there is some confusion about their exposure to tariffs. We opted to run a correlation between the gross margin of different market cap indices in the US and the US$ in order to assess whether SMid is more or less exposed to imports than Large-Caps are. In theory, the more exposed to imports relative to exports a company is, the higher the correlation between its gross margin and the US$ should be. As one can see in the chart below, the S&P 500 equal weighted has the highest correlation of any index, with the S&P 400’s correlation against the US$ being much weaker and the Russell 2000’s weaker still. This would suggest, as we always thought was the case, that Smaller-Caps are more shielded from tariffs as they are more domestic in their purchases. Passthrough to core inflation may become a little bit more tangible then, introducing more stickiness into early 2027 on that metric, too. Growth would take a bigger hit. We could see 2026 growth at 0.8% on average, with 2027 at 1.3%. End-point GDP levels would be c 0.5% lower than in our current base case. 1H26 growth could be close to 0, perhaps 2Q26 could even see a quarter of contraction. The bounce-back thereafter could be more partial – energy prices are the Achilles’ heel to confidence since the energy crisis. We wouldn’t rule out a stronger than usual response from households and corporates to even a short lived energy spike. This would intensify downward pressure on underlying inflation, eventually. Scenario 3: 4 months of high energy prices Under the assumption of 4 months with Brent at USD 80 and TTF at 50, we would see inflation at 2.2% this year and 1.4% next. The peak would remain around 2.5% near term, but 2Q average inflation would be close to 2.5%. Second-round effects into core would likely be bigger than under scenario 1, too. records.text: M Update Morgan Stanley Research 3 Weak private payrolls, a slightly higher unemployment rate Payrolls fell 92k in Feb (MS estimate +25k, consensus +55k), with net revisions of -69k. The slowdown was partly one-offs—weather probably subtracted perhaps 30k, strike subtracted 30k, and payback for a strong Jan was worth another -40k. These won’t repeat. But there was some breadth to the slowdown across other industries, plus the unemployment rate rose 0.1 to 4.4% vs our forecast for no change. On net, private payrolls are now rising at the same pace so far in 1Q as in 4Q, rather than accelerating. That pace is slow enough to continue to put gradual upward pressure on the unemployment rate. The January employment report had suggested a decisive reacceleration in labor demand across 4Q and into 1Q. But with February weakness, there's still a hint of ongoing slackening—even if not as rapid as last summer. Some on the FOMC will continue to tilt toward cutting rates because of labor market slackening. We continue to expect 25 bp cuts in June and September. Oil price pressures risk delaying those cuts. Payrolls and earnings Despite the February slowdown, 1Q-to-date aggregate hours worked are up 1.3% at an annual rate from 4Q—vs a 0.5% pace in 2025. They did however fall 0.2% m/m, underlining the February deceleration. In particular, under the current situation where underlying inflation is approaching 2%, unless the policy rate is raised in response to rising inflationary pressure, the inflation rate could very well overshoot 2% (Exhibit 4). In that case, the yen could depreciate further from the perspective of purchasing power parity, potentially increasing inflationary pressure even more. The government has continued with expansionary fiscal policies (Exhibit 5). Particularly during the deflationary period, a lack of effective demand and continued low interest rates meant that an increase in government spending did not cause the crowding out of private investment. However, the current phase is one where crowding out would likely occur due to supply constraints and rising interest rates. For this reason, an increase in fiscal spending to stimulate effective demand would also carry the risk of crowding out high-value-added private-sector investment, which could, in turn, lower the potential growth rate.2 2 In this case, in addition to the increase in fiscal spending, interest payments on higher-coupon JGBs issued during a phase of accelerated rate hikes to address rising inflationary pressure would continue into the future. Historically, there tends to be volatility on the day or week of the start of geopolitical risk events (see Appendix: Market Performance Around Geopolitical Events ) but fundamentals tend to reassert themselves over the medium to long run, and there's no clear pattern on asset-class performance coming out of these episodes. The main exception is Brent, where fundamentals can be driven by geopolitical events via impacts on demand-supply imbalances, which in turn have knock- on effects on macro, which in turn have knock-on effects on asset class returns, which in turn have knock-on implications for multi-asset allocation. Below, we lay out probable scenarios for the conflict in Iran from our US Public Policy team, based on how our oil strategist sees the skew of risks. So the Sell America and rotation toward RoW equity markets has paused given the lower sensitivity of US assets to energy costs. In fact, S&P500 is barely down on the week and Vix hasn't spiked much, showing little concerns about the war. Sector performance has been distinctly stagflationary in Europe, with Energy and Defensives outperforming while Banks and broader Cyclicals lagged. The conflict’s endgame remains uncertain, but we stay of the view that the Trump administration’s incentive to support the US consumer, especially ahead of the midterms, argues for a shorter lived confrontation and energy shock. This is arguably consensus, with most of our clients inclined to buy the dip and oil futures in backwardation, suggesting markets expect supply disruption to be temporary. This may prove complacent, and the longer the conflict persists, the greater stagflation risk, especially for energy dependent regions outside the US. Indeed, if oil were to rise to $100/bbl, we estimate the SXXP could retrace further toward ~550 (we added to UK as a hedge - see From greed to fear – March Chart Pack, 4 Mar). This phenomenon is material because elevated jump risk is not healthy for the provision of liquidity (as can be seen in the sharp decline in market depth), and thus liquidity conditions seem destined to remain poor for a while longer. In addition, elevated jump risk can bias implied normal basis point volatility consider- ably higher because of the nonlinear gains to long gamma positions from large jumps. This also makes carry-seeking short gamma strategies unattractive, as a single day of “jump” can erode multiple days of carry (Interest Rate Derivatives, US Fixed Income Mar- kets Weekly, 2/6/2026). To illustrate this in stylized fashion, we may imagine that each day, the market realizes either a “jump” of 8bp or a “regular sized” move of some magnitude. Figure 6 shows the magni- tude of the “regular sized” move required to break even on long gamma positions versus the assumed frequency of jumps. This figure tells us, for instance, that a 2-sigma jump probabil- ity of ~7% requires non-jump-day volatility of only 4.5 bp/day for an option trading at 5bp/ day. By contrast, under the same swap-spread model, the 30y ASW is around 3bp cheap. From a macro perspective, concerns over stagflation stemming from Middle East developments (ie, the risk of delayed BoJ rate hikes), as well as upward pressure on inflation risk premia under Takaichi's "high-pressure economy" policies and the associated potential for higher yields, remain intact. These factors are more likely to translate into steepening pressure in swaps than in JGBs. On the JGB side, issuance in the superlong sector is set to be reduced from the next fiscal year (April), while issuance in the long sector will remain unchanged. Including BoJ QT , stock-based net supply points to flattening pressure in the 10y/30y curve (Figure 9). Which countries could see currency pressure? Because government debt ultimately impacts economic growth, investor confidence, and currencies, we believe investors ought to keep an eye on government debt levels around the world. The table below shows how Debt to GDP should progress this year. As we can see, nearly 60% of the world’s GDP rests in the hands of governments that are sporting>100% Debt to GDP prints, and the majority of them are running deficits large enough to keep that metric heading north. At best, this impacts investor returns as the currencies of some of the most indebted countries lose ground against the rest (i.e. Japan since 2019, US last year, etc). At worst, this situation could result in a loss of confidence on countries running over-leveraged balance sheets, which would in turn push up their financing costs, dampening their growth outlook. Third, management from major lifers gave interviews to Reuters and Bloomberg, indicat- ing they will continue switching from low-coupon to high-coupon JGBs, using equity gains to offset realized bond losses. As we argued last week, as long as equities perform well, we anticipate continued sales flows primarily in the off-the-run JX space, regardless of the recent accounting developments (Figure 6O f f - t h e - r u n s c a m e u n d e r c h e a p e n i n g p r e s s u r e , c o n t r i b u t i n g t o t h e w e a k n e s s a t t h e b a c k e n d ). Additionally, the 15-year sector reversed about half of the richening seen last week. We believe this was driven by profit-taking from fast- money accounts and unwinding of legacy ASW exposures. Next week, JPX will release cash equity transaction data for this week, which we will monitor closely for any signs of a change in activity by lifers, banks or trust banks. Lastly, anecdotal evidence suggests that foreign flows into the super-long sector have slowed. We believe that another wave of foreign buying is likely only if yields approach local highs. While we remain constructive on SMid’s outperformance for full-year 2026, we expect moderating outperformance over March-April and likely reversal in April. • Separating the wheat from the chaff: Regulatory actions are dampening valuation premiums in thematic plays with weak revenue/earnings. On Jan 14, Chinese authorities hiked the minimum margin financing requirement from 80% to 100%, among other things. There are concerns that regulators may reinstate securities refinancing (转融券) that facilitated shorting of SMids. This tool was suspended on 11 July 2024 and contributed to SMids’ impressive outperformance since then (CSI500/1000/2000 +75%/74%/95% vs. CSI300’s 37%). • SMids’ best January outperformance (+8%) since 2016 may mean weaker returns over March-April. Challenges from private credit and AI‑related software‑company valuations have led to a broad risk‑off tone, exacer- bated by the conflict in Iran and rising commodity prices (oil/gold). Increased volatility implies nominal spreads are likely to widen. This has carried over to the non‑agency space, with non‑QM AAAs in the ~130bp context, at least 30bp wider than their tights in January. The Iran conflict is also fueling inflation fears and pressuring Treasuries, likely pushing mortgage rates back above 6%. Even so, issuance is full‑steam ahead, with large deals com- ing to market in both non‑QM and closed‑end seconds. Any widening pressure should be viewed as a technical buying opportunity in both segments. Last week, we shifted our mid- year price target for non‑QM to 115bps (up from 95bps earlier in the year). The move was driven primarily by positioning and views on the BoJ’s potential reaction function should geopolitical risks intensi- fy further. OIS pricing was stable, implying a 65% probability of a 25bp hike by the April MPM. We showed that the greater the rate dispersion for any given incen- tive bucket, the higher the at-the-money speeds and the softer the deep in-the-money speeds should be, all else equal. In that exercise, we assumed that all borrowers faced both the same average rate and the same (normal) distribution of rates around this average. When we looked at a sample of the McDash transition data connecting WACs on loans that executed rate-term refis to their new WACs, we noticed that these assumptions did not necessarily hold. Instead, we saw that higher WAC borrowers actually typically settle for worse refi rates, responding to less incentive than we had initially modeled. Though this effect is not new, it was stronger in late 2025 versus early 2021. This phenomenon, in addition to the fact that new rate dispersion for higher WAC loans was greater in late 2025 but stable in early 2021, has likely contributed to late 2025 s-curves being relatively flatter compared to early 2021. Bank of England Preview Caught between a cut and a hard place Global events leave this MPC meeting on a knife-edge. We expect the committee to deliver a 25bp cut, but if geopolitical uncertainty does not subside, or data come in hotter than we expect, then the balance could easily tip to a hold. • We expect the MPC to cut Bank Rate at its March meeting by 25bp, most likely with a 5-4 vote.• However, we think the decision is incredibly finely balanced. Although recent UK data flow has been supportive of a cut in March based on our interpretation of the MPC's position, the emerging energy price shock risks reawakening concerns within the committee that second- round effects could keep inflation sticky. • If data over the next two weeks come in line with our expectation, our confidence in a cut• being delivered would strengthen. However, if energy prices and geopolitical uncertainty stay elevated going into the week of the meeting, that would pose a material risk to our call. • Guidance is likely to be cautious and we expect the MPC to remove text that says "on the basis• of the current evidence, Bank Rate is likely to be reduced further", emphasising a meeting-by- meeting, data-driven approach. If there is no long-lasting disruption in the Strait of Hormuz, J.P. Morgan forecasts oil prices to stay elevated around $80-85/bbl before retracing down to approximately $70/bbl later in 2026. In this scenario, the energy price spike is expected to increase global CPI inflation by 1% and reduce GDP growth by 0.6% in 2026. The overall macro impact would be modest in such a scenraio and unlikely to derail the global expansion or significantly alter monetary policy paths . However, there are growing risks of more severe and persistent disruptions in the Middle East (e.g. an extended closure of the Strait of Hormuz): this would lead to larger/longer-lasting impact on energy prices (Brent price spiking above $100/bbl and TTF gas above €60-80/MWh) as well as a more substantial hit to growth owing to supply chain distruptions and weaker business sentiment. History suggests that a clear geopolitical risk pattern unfolds: risk-off immediately after, and risk-on within two weeks. That’s provided the event doesn’t disrupt the global economy with further escalation. Vol is a clearer expression of the pattern than spot equities. Drawing on our historical analysis of geopolitical risk events since the early 2000s, the initial risk-off phase is already under way, with expectations of a risk-on rally once headline shocks fade into background noise (typically after peak fear subsides and investors recognise that the impact is contained or localised). That said, the current episode may differ in magnitude given the scale and systemic nature of the actors involved. Inflation market seems to price a relatively quick resolution If inflation only reacts to persistent oil price shocks, what about inflation expectations? For the most part, while it is well known that market-based inflation measures (breakevens, inflation swaps) are sensitive to oil prices at a high frequency, rallies in the 1-year inflation swap have rarely been long-lived in response to oil prices. The main exception to this is the persistent increase in market-based inflation expectations after COVID and the war in Ukraine (Exhibit 2). Since the Iran conflict erupted last week, the 1y inflation swap jumped c 25bp, but that may be mostly attributed to the surprise in the prices paid component of the ISM survey. Overall, considering that the jump in oil prices has been contained so far, the market is still pricing a largely benign scenario with a relatively quick resolution. A little bit more explanation – clarity by June would be key Our second point above is a key one. Even if the shock was a bit more persistent (or short but larger (ie scenarios 1 and 2 in Exhibit 3), as long as there is clarity on the normalisation by the June meeting, we think the ECB could “look through” if expectations remain well-behaved. Perhaps the cuts we currently expect in Mar/Jun-27 would move towards the second half of 2027, particularly if the shock keeps growing larger. But in a scenario where the shock is longer (ie no clarity by the June meeting on how it plays out) we think the ECB would be tempted to hike then given inflation would be somewhere around 2.5-3%, with no clarity on the persistence of the shock, and hence growing risks of second-round effects. Though not our base case, the cumulation of shocks is also starting to increase our concerns around non-linear effects, something the ECB dubbed a “latent risk of rolling recessions”. The risk balance to our current base case of cuts in Mar/Jun-27 has moved from earlier to tentatively later cuts to below 2%. But even if the ECB hikes in the summer, our conviction that the policy rate will be no higher than current levels by end-27 – and more likely below 2% – remains unbroken. UK: March at risk As argued above, the size and persistence of the shock matter for the eventual direct impact as well as the effect on inflation expectations and the BoE’s reaction function. If energy price moves reverse quickly, within the next couple of weeks, then the BoE will likely resume its cutting cycle as per our base case of March and June. But a March cut would be in doubt if energy price moves don’t reverse by then. If these moves reverse within a few months, we would still expect two cuts this year, even if there is a delay. More persistent or larger moves last could cast doubt on whether the BoE can cut twice this year but may mean deeper cuts next year. The bar for a hike is still likely to be high, and probably higher than for the ECB given the BoE tends to be more forward-looking (and has historically tolerated higher inflation). records.text: FOCUS F O C U S KEY MESSAGES The outlook for European equities has become more uncertain due to geopolitics. The distribution of risk has shifted and downside scenarios have been repriced, particularly in Europe. The region’s economic recovery could be facing headwinds. These include spiking energy prices and changes in monetary policy that would stand to impact corporate earnings growth. Reduction of exposure to European equities was amplified by overweight and overcrowded allocations. Now seems too early to add risk aggressively, as valuations do not offer a sufficient margin of safety. Investors might consider hedges that benefit from high skew and rotate into defensive sectors. These geopolitical events occur after a period of low volatility and tight spreads, which is likely to have led to an increase in leverage in financial markets. Cracks were starting to appear in sectors at risk of AI disruptions. Rather than the macro impact, the most immediate concern may come from the unintended consequences of a system-wide reduction of leverage triggered by higher oil prices, higher volatility, and higher risk aversion. This leads us to reduce risk in our portfolio and exit the short Bund. Despite the increase in oil prices, our inflation strategists still expect inflation to remain close to target this year. Thus, in the case of a significant spike in risk aversion, inflation should not be a constraint for potential ECB policy easing. This leads us to maintain the long Dec-26 ESTR as a hedge to our remaining bearish UST10Y position. We will reassess again if our remaining trades reach their indicative stops. We note that the bulk of this week’s repricing higher in monetary policy expectations was concentrated in 1H26 (+5bp in EUR/USD and +15bp in GBP) and 2H26 (+15/20bp on the week), while changes in 2027 pricing have been more contained. Notably, after the attack on Iran last weekend, the ECB OIS curve went from reflecting some probability of cuts to hikes (previ- ously about 10bp of cuts priced in by end-26 vs. around 27bp of hikes currently). Markets have shifted to price only 11bp BoE cuts this year (vs. ~55bp priced in previously) and around 37bp cumulative easing for the Fed (vs. ~43bp before the weekend strikes). Such a hawkish market reaction suggests that rate markets have assigned more weight to the risk of a significant inflation shock that prompts less easing or tighter central bank policy, rather than to the potential growth hit due to supply chain disruptions and overall weaker global business sentiment. But, instead, they have stood their ground, and in fact outperformed Large-Caps in half the world since the US/Israel campaign began on Feb 27th. His successor, Ronald Reagan, during the 1980s Iran-Iraq Tanker War, prioritized protecting shipping and targeting Iranian vessels and missile batteries, leaving Kharg untouched. Although Iraqi forces struck some terminals and tankers during the eight- year war, Kharg remained largely operational and damage was typically repaired quickly, demonstrating that disabling it would require sustained, large-scale attacks. So far, American and Israeli forces have tried to avoid striking Iran’s oil infrastructure. What would be the implications if Kharg Island were seized? If Kharg Island were disabled, the loss of its storage buffer and the scarcity of viable export alternatives would rapidly trigger upstream shut‑ins across major southwest fields. With production near 3.3 mbd and exports around 1.5 mbd, as much as half of national output could be at risk if the hub remains offline, and the previously assumed 20‑day buffer would vanish from day one. What is the latest tally of production cuts? Today’s reports indicate Iraqi output is down by 3 mbd—nearly its entire pre‑conflict export flow via the Strait of Hormuz. With a strong tendency for companies to align with their peers, the downward revisions proved modest ( Figure 13). Originally, S&P placed the company on CreditWatch Negative on July 7, 2025, after CNC removed its FY25 earnings guidance amid growing pressure in its ACA business. it then extended the Watch on October 6, 2025, based on unresolved legislative risks (ACA subsidy extension). Now that we have more clarity on the company's outlook for 2026 and with the extension of ACA subsidies increasingly unlikel,y we remain convinced that a downgrade to high yield is only a matter of time. S&P plans to resolve the CreditWatch in the first quarter of 2026. While management has laid out a path to incremental improvement through 2026, there are considerable unknowns in the story. We continue to think there are challenges to the ACA business and specifically the acuity of the risk pool. While ACA enrollment remains healthy, we will learn the true health of the market in 1Q, when premium grace periods expire. It remains difficult to expect adverse selection risks to decline in the ACA marketplace through 2026. Impact on GDP, unemployment and inflation We break down how our projections would look like based on the above scenarios, focussing on growth, unemployment, and inflation. records.text: Global Economic Weekly | 06 March 2026 3 It is supply shocks that matter Since the OPEC crisis and the Iranian Revolution of the 1970s, the only clear examples we find of a long-lasting inflationary impact emanating from an oil price shock are the OPEC cuts of 1999 and the spike following the COVID recovery and the Russia-Ukraine conflict. Outside of that, the oil price spike of 2007-2008 coincided with a jump in (headline) inflation, but the experiment was halted by the GFC, where the global recession that followed drove down both inflation and oil prices. Similarly, higher oil prices after 9/11, Afghanistan, and Iraq generated a persistent increase in oil prices that may have contributed somewhat and very gradually to headline inflation. However, it did not really materialize into a major inflationary cycle, especially given that core inflation that remained largely stable. In addition, a glance at inflation dynamics over the same period in the Euro area and Japan shows very little reaction too. Inflation risks remain modest for now The new conflict that just emerged in Iran, the consequences for the Strait of Hormuz, and the risks involved certainly amount to an oil supply shock. However, a market reaction like we have seen so far, with oil prices moving about 30% higher than the average of 2025, or 20% higher than a year ago may lead only to a modest transitory inflation shock absent further and persistent escalation.
