records.text: E and SNB; US CPI & 4Q GDP A sudden neutral We have turned neutral on USD for the first time since March of last year, reflecting a tactical but decisive change in our FX strategy. The catalyst for this shift is the emergence of an energy price shock with tail risks still a con- cern. Our core view of “Bearish USD, bullish beta” had been anchored in two main themes: (a) robust global growth which had recently culminated into an equity rotation story, and (b) bounded Fed policy, both of which favored cyclical curren- cies. The sharp rise in energy prices brings back shades of US exceptionalism via the terms of trade channel and thus chal- lenges the former, the global growth pillar. The related dynamic of equity rotation away from the US to RoW which had been leaning USD bearish, has already been rudely interrupted this week (Figure 1T h e e q u i t y r o t a t i o n a w a y f r o m t h e U S w a s i n t e r r u p t e d t h i s w e e k ; t h i s w a s o n e f a c t o r d r i v i n g U S D w e a k n e s s i n r e c e n t w e e k s ) stalling momentum in the dollar as well. records.text: M Idea 2 On oil and uncertainty shocks Prices of important energy commodities like oil and natural gas moved higher following US strikes on Iran. WTI and Brent both moved about $10-15/bbl higher, while natural gas prices in Europe rose by about $15/MMBtu. In addition, the response by Iran to the strikes temporarily halted the passage of ships through the Strait of Hormuz. The closure is noteworthy since about 30% of the world's oil consumption flows through the strait, much of which eventually ends up in Asia. Qatar halted LNG production, putting about 20% of global supply at risk. About 15% of this supply reportedly goes to Europe, while the remainder flows to Asia. Our commodity analysts continue to track the flow of ships through the Strait of Hormuz on a daily basis (see here and here). Importantly, in the eyes of our commodity research team, the closure of the strait is better described as a logistics shock rather than a production shock; we see no lost barrels from production as of yet, but view market moves as a repricing of deliverability (see Iran Scenarios - Updated). This is good news in the sense that it may be easier to restore the movement of ships through the strait than it would be to rebuild lost production. A modest sustained rise in oil prices could delay Fed easing The moves – if sustained – could have implications for our outlook for the US economy and monetary policy in 2026. The presented draft regulation proposes that the preferred risk weight under the CRR standardised approach (currently only applying for domestic UK CB in the UK) will also apply to non-UK CB from HMT-approved countries. The current list of countries includes not only EEA member states but also Australia, Canada, New Zealand, Singapore, Switzerland, South Korea and others. However, the respective CB laws also have to meet certain requirements. Hence, at this stage, it is not fully clear which non-UK CB will benefit from the new rules. In addition, the PRA published a consultation paper, inviting market participants to comment by 2 April. “The PRA considers that, where it has been judged appropriate for overseas CB to be eligible for preferential treatment under the SA on the same basis as UK CB, it would be consistent for them to also receive preferential treatment under the FIRB approach and the credit risk mitigation framework on the same basis as UK CB." According to the PRA, the preferential risk weight should therefore not be limited to the standardised approach, but should also apply to the IRB approach, i.e. a lower LGD could be assigned (which is important for larger UK banks). No specific adjustments to the LCR rules are included so far. We also have micro level data at the HS-2, HS-4 or HS-6 levels, which drove much of the analysis in the Supply Chain Strain note. The primary driver of the data in the first three interactives, as indicated above, is UN Comtrade data. This ties to the reported trade statistics from national statistical offices (see the grey box below for further granularity). Additionally, we provide a fourth interactive that scopes value add production. Globalized supply chains mean that tracing value add production is not straightforward. National statistical agencies, international organizations like OECD, and academic projects all study where value is added — both internationally and domestically. We use data from Eurostat's FIGARO Inter-Country Input-Output (ICIO) database, which examines the value add for 64 industries across 45 countries. Ultimately this cross section allows for analysis of more than 2,500 industry nodes to see the inputs a given industry uses from other industry nodes — a proxy for value add across supply chains. Unfortunately, the next comprehensive NZ labour force survey is not due until early May. This lack of a trigger links to a common topic in client discussions: the difficult carry set-up to play NZ policy normalization. NZD 1s/2s is steep, and the RBNZ is likely to normalize, but doesn’t show urgency to start. The relative underreaction of NZ assets to the survey and growth data is then partially justified in the sense that excess capacity buys the RBNZ time, pushing policy normalization into the forwards, which are now close to fair value (Figure 8N Z D 1 Y x 1 Y i s a b o u t f a i r i n o u t r i g h t t e r m s g i v e n m a c r o i n p u t s a s t h e y s t a n d ). The precise timing of the coming unemployment rate decline in a sense summarizes the carry headwind, as an imminent tightening of the labour market would overcome negative carry concerns. In our models, every 1%-pt lower on unemployment flattens 2s/10s swap by 40bp, and 6m forward 2s/10s is about 15bp below spot. A roughly 0.3-0.4%-pt fall in unemployment in the next six months is then needed to beat the forwards. If current curve shape is preserved, we look to re-enter NZD flattening trades closer to the 1Q labour data. Constitutional protection mechanisms (e.g. federal loyalty principle, financial strength equalization, eternity guarantee for federalism) will continue to provide support to federal states. Japan: CPI inflation set to moderate further despite upside surprise in Feb In Feb, Japan-style core CPI inflation (ex. fresh food) fell below 2%, for the first time since Oct 2024, on lower energy prices. However, BoJ‑style core CPI inflation (ex. fresh food and energy) rebounded to 2.5% yoy and beat market expectations. records.text: Global Strategy9 March 2026 ab 3 UBS energy research summary: Why Straits of Hormuz disruption has shades of 2022 Below we summarise the key points from UBS' energy research team over the last week, adding our own perspectives on the transmission channels to EM. - Global oil consumption was 104Mb/d last year. ~20Mb/d of oil supply transits the Straits of Hormuz (inc crude, condensate, oil products) - which are now, de facto, closed. Gulf states such as Iraq and Kuwait have reportedly already reduced production in response, with Qatar warning of broader production stoppages in the coming days. - Henri Patricot , our global oil analyst, sees only 5mln of this 20mn supply being potentially redirected away from the Straits of Hormuz via pipelines, leaving a potential 15mln bpd at risk of extended disruption. After accounting for other forms of offsetting supply relief - such as US and Chinese strategic reserve depletion - UBS still sees at least 10m bpd at risk of disruption. This suggests that 2022, when Russian supply was reduced, is the closest historical parallel for oil and gas markets to today – Russia produces ~11Mb/d of oil and other liquids. - UBS estimates OPEC+ had 3.8Mb/d of effective spare capacity in February. Relative to previous similar events, the response of DM rate markets to this week's Middle East tensions has differed substantially in both magnitude and direction from previous comparable geopolitical flare ups, such as last year's 12-day Iran-Israel conflict and the Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Firstly, we note that, in terms of energy prices, this week’s shock is substantially different from the start 2022 Russia-Ukraine episode (Figure 4T h e e n e r g y p r i c e s h o c k i s n o w s u b s t a n t i a l l y d i f f e r e n t f r o m t h e 2 0 2 2 R u s s i a - U k r a i n e e p i s o d e ). Indeed, back then, both Brent and TTF gas were already at much higher levels ahead of the invasion of Ukraine ($97/bbl and €88/MWh respectively) than last Friday and the subsequent spike in TTF gas was much larger (+€50/MWh in a single day, +€90/MWh after a week) than what was seen this week. The energy market pricing around the latest events is more similar to what observed for the 12-day war. Brent and TTF gas prices were at comparable levels ahead of the conflict (~$70/bbl and ~€30-35/MWh respectively), although the magnitude of the move especially in TTF has been larger this time around. All in all, the magnitude of this week’s market moves and anecdotal evidence suggest that unwinds of crowded positions has played an important role in exacerbating the market reaction to the energy price shock. For instance, carry trades in intra-EMU spreads and vol space had been widely subscribed in recent month. We had previously highlighted that the slim carry levels would not be enough to cushion against potential risk-off moves and our cautious stance has been vindicated this week. At the peak of this week’s widening, carry trades in intra-EMU spreads have cost, on average, 5-10 months worth of carry if implemented vs. Germany and 3-5 months for trades implemented vs. €STR (Figure 6T h i s w e e k ’ s p e a k s p r e a d w i d e n i n g i n i n t r a - E M U s p r e a d s h a s c o s t 3 - 1 0 m o n t h s ' w o r t h o f c a r r y ). While PCG CDS has been volatile (trading as wide as 200bp prior to SB254's passage), levels have tightened back to pre-Eaton Fire levels. We think incremental progress on wildfire reform (catastrophe fund, broader contributors, durable fund, some level of liability cap color) should support CDS tightening. We see scope for 30-40bp of compression, which would still leave PCG well wide of regular way-regulated utilities such as SRE or FE, but be more reflective of the substantial de-risking we anticipate from Phase 2. We think going back to around 150bp or wider is unlikely absent another large catastrophic fire, given the SB254 Phase 1 protections in place. 6 March 2026 9 Barclays | US Credit Alpha: The power of yields

Indeed, our base case is that the Iran conflict will not affect the trajectory of Fed policy, though it will probably strengthen the consensus around staying on hold at the next two meetings. At the time of this writing, markets have almost perfectly priced this outcome. A large and longer-lasting shock would be stagflationary. This would mean renewed tension between the Fed’s two mandates. In the near term, substantially higher oil prices would make it harder for the Fed to cut. With inflation already above target, we think most of the FOMC would prefer to err on the side of caution by staying on hold. Some policymakers might even call for hikes if inflation expectations, which are typically sensitive to oil prices, were to move up meaningfully. But we think the bar to raise rates will be high under Warsh. In the medium term, however, the Fed might get concerned about demand destruction from the energy supply shock. The saving rate is already low by historical standards, so consumers don’t have much buffer against a spike in energy prices. A spending slowdown would weigh on both job growth and inflation (once oil prices stabilize), pushing the Fed in a more dovish direction. In addition, the KEY MESSAGES The conflict in the Middle East and associated spike in oil and gas prices challenge both our optimistic outlook for the eurozone economy and already subdued outlook for the UK. As a large net energy importer, Europe is among the most vulnerable to rising energy prices, while the potential impact on sentiment threatens to stamp out the nascent economic momentum. Defence and infrastructure spending have a high energy intensity, so the fiscal multiplier could fall if energy prices remain high. If the shock is short-lived and/or contained, we retain our view of an accelerating eurozone economy and the ECB remaining on hold this year. It would reinforce our view of a prolonged policy pause for the Bank of England after a final rate cut in H1. A rise in gas and oil prices to triple-digit figures would make us reconsider our forecasts and raise the risk of rate hikes to mitigate second-round price effects. In December 2025, Congress passed the Modernization and Reauthorization Act, which significantly expands the US Development Finance Corporation’s capacity and tools. The Act raised the maximum contingent liability from US$60 billion to US$205 billion, created a US$5 billion equity revolving fund to enable more effective equity investing, and extended authorization through 2031. It also broadened financing flexibility (including subordinate debt and up to 100% loan guarantees) to support larger, more complex projects and better compete with state-directed finance while preserving DFC’s development mission. We run a few scenarios for energy prices, impact on inflation and BoE’s reaction function Scenario 1: If gas and oil prices are sustained at current levels (£60/barrel and 140pence/therm) Energy is ~6% of the UK’s CPI basket. Oil prices at ~£60/barrel are around ~25% higher in sterling terms. If this move is sustained and doesn’t reverse, it can add ~20-25bps to inflation in 2026. Petrol prices usually reflect the moves in oil prices fairly quickly. In terms of gas, while the Ofgem price cap has already been set for April and is set to see a ~7% drop, a sustained rise in gas prices can affect price caps in H2 (July and October). If we assume British natural gas prices of around 140pence/therm, that is an an increase of more than ~70% from an average of 77 pence/therm. We estimate this could raise the energy price cap by ~11-12% in July assuming this is sustained. In the near term, inflation could be 20-25bps higher from March- June and be around ~55-60bps higher in H2 2026 (vs. 1.9% in our current forecasts), with December inflation likely at 2.5%. Overall inflation could be ~35bps higher in 2026 (vs. 2.2% in our current forecasts) and 20bps higher in 2027 (vs. 2.0% in our forecasts). Not all hope should be lost at this stage, as a revision to 3% or below by April, could still allow the Italian government to apply for an exit from EDP. What are the implications of remaining in EDP? 1. Eligibility under TPI: In order to be eligible for asset purchases under the ECB's TPI, a member state needs to either avoid EDP, or if placed in EDP respect the annual fiscal adjustments requested by the European Commission. For Italy, remaining in EDP would not necessarily represent an obstacle to TPI eligibility, as long as the country is able to maintain the nominal growth rate of net expenditure at 1.3% in 2025 and 1.6% in 2026. Additionally, complying with the net expenditure growth path is not a strict requirement, as some deviations are permitted. Notably, the Commission records these in a control account, and countries may exceed their expenditure path by up to 0.3pp of GDP per year, or 0.6pp cumulatively over the implementation period of their plan (see here). This supports the idea that Italy would still be eligible for TPI despite being in EDP. 2. Limiting defence spending: The Italian government had linked any take up of the Safe loans to its exit from EDP - see here. Admittedly such rescaling may not be innocu- ous if the drag on GDP is nonlinear in the price change. • Our global colleagues find that a 10% rise in oil prices reduces developed market GDP by 14bp. • In past work, we found that a 8% price increase lowered US GDP by 27bp after two quarters, with the drag fading to 15bp over a year (34bp and 19bp under a 10% price move). Our approach is similar to Kilian (2009). • Gagliardone and Gertler (2025) found a 6% price increase reduced GDP by 25bp after a year using a structural V AR, or 10bp using a DSGE model (42bp and 17bp, respective- ly, per 10% price move). • Presno and Prestipino (2024) estimated a 10% price increase reduces GDP by 8bp, although it takes around two years for the full effect to be felt. • Kilian, Plante, and Richter (2026) develop a DSGE model to estimate the economic effects of oil shock probabilities, in which an anticipated disaster (like the closure of the Strait of Hormuz) drives up prices even if the disaster doesn’t actually occur. records.text: 6 March 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Page 38 Deutsche Bank AG Treasury basis: Lower returns and lighter positioning Profitability of the Treasury basis trade has compressed substantially since last year. Today's chart shows the implied repo rate from owning the CTD bond against 5-year futures, minus SOFR funding, which approximates the expected return of the basis trade. As seen in the chart, the expected return has fallen from the mid- teens basis points over the last few years to low single digits currently. Returns for owning the basis in the 2-year (TU) and 10-year (TY) sectors have declined similarly. Positioning in the basis trade has likely become lighter as a result. In CFTC data, leveraged fund net short positions in the 2-, 5-, and 10-year sectors have declined as a percentage of open interest compared with the last quarter. The decline in basis activity is reflected in the softer funding markets since start of this year. The Fed's funding backstops may have played a role: by reducing the risk premium embedded in basis trades, they may have directly contributed to the compression in the basis. Asset managers have also stepped back on their futures positions across the curve, with buying concentrated in the ultra long-end. Additionally, as we highlighted recently, foreign allotments in Treasury auctions have been unusually strong since December, which suggests increased foreign real money demand for cash securities further compressing basis opportunities. The larger and more sustained the increase in oil prices, how- ever, the greater the risk for larger nonlinear reductions in growth and the corresponding likely drag on employment. While this would also result in a larger surge in headline inflation, the scope for direct pass-through of higher energy prices into core inflation appears limited, whereas the risk for weaker demand to weigh on core inflation increases with a larger oil supply shock. Thus, in an alternative scenario in which oil prices spike to $120/bbl or higher on realized and expected sustained reduction in supply, we expect the Fed to be biased toward easing as downside risks to activity once again move to the fore. Another factor in how the Fed might trade off divergent growth versus inflation moves from an oil price shock is how much inflation expectation rise as a result. Concerns about tariffs have already boosted near-term inflation expectations in consumer surveys—although they are down moderately from their peaks last spring—and a surge in gasoline prices would risk a further move higher in expectations. Fed offi- cials often suggest it is most appropriate for policy to look past the volatility in near-term inflation expectations and focus on medium- to longer-term measures. records.text: 2 Global Economic Weekly | 06 March 2026 Global Letter Claudio Irigoyen BofAS Antonio Gabriel BofAS Only persistent oil spikes really matter Since the US-Israel operation in Iran started, oil price volatility reignited inflation concerns. But how worried should we be about an increase in global inflation? While market and survey-based inflation expectations can be sensitive to oil at high frequency, history suggests only marked and persistent spikes in the price of crude trigger persistent inflationary cycles. If the status quo persists, with oil prices around $15 higher than the pre-war level, we would fade (oil induced) inflation concerns. But an escalation driving oil prices persistently above $100 would become more concerning. Looking at oil price shocks of the last 50 years To gauge the potential correlation between inflation and oil prices over the past several decades, we start by looking at PCE and core PCE inflation in the US, side by side with the change in oil prices (WTI). Note that comparing inflation (the rate of change in the price level) with the level of oil prices would be comparing apples to oranges, so we abstain from doing that. Exhibit 1 shows the inflation and oil price series for the US, where at a first glance one can see that there is not a very marked correlation between oil prices and inflation at any given point in time. Financial markets would likely price in the impact much faster. Transit-avoidance pipelines in Saudi Arabia and UAE: The largest transit- avoidance pipeline is the East–West pipeline in Saudi Arabia, with a capacity of up to 7mbd. A smaller pipeline in the UAE can flow up to 1.8mbd at maximum utilisation. These capacities are impressive; however, the three caveats here are that part of this capacity is already utilized, flow through the EW pipeline is constrained by loading capacity of the Yanbu port; and EW barrels would evacuate in the Red Sea, where Houthi attacks impeded flows until recently. Inflation concerns were rebuffed Unusually given German stereotypes, inflation concerns from the upcoming fiscal growth spurt were very limited – that was the unanimous view among our interlocutors. The output gap has opened up to the downside over the past few years, leaving enough room for some growth to come through without affecting price dynamics much. Fiscal discipline isn’t quite as dead as many think We were caught by surprise when we heard that finance ministry working groups were already looking into how and when to phase out the carve-out for defence spending from the national fiscal rule. Mea culpa, it is not a secret, the working group agenda is on the ministry’s website, but has largely gone unnoticed. Perhaps it is because the majorities to deliver constitutional change to alter the carve-out are elusive. That's what the central bank is designed to do, prevent liquidity spirals … To that end, the liquidity coverage ratio requirements and other liquidity rules should give appropriate capped recognition of borrowing capacity associated with col- lateral prepositioned at the discount window.” Our interpretation of their remarks is that liquidity coverage ratio (LCR) reform is likely to follow capital rule changes (Basel III endgame and GSIB calibration) this year. One poten- tial change is that banks may be allowed to include their collateral pre-positioned at the discount window (with a haircut) in their LCR calculations and internal liquidity stress testing (ILST). If so, this would unlock some liquidity and allow banks to hold less cash, but the benefit is likely to be much less than the current collateral value (which was ~$1.1tn for institutions with assets above $100bn as of 4Q23). We expect reserves to stabilize around ~$2.4-2.5tn if such a change were to occur. This change would be positive for markets, as banks would be able to deploy more into repo and other assets, and we expect higher-ROA assets (which currently have no liquidity value) to be the first option. In that scenario the BoE is likely to worry more about second round effects, especially as wage expectations are still elevated. A March cut would be in doubt if the energy price moves don’t reverse by then (unless the labour market report released on 19 March is fairly weak), increasing risks of a delay of the next cut potentially to sometime in Q2 and the second cut to H2. We don’t change forecasts yet and will reevaluate our March cut call next week. Overall, if the energy price moves reverse quickly say within the next couple of weeks, then the BoE can likely resume its cutting cycle as per our base case of March and June. If these moves reverse within a few months, we would still expect two cuts from the BoE this year, even if there is a delay. If the moves are sustained for much longer or become larger, it can add to doubts on whether the BoE can cut twice this year but may mean deeper cuts next year given deteriorated growth outlook in the medium term. The bar for a hike is still likely to be high and would need a de-anchoring of inflation expectations. records.text: 6 March 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Deutsche Bank AG Page 43 Oil, Natgas & inflation implications The recent geopolitical events in the Middle East have led to large moves in energy markets, with significant implications for the near-term inflation outlook. While the Strait of Hormuz remains officially open, and oil infrastructure has remained largely unaffected, higher insurance and freight costs as well as some persistence in risk premia could keep prices elevated for now and energy market futures curves reflect these concerns. While the front-end has seen the largest price increases, implied prices remain relatively elevated through most of this year, at least in Europe, before fading more clearly into next year (Figure left); by the summer of next year, prices converge back close to the levels seen last week. Price increases in US energy markets are much smaller in magnitude, with natural gas futures rising only modestly and gasoline futures up ~5% at the front-end (Figure left). This has moderate implications for the expected inflation profile. In month-on-month terms, only March and April see significant upward revisions, while the overall impact at the end of this year is limited to just under ~10bp. For next year, year-on-year inflation remains broadly unchanged (Figure right). The potential implications for the euro area inflation outlook are much larger. These flows are highly sensitive to interest-rate differentials and FX moves and can reflect corporate treasury operations rather than fresh strategic commitments of capital. The cross‑country pattern is similar, likely driven by taxes, price controls and administered pricing. Combined with the ongoing and steady deceleration in inflation, confidence is rising in a scenario where improving real wages provide meaningful support to economic activity. Indeed, core real wages (deflated by headline CPI) turned positive in December, rising 0.1%, marking the first positive reading in nearly a year. In January, amid a sharp slowdown in inflation, real wage growth is expected to improve further to around 0.7%, assuming nominal wages remain broadly flat. That's what the central bank is designed to do, prevent liquidity spirals … To that end, the liquidity coverage ratio requirements and other liquidity rules should give appropriate capped recognition of borrowing capacity associated with col- lateral prepositioned at the discount window.” Our interpretation of their remarks is that liquidity coverage ratio (LCR) reform is likely to follow capital rule changes (Basel III endgame and GSIB calibration) this year. One poten- tial change is that banks may be allowed to include their collateral pre-positioned at the discount window (with a haircut) in their LCR calculations and internal liquidity stress testing (ILST). If so, this would unlock some liquidity and allow banks to hold less cash, but the benefit is likely to be much less than the current collateral value (which was ~$1.1tn for institutions with assets above $100bn as of 4Q23). We expect reserves to stabilize around ~$2.4-2.5tn if such a change were to occur. This change would be positive for markets, as banks would be able to deploy more into repo and other assets, and we expect higher-ROA assets (which currently have no liquidity value) to be the first option. If oil prices were to rise to around USD 100, equivalent to the average level in 2022 following the outbreak of the Russia–Ukraine war, the drag on GDP could reach approximately 0.2ppt. Implications for BoJ monetary policy: we continue to expect rate hike in April As expected in our report earlier this week, during the House of Representatives’ Financial Affairs Committee meeting on 4 March, BoJ Governor Ueda commented on the impact of higher oil prices on inflation. In this context, he highlighted the presence of both upside and downside risks to inflation. records.text: an tactical signals: A buying opportunity emerges when positioning is light, sentiment is bearish, volatility is excessive and short-term valuations are cheap, but macro conditions and earnings momentum are rebounding. In contrast, a selling opportunity is reached when positioning is overcrowded, sentiment is bullish, volatility is depressed and short- term valuations are expensive, but macro conditions are tight and earnings momentum is negative. Our study reveals that buy opportunities are indicated for US TEI levels below 35 (scale of 100) and sell conditions are implied for readings above 75, with respective hit ratios of 64% and 44%. This asymmetry arises from the different nature of buying opportunities, which tend to be deeper and briefer, and selling conditions, which can be more drawn-out. Providing alpha: Back-testing against the S&P 500 suggests that the US TEI is a useful tactical tool for contrarian plays, aiming at attractive positive (negative) average forward returns at low (high) levels of the indicator. records.text: M Idea 4 3-8 months after the initial shock as GDP experiences a level shift down that does not reverse. …weakening activity and putting more Fed cuts in play In this scenario, we would expect other variables to deteriorate, including equity markets, which could trigger precautionary saving from upper income households. As we noted in last week's edition of the US Economics Weekly, consumptions spending by US households is overshooting its wealth-implied fundamentals (see Dissaving limits consumer upside). At 3.6% in December, there is limited room for the saving rate to move lower to smooth consumption through this type of shock. We also find that a shock to uncertainty bites harder when confidence is low. As we show in Exhibit 5 below, shocks to the VIX tend to correlate with declines in payrolls if NFIB sentiment is below 100 (it was 99.3 in January). Put simply, uncertainty shocks can delay spending and hiring plans and large shocks can lead to spending cutbacks and layoffs. Even though we think AI-related capital expenditures can continue, other business spending may not be so resilient. To date, any rise in the VIX has been limited, as has the decline in US equity markets. We think the more relevant risk to our outlook for monetary policy is that Fed cuts are delayed. CITI'S TAKE A mechanic reflation could be unfolding in China, in our view, driven by global oil prices. Both CPI and PPI surprised on the upside in February. Chinese New Year seasonality helped with CPI, especially via services prices. Sequential PPI stayed solid even as much of the oil price surge hasn’t surfaced. The current oil price surge could be sufficient to drive PPI back to positive territory despite more nuances on price transmission. We think an organic reflation could still be absent. Post-CNY seasonality could drive CPI lower in March, while the downstream price passthrough could still be limited, weighing on downstream profits further. Such a backdrop could put policymakers in a difficult position, in our view, trying to keep supply risks subdued amid elevated uncertainties and support downstream sectors via structural tools. The PBoC’s rate decision could be complicated further post the downgrade of the growth target at the NPC. records.text: Furthermore, this analysis suggests that if intangible assets were to increase to a certain level partly due to government initiatives in sectors where there is currently under-investment in intangible assets, they might increase organically thereafter, through a rise in the return on intangible assets caused by a rise in productivity. For this reason, government initiatives to promote investment in intangible assets such as AI, software, and R&D, is considered effective for improving Japan’s productivity. Even in the case of increased fiscal spending for productivity improvement, inflationary pressure would be expected to rise in the short term, because the increase in demand would precede the increase in supply capacity, and the BOJ would need to steadily raise rates in response. However, compared to Case 1 above (government spending focused on boosting demand), the yen’s weakness could be corrected by productivity improvements (Balassa-Samuelson effect, Exhibit 9), so the inflationary pressure would be smaller, and the magnitude of rate hikes required to suppress inflationary pressure would likely also be smaller. Another important difference in the implications for monetary policy is that in this case, over the longer term, it would be necessary to gradually raise the policy rate in line with the rise in the natural rate of interest caused by the rise in the potential growth rate (see BOX on this point). However, geopolitical risks with higher oil price challenges improving real wages That said, the favorable macro scenario we envision—sustained real wage growth and improving consumption—faces downside risks from recent geopolitical developments driving higher oil prices. On the inflation front, if crude oil prices remain around USD 80 per barrel, compared with our baseline assumption of USD 70, we estimate that our forecast for average core CPI inflation in 2026 would need to be revised upward by 0.2ppt to 1.9%. Should geopolitical tensions intensify further and oil prices rise to USD 100 per barrel, the inflationary impact would widen to 0.5ppt, pushing core CPI inflation to around 2.3%. Under such a scenario, our current baseline assumption of inflation decelerating below 2% would no longer hold, and inflation could remain near 2.5% from the second half of 2026 through the first half of 2027 (Figure 7). Recently, pass- through from import prices to consumer prices—particularly food—has strengthened compared with the past, suggesting upside risks to inflation may be larger than assumed. What happens after that depends crucially, again, on the size and persistence of the shock. We try to shed some (limited) light in our main pieces for the Euro area and the UK . Euro area: a blast from the recent past We would argue that the ECB’s sensitivity to large and persistent energy price shocks is now higher than in the past after the recent 2022-23 episode, when some observers (not us) felt the ECB probably reacted late. Additionally, as we have argued before, this is an ECB that is not perfectly forward looking. With that in mind, while the ECB is likely to look through short-lived shocks, even if sizeable, there is a limit to that, we think. In our baseline scenario, we would not expect much of a reaction from the ECB and our call for cuts in 1H27 would still hold. How large and persistent a shock would need to be to materially change our call, or prompt the ECB to act, is clearly subjective and there are no magic thresholds. But thinking beyond the March meeting, we make three important points, particularly looking at how ECB pricing has moved in the past few days: 1. If by the June meeting there is no clarity on when the shock might fade, we see a significant likelihood of the ECB hiking rates then or shortly after. 2. In this weekly, we take a quick look at what the Middle East war means for the UK economy. We briefly touch on growth (GDP), the labour market, and inflation. Policy won't be immune to the recent energy shock too. To be clear: we are not changing our baseline projections - not yet at least. Given how fluid the current situation remains, we will re-assess our baseline as we get more clarity on the unfolding war. Our baseline: resilient growth, stabilising labour market, and strong disinflation We start off by restating our baseline projections - these have not changed yet. On growth, we expect GDP to have seen a resounding bounce in Q1-26, rising by 0.5% q-o-q. We then expect growth to track around 0.3% q-o-q for the remainder of the year, taking annual real GDP growth to 1.1%. Thereafter, we expected GDP growth to ramp up to 1.4% in 2027 and 1.5% in 2028. On the labour market, our baseline projections include a further rise in the jobless rate to a peak of 5.4%. Some stabilisation thereafter remains our basecase, with a gradual decline in the jobless rate likely in the second half of the year. We saw wage growth (AWE Regular Pay) edging lower to 3.3%. For instance, there was a leftward move in the 2022 Senate elections, indicating the mood of the presidential election (Figure 3). And in 2018, the center-right bias in Senate voting was also seen in the presidential election (Figure 4). The 2026 Senate election clearly shows a shift in the number of votes towards the left, pointing to Pacto Historico’s strength going into the presidential election. We note that the increase in votes for Pacto Historico relative to 2022 is higher than the increase for all other parties put together (Figure 5). Given that the outstanding volume of EU bonds will increase further in the next years, its dominance in the EUR SSA trading volume is also likely to increase further. Fitch highlighted in a recent update on its top 50 SSA issuers globally, that their total outstanding debt rose to about USD 5.6tn at end-2025, up more than 4% from a year earlier. Based on our data, the EU accounted for over 60% of the increase. For investors willing to invest only in large-sized EUR SSA (for example, EUR SSA bonds with an outstanding volume of at least EUR 5bn), the sector has only six issuers, with a total outstanding volume of EUR 1168.9bn (133 ISINs). With EUR 700.884bn, the EU is by far the largest issuer, followed by EIB (EUR 135.5bn), KfW (EUR 214bn), EFSF (EUR 67.5bn), CADES (EUR 46bn) and the ESM (EUR 5bn). There may be something in that argument, as we have seen structural under-delivery of investment plans over the last decade(s). And what wasn’t spent, was lost. The SVIK is indeed different here: by design, money that doesn’t get spent as planned isn’t lost, but available for future budgets. But that's a different question to the quality of additional spending. We still feel comfortable that a little bit of extra capex plus the defence sector spending may be enough to keep German growth in the 0.5-1% range rather than close to zero for some time after the initial growth spurt, but insufficient for something more exciting. Cash vs accrual: the methodology challenge of translating spending into growth We are still uncertain exactly when fiscal spending will show up in growth. Remember the finance ministry data comes in cash, not accrual. The money is raised and spent, but we don’t know on what (downpayments, imports, immediate deliverables, medium term deliverables…) – a proper dashboard seems to be in the making, though. We continue to feel comfortable assuming particularly strong GDP growth in 2H26, with risk of earlier materialisation, and/or perhaps an even bigger stimulus this year compared to our expectations (remember we assumed a delivery ratio similar to last year’s at federal level). records.text: on consumers There are two considerations for growth: how is aggregate output affected, and how is that spread between consumption and investment. Higher energy prices are unambiguously neg- ative for most households and real consumer spending should decline. They are also negative for energy-intensive industries but positive for domestic energy producers, and this latter channel can generate a partially offsetting rise in investment. However, to the extent that the shock is seen as short-lived, any investment gain may be a tepid offset to the consumer spending decline, and is likely to take shape more slowly than the consumption response. One way to approach this question is by looking individually at the response of consumption and investment. As noted above, energy commodities are about 2% of consumer spend- ing, mostly gasoline. We often assume that households will hold real gasoline consumption steady in the short run and offset the higher price of gasoline with an equivalent cut in other spending. If a 10% rise in oil prices leads to a 10bp rise in the PCE deflator, then real consumption will fall about 10bp, which would subtract 7bp from GDP. On the investment side, structures investment in oil and natu- ral gas well drilling has tended to follow oil price movements with a slight lag (Figure 3), although the relationship was less tight in the 2000-2010 period. As we show below, the composition of Chinese investments related to BRI speaks to the aforementioned goals, showing a large deployment of capital to the energy, mining, and transportation/infrastructure sectors in recipient economies. Implicit in the BRI agenda was to leverage the investments to gain political and military influence, especially in smaller, developing countries in Africa, Latin America, and Central Asia. After the initial success (e.g., China hosting the African summit), how successful this has been is questionable. Political backlash erupted in various countries amid allegations of corruption, questions about the contribution of these projects to domestic development, and concerns over infrastructure, such as ports, being used as military bases. Parsing the pieces of BRI The BRI consists primarily of the New Silk Road Economic Belt, which envisages connecting China with Europe through Central and Western Asia, as well as the 21st Century Maritime Silk Road, connecting China with Southeast Asian countries, Africa and Europe. According to the Chinese government, it has signed cooperation agreements with 155 countries (mostly developing economies) to work under the framework of the Belt and Road Initiative, including 41 economies in Asia, 52 in Africa, 27 in Europe, 13 in North America, 10 in South America, and 12 in Oceania. Higher trading volume in CB ytd - slightly less in SSA There has been no supply of EUR benchmark CB for almost two weeks. So far, in line with our "safe haven" assessment, only German federal states tapped the primary market in the CB and SSA sectors amid the "war in the Middle East"- driven market turmoil. In our view, higher new-issue premiums - particularly for CB - will be necessary to reopen the primary market. Bloomberg reports EUR 54bn of EUR benchmark CB (EUR denominated, at least EUR 500m outstanding, fix rate, "not retained") traded ytd (as of 3 March). This compares to EUR 42bn of EUR benchmark CB traded in 2025 ytd. Given higher supply of EUR benchmark CB of EUR 52.3bn ytd versus EUR 42bn in 2025 ytd, the increase in the trading volume seems plausible. Using the same EUR benchmark definition for (non-sovereign) SSA, the trading volume reported by Bloomberg amounts to EUR 328.6bn ytd versus EUR 335.6bn in 2025 ytd (as of 3 March). Given that EUR-denominated supply by European SSAs is slightly down ytd (see details here), the slightly lower total trading volume of EUR benchmark SSA seems also plausible. This is because variable annuity (V A) hedgers’ receiving needs increase in an equity sell-off or rates rally, and because their assets are longer-dated, they receive in the 10+ year part of the curve. With the rally in equities in the past year and still-el- evated rates, V A hedging needs have been low. However, Figure 11 shows that their hedging needs can increase in a further selloff or a rally, and in an accelerating fashion, making long-end spread narrowers attractive hedges against such scenarios.

It is worth noting that UK consumer energy prices are regulated via the quarterly Ofgem price cap (and are now fixed for April) which is based on NPB forward curve rather than wholesale prices. We currently estimate a mechanical 0.3% impact on headline CPI from the move in the forward curve and taking into account second round effects we currently estimate the recent energy shock might increase headline CPI by around 0.6% by July to 2.7%. We acknowledge that increased gas prices limits the ability for the BoE to ease in the near term but assuming the conflict does not extend beyond several months into the summer, we think BoE easing later this year is still a possibility against a backdrop of an ongoing easing in the labour market. In addition, global downside growth risks likely increase if oil were to persistently rise above 100$/bbl. Given this, we recommend recveiving Dec26 MPC OIS with a few bp of easing priced. We judge this to be particularly true for Governor Bailey who is likely to be one of the deciding voters in March's meeting. With 12 days until the MPC casts its votes, there is a chance that the situation calms and the current levels of uncertainty and commodity prices wane. That said, downside risks to our forecasts are building from latest geopolitical developments and the energy price rise, Germany’s particular weak spot. The SVIK spending shortfall of 2025 (c EUR13bn vs plans) will not be made up this year – this would need to be in the 2026 budget, but isn’t. Our working assumption is that the “leftovers” will be smoothed over the remaining lifetime of the SVIK, rather than delivered in bulk in any given year. Potential growth challenges trump fiscal fireworks We also left Berlin with an acute sense that long-term structural challenges are almost overwhelming, or in any case much bigger than the fiscal support in the pipeline. The two most prominent factors: • Energy prices and supply: the Russian invasion of Ukraine and the energy crisis have created very long-term challenges, both via prices and supply, with no quick fix in sight (and returning to Russian supply wasn’t a solution).

Across past conflicts, the few episodes with negative IG total returns occurred when the Fed was hiking, while periods when the Fed was paused or cutting delivered positive returns despite the conflict. The very wide distribution of outcomes in the table below underscores the absence of a clear “war effect”; e.g. the standard deviation of the distribution is much larger than the average. There is more of a pattern when we look at the periods through the lens of the Fed instead: in hiking cycles, average spreads widen meaningfully during war periods with negative total returns (around +10bp / -4.3% at the 3m mark). In paused or cutting cycles, spreads tend to tighten with positive total returns (around −6bps / +3.0% at the 3m mark). In other words, while geopolitical headlines can lift near-term volatility, the direction and magnitude of US IG spreads and returns are primarily a function of whether the Fed is tightening financial conditions or easing them in response to the conflict. Escalation that sees shipping flows through the Strait of Hormuz constrained, driving oil and gas to USD130/bbl and EUR110/MWh, respectively. For energy markets, we view gas as more vulnerable than oil. Qatari LNG cargoes cannot be diverted if the Hormuz passage is constrained, for example. In addition, the European gas market will end this winter with lower-than-expected storage levels, and unlike oil markets, there are no strategic gas reserves. Oil in contrast has five key circuit breakers that can help to insulate against rapid upside: OPEC+ supply increases, diversion of pipelines in Saudi Arabia and the UAE, high Chinese stocks, significant volumes in floating storage, and strategic reserves. But going forward, activity in the Strait of Hormuz is critical to the outlook, as the channel sees approximately 15mbd of crude flow that has been disrupted. Even in the best-case scenario of full usage of all these circuit breakers , the market would still run short by 2.5mbd, implying a price of ~USD85/bbl. Average Q4 y/y inflation would be around 0.5pp higher in 2026 (Figure 12), when accounting for direct and indirect effects, which would take the annual average to around 2.3%. We would expect the ECB to ‘look through’ the shock, rather than try to offset it by tightening monetary policy. After all, it would fit into the bucket of mid-sized but persistent shocks that ECB Chief Economist Philip Lane has argued does not necessarily warrant a response if it represents a supply-driven shock to relative price levels (speech, 3 December 2025). The combination of the February CPI/PPI print and much higher energy prices due to Hormuz disruptions suggests higher CPI/PPI inflation at least in H1 than we previously anticipated. Our commodity strategy team have revised up their 2026 full-year average oil price forecast by more than 10% since our last PPI inflation forecast change, while crude oil future prices imply a potential additional 20%+ upside risk. March headline CPI inflation is likely to remain at around 1.0% yoy, and headline PPI inflation could rise further towards 0% yoy. Therefore, we revise up our 2026 full-year CPI/PPI inflation forecasts to 0.8%/0.3% (vs. 0.6%/-0.5% previously), driven by stronger sequential price gains in Q1 and Q2. Under the revised path, year-over-year PPI inflation is likely to turn positive as early as the start of Q2 2026. Given the elevated uncertainty around oil prices, further upside risks to China’s inflation remain should oil prices move higher. Moreover, if imports from the Middle East were cut off and this situation became prolonged, the impact on Japanese economy could be severe. Estimates by Sano and Nagamachi (2022) using the 2015 input-output tables 7 suggest that under a tail-risk scenario in which imports of coal, crude oil and natural gas from the Middle East are permanently disrupted with no alternative supply found, nominal GDP would decline by just under 3%. That said, Japan’s dependence on oil has likely declined since the time of those estimates as domestic supplies of oil (crude plus petroleum products) in primary energy have fallen around 30%, from 7,406P J in FY15 to 5,138P J in FY24, proportionally reducing any negative impact. Over the medium to long term, securing alternative supply sources could mitigate the damage to some extent. We note that the bulk of this week’s repricing higher in monetary policy expectations was concentrated in 1H26 (+5bp in EUR/USD and +15bp in GBP) and 2H26 (+15/20bp on the week), while changes in 2027 pricing have been more contained. Notably, after the attack on Iran last weekend, the ECB OIS curve went from reflecting some probability of cuts to hikes (previ- ously about 10bp of cuts priced in by end-26 vs. around 27bp of hikes currently). Markets have shifted to price only 11bp BoE cuts this year (vs. ~55bp priced in previously) and around 37bp cumulative easing for the Fed (vs. ~43bp before the weekend strikes). Such a hawkish market reaction suggests that rate markets have assigned more weight to the risk of a significant inflation shock that prompts less easing or tighter central bank policy, rather than to the potential growth hit due to supply chain disruptions and overall weaker global business sentiment. We expect a finely balanced 25bp cut, on a knife-edge Given our expectation that the data will move in a way that suggests a sharper labour market loosening than the BoE forecasts and the possibility that we see relatively short-lived energy price shock and some reduction in uncertainty in advance of the MPC meeting, we retain our call that the MPC will cut 25bp. However, whereas previously we had a firm conviction of this outcome, we now view the probabilities as finely balanced and acknowledge the sensitivities outlined above on data and geopolitics. We expect the decision to be finely balanced for a number of members of the committee (most pertinently Bailey and Mann, but also, we think, DG Ramsden and potentially DG Breeden too), we think the most likely vote split would be a 5-4 majority, with Mann making the switch to support a cut, but Governor Bailey inclined to follow the behavioural pattern he used in November around the budget uncertainty, weighing caution more than the data flow. It is notable that such a vote would see the Governor in the minority – something that has not yet happened in his tenure – alongside his DG for Monetary Policy and his Chief Economist. Looking at 1y OIS swaps, the market in early February was pricing in semiannual hikes starting in March, but is now pricing in semiannual hikes starting in April (Figure 2). With the tally of FY26 labor union wage hike requests also coming in firm as expected, we likewise forecast semiannual rate hikes starting in April. If concerns of stagflation strengthen on prolonged Middle East tensions and high commodity prices, fueling market expectations for a potential delay to BoJ rate hikes, there would initially be scope for short-tenor swap rates to decline toward levels consistent with a scenario where hikes resume in June. That said, higher oil prices could simultaneously reinforce contrasting currency pressures on the US, now a net oil exporter, and on Japan, which remains highly dependent on external energy supplies (ie, USD strength and JPY weakness). As such, unless the situation clearly deteriorates further and becomes prolonged, sharply increasing concerns about domestic economic deterioration, short-tenor swaps are unlikely to show a strong directional move from current levels. If we focus on survey based 1-year-ahead inflation expectations from the Michigan survey, we find they have not been persistently responsive to oil prices outside the 2007-2008 period and the post-COVID inflation cycle either (Exhibit 2). And it is even difficult to argue that the 2007-2008 spike was purely a supply shock, though it may have been from the US’ perspective. The Euro area and Japan offer a similar story Broadening the scope of the exercise, we find that the sensitivity of inflation in the Euro area and Japan appears larger than in the US, especially on headline, which likely reflects a larger incidence of energy in the CPI and a greater dependence on energy imports. Moving away from T-bills, the BoJ announced last Friday its decision to apply regular conditions to the upper limit on consecutive-day purchases of the same issue under the SLF (a maximum of 50 business days, in principle) to CTDs starting this Monday. With generous Gengaku Sochi now fully utilized and futures rollovers underway, the BoJ has taken another step toward “normalization” of the SLF (Figure 15R e g u l a r c o n d i t i o n o f t h e u p p e r l i m i t o n c o n s e c u t i v e - d a y p u r c h a s e s o f t h e s a m e i s s u e n o w a p p l i e s t o C T D s ). While map- ping the future direction of the conflict is beyond the scope of this piece, the most immediate risk to the US economy comes from rising energy prices. At the time of writing, WTI and Brent crude oil prices had both increased around 35% from their average over the past year. These increases are coming off of a low base, with prices recently having reached their lowest level since the outbreak of the Russia/Ukraine war in 2022 (Figure 1). Natural gas prices, meanwhile, have been essentially unchanged in the US, in contrast to a spike in Europe. Conversely, a quicker de-escalation of the conflict would likely drive a faster drop in TTF back to the coal switching range in the 40 EURs/MWh. While we observed at times during the last week some sympathy in intra-day Henry n Hub trading relative to TTF, we maintain our view that US natural gas prices are likely to remain insulated from the spike in European gas and global LNG prices, given the US is a net exporter of LNG, with essentially no spare capacity at export terminals. This revision lowers our global LNG supply by 2.8 mtpa on average in 2027-2030, which does not derail our very bearish global gas price view for 2028 and 2029. The starting point is already relatively positive, hence the hit to growth and upward pressure on inflation should be manageable if the spike in oi l prices is relatively short-lived. While the US can to some extent absorb an energy shock due to domestic production and China has large strategic reserves and bilateral agreements, Europe lacks both of these, leaving the region uniquely exposed (particularly in gas). For central banks, this seems unlikely to prompt a meaningful reaction. There is little that monetary policy can do to address a temporary price shift driven by an exogenous shock . Rather, this reinforces our view of an on-hold ECB this year, as well as a prolonged policy pause for the BoE after a final rate cut in H1. Likewise, we see the BoJ proceeding with hikes and retain our call for the next move to be in April. When mapping economic scenarios, our primary consideration is the duration of the conflict. We would consider changing our views if oil were to both rise above USD100/bbl and remain there for a prolonged period. This reaction has been similar in terms of direction to what was seen last year after the outbreak of the 12-day Israel-Iran conflict, although DM curves had remained little changed back in 2025 and the magnitude of the moves was more contained. Instead, this week’s market reaction to the Middle East conflict has been broadly opposite relative to the Russia-Ukraine episode of 2022. In the aftermath of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, DM curves had indeed bull steepened across the board with the front-end rallying 20-25bp in a week, as markets priced in a slower pace of policy tightening from major central banks and resorted to flight-to-quality into govies. Swap spreads widened on risk-off sentiment, while intra-EMU spreads tightened 5-15bp on the week given the ECB's implicit commitment to prevent fragmentation, the symmetric nature of the price shock and the announcement of fiscal responses across the whole Euro area. It is worth noting that UK consumer energy prices are regulated via the quarterly Ofgem price cap (and are now fixed for April) which is based on NPB forward curve rather than wholesale prices. We currently estimate a mechanical 0.3% impact on headline CPI from the move in the forward curve and taking into account second round effects we currently estimate the recent energy shock might increase headline CPI by around 0.6% by July to 2.7%. We acknowledge that increased gas prices limits the ability for the BoE to ease in the near term but assuming the conflict does not extend beyond several months into the summer, we think BoE easing later this year is still a possibility against a backdrop of an ongoing easing in the labour market. In addition, global downside growth risks likely increase if oil were to persistently rise above 100$/bbl. Given this, we recommend recveiving Dec26 MPC OIS with a few bp of easing priced. records.text: M Global Foundation 16 The Structure of Global Trade Data The Harmonized System In 2023, US$24 trillion worth of global goods traded across 200+ categorized trade countries/groups. The World Customs Organization's "Harmonized System" is the framework most commonly used to create a standardized economic language that organizes the colossal amount of data that describes trade flows. The Harmonized System is a globally accepted product nomenclature that assigns product codes to individual goods, which allows customs authorities globally to determine the taxes, tariffs and duties for exporting or importing any good. It is also used to gather globally comparable trade statistics. For fundamental equity analysts more familiar with the Global Industry Classification Standard (GICS), North American Industry Classification System (NAICS), or the legacy Standard Industrial Classification codes (SIC), HS codes are similar in concept and can be mapped. They operate on a similar principle, with a sequence of digits offering more granularity on a product's specifications. Harmonized System of tariff Nomenclature (maintained by the World Customs Organization) The HS system uses 6-digit codes. Each code is structured in the same way: • Chapter — the first 2 numbers represent the HS2 code, e.g., 08 for "Edible fruit and nuts, peel of citrus fruit or melons." • Heading — adding the next two numbers (08.04) gives the HS4 code for "Dates, figs, pineapples, avocados, guavas, mangoes and mangostee

If there is no long-lasting disruption in the Strait of Hormuz, J.P. Morgan forecasts oil prices to stay elevated around $80-85/bbl before retracing down to approximately $70/bbl later in 2026. In this scenario, the energy price spike is expected to increase global CPI inflation by 1% and reduce GDP growth by 0.6% in 2026. The overall macro impact would be modest in such a scenraio and unlikely to derail the global expansion or significantly alter monetary policy paths . However, there are growing risks of more severe and persistent disruptions in the Middle East (e.g. an extended closure of the Strait of Hormuz): this would lead to larger/longer-lasting impact on energy prices (Brent price spiking above $100/bbl and TTF gas above €60-80/MWh) as well as a more substantial hit to growth owing to supply chain distruptions and weaker business sentiment. In terms of strategy, in Euro space, we find this weeks’ pricing of ECB tightening expecta- tions excessive, but do not find risk-reward attractive in outright duration exposure near term. We enter OW 5Y Germany vs. US as low-beta way to fade recent cheapening in Euro rates. We also recommend bullish duration proxies via options. I

Morgan Securities LLC Global Markets Strategy U.S. Fixed Income Markets Weekly 06 March 2026 J P M O R G A N • We are revising our JULI spread target to 85bp or 12bp tighter than current levels (our 85bp JULI target is roughly equivalent to 73bp OAS for the Bloomberg IG index). Our prior forecast in late November was for 110bp, or +15bp from levels at the time. In the interim, the market hit new all-time tights of 82bp in late January, with the following February the worst month for spreads (+14bp) since September 2022, leaving spreads now marginally wider versus their 1yr average. So what’s changed in our thinking? • First, fundamentals are strong with growth and earnings surprising to the upside, but higher uncertainty from tariffs and commodities should now restrain ‘animal spirits’. Second, the ongoing conflict with Iran may move markets near-term and provide a slightly better entry point, but it’s unlikely to be a negative for spreads unless it compels the Fed to hike. Third, a worsening fiscal outlook portends higher UST issuance over time such that their share of the bond market is increasing, incentivizing an overweight to spread products. records.text: 8 06 March 2026 Even where female labor market integration looks strong on the surface, large reserves remain once hours are considered. Higher female employment rates often come with much lower hours than men. Germany is a good example: the female employment rate is high at 74.1%, only 6.6%-pts below men (Figure 4E U e m p l o y m e n t r a t e a n d w o r k i n g h o u r s r e l a t i o n s h i p ). But the share of women working part-time is 7.4%-pts higher. Survey evidence from the European Commission points to the usual frictions: unpaid care responsibilities, limited/expensive childcare, and tax-benefit designs that penalize second-earners. This means policymakers can still play a significant role in integrating women into the labor market by expanding affordable childcare and eldercare; reducing secondary earner-tax wedges and removing “part-time traps”; and supporting flexible work arrangements that enable progression to longer hours. This is especially important in laggards such as Italy, where female participation remains low and progress has been slow despite NGEU-related reforms. The price change so far should be marginally hawkish for monetary policy and reinforces our call for the Fed to remain on hold. However, we recognize a prolonged surge in crude oil to $120/bbl or more would result in a much larger drag on growth and could precipitate a dovish turn by the FOMC (see US: Oil and the economy, Abiel Reinhart and Michael Hanson, 3/6/26). Data took a backseat to geopolitical developments this week, but the February employment report came in weaker than expected, showing a notable reversal in January’s private sector job gains and a tick up in the unemployment rate to 4.4%. Although last year’s downward momentum in labor demand appears to have been arrested, there is not yet a clear sign of reacceleration. For now, we think the FOMC will probably be comfortable looking through the recent noise in job growth as they await more clarity on the labor market and any inflationary developments stemming from the Iran conflict (see US: What January gives, February takes (jobs), Abiel Reinhart, 3/6/26). If there is no long-lasting disruption in the Strait of Hormuz, J.P. Morgan forecasts oil prices to stay elevated around $80-85/bbl before retracing down to approximately $70/bbl later in 2026. In this scenario, the energy price spike is expected to increase global CPI inflation by 1% and reduce GDP growth by 0.6% in 2026. The overall macro impact would be modest in such a scenraio and unlikely to derail the global expansion or significantly alter monetary policy paths . However, there are growing risks of more severe and persistent disruptions in the Middle East (e.g. an extended closure of the Strait of Hormuz): this would lead to larger/longer-lasting impact on energy prices (Brent price spiking above $100/bbl and TTF gas above €60-80/MWh) as well as a more substantial hit to growth owing to supply chain distruptions and weaker business sentiment. In terms of strategy, in Euro space, we find this weeks’ pricing of ECB tightening expecta- tions excessive, but do not find risk-reward attractive in outright duration exposure near term. Morgan It’s interesting that the moves in swap spreads this week differed from those following “Lib- eration Day.” As we noted earlier this week, swap spreads narrowed in an almost parallel fashion in April last year, and zero duration spread sharply narrowed. However, this week’s moves have been in the swap spread curve, as term funding premium has increased sharply and appears to be over one standard error above our estimate of fair value (Figure 10). We think this could be due to a confluence of factors. One, as we have noted before, an increase in volatility makes carry-seeking strategies appear less attractive on a carry-to-risk ratio basis. records.text: 26 Eduardo Lecubarri AC (44-20) 7134-5916 eduardo.lecubarri@jpmorgan.com Global Markets Strategy 08 March 2026 J P M O R G A N SMid vs Large We stick to our Nov 3, 2023 OW of SMid vs Large in DMs ex-J and note this trade has delivered alpha, with SMid flattening out vs Large through Mar 2025 and outperforming since then. After a >2 yr 20-35% underperformance of SMid vs Large across DMs (i.e. 2021-23), the relative performance of SMid vs Large flattened out since Nov 2023 and rallied since Liberation Day in most DMs. We see SMid-Caps benefiting from their oversold state, undemanding valuations, improving fundamentals (relative to those of Large-Caps), and their more domestic exposure within a world that is facing turmoil in global trade. We also remind investors that, contrary to common belief, even if we were to hit a bear market, SMid should do well vs Large (it wouldn’t be the first time – Sep 2000 to Oct 2003 and Nov 2008 to Mar 2009 are 2 examples of SMid outperforming in a bear market). In short, we continue to see SMid offering a very asymmetric investment opportunity, with the potential to underperform short term by 0-5% in a worst-case scenario, but within what we consider to be a 30-60% alpha opportunity relative to Large over the coming 3-5 years. records.text: US Rates Weekly 06 March 2026 Citi Research 15 Vol: Sell the overly rich receiver skew Due to the spike in oil price and growing inflation worries, swaption vols have increased amid the rates sell-off, which goes against the extremely flat risk reversal (pay-rec) skews. We recommend monetizing the elevated vol and rich receiver skews by owning costless 3m1y receiver ladders to position for a modest rate rally. Growing inflation concerns widening policy rate distribution The unexpected escalation in the Middle East conflict over the past week and the associating higher oil price/inflationary concerns have led to higher implied volatilities across all assets, with the repricing in EUR rates vol being the most extreme on a z-score basis (Figure 23). For both US and EUR, short-expiry vols on front-end rates have led the richening across the swaption surfaces as market expectations for central bank policy rates have changed meaningfully on the growing inflationary concerns. The increase in upper-left vols in both US and EUR over the past month has been the largest in recent years (Figure 24). The richening in EUR implied vol has been relatively straight forward in that gamma was at an extremely low starting level, pricing for essentially unchanged ECB policy rate with only a slight dovish bias just a week ago. Moving away from T-bills, the BoJ announced last Friday its decision to apply regular conditions to the upper limit on consecutive-day purchases of the same issue under the SLF (a maximum of 50 business days, in principle) to CTDs starting this Monday. With generous Gengaku Sochi now fully utilized and futures rollovers underway, the BoJ has taken another step toward “normalization” of the SLF (Figure 15R e g u l a r c o n d i t i o n o f t h e u p p e r l i m i t o n c o n s e c u t i v e - d a y p u r c h a s e s o f t h e s a m e i s s u e n o w a p p l i e s t o C T D s ). In our 2026 Outlook, we flagged that conditions were set for the normalization of the SLF, and we see a reasonable likelihood that the BoJ will raise the minimum lending fee back to 50bp during the interim QT assessment in June. We continue to think the BoJ is on track to take this action. That said, we expect the overall impact to be relatively contained, given the limited usage of the Facility. It's not just about returns, it's about correlations too Equities and bonds selling off together at various points this week sparked by the conflict in Iran have brought up the spectre of markets coming out of the pandemic, when stocks-UST returns correlation stayed stubbornly positive. Back then, 60/40 equity-bond portfolios saw the worst annual performance in nearly a century, and the memories of that experience run so deep that even now, several years on, we often have long debates with investors on whether bonds work as diversifiers. By law, EXIM must reserve at least 20 percent of its total financing authority (i.e., US$27 billion out of US$135 billion) for support under this program. That weighs on labour supply and social security systems. The need for reform seemed obvious, the political capital available much less so. From reform needs to proposals, but perhaps not implementation “Keeping social security contributions stable” seemed to be the primary policy ambition flagged. That doesn’t sound very ambitious as a policy ambition. But given the state of the economy and underlying challenges, it is. It requires either great efficiency gains in the system, outright spending cuts, much stronger growth dynamics, or a combination of all three. The social welfare state reform proposal by an expert commission in January would be a bold step in that direction, we think. It’s a long-term project, that would merge social security institutions and require digitalisation efforts. This alone could reduce bureaucracy and operating costs. In a second step, means-testing social transfers could follow. The sub-optimal interplay between taxation and social security contributions and payouts for a large group of middle-income households creates a long-lamented disincentive to work. In Germany, we expect a drop in January manufacturing orders (-2.5%M) after two strong months boosted by military spending. January industrial production should instead see an uptick (1.4%M), due to a correction from a weak December print in auto and other larger sectors. In Italy, we expect flat industrial production, while at euro area level, we expect IP to rebound in January at 0.8%M. Germany will also see the release of its January trade data, where we forecast another uptick in exports and trade balance at EUR15.1bn. Last but not least, next week will also bring the final February inflation prints for the Netherlands, Germany, Portugal, France and Spain - we expect all of these to come in in-line with their flash estimate. Outside of data, the weekend will see State elections taking place in Baden- Württemberg. Exit polls are expected on Sunday shortly after 6pm CET. Source: Barclays Research JPY Outlook (last updated 18 November) • Although the JPY has weakened nearly 5% since PM Takaichi won the party leader election,• we expect USDJPY to remain elevated, with risks skewed to the upside. Our bullish USDJPY view is based on domestic and global factors. On the domestic front, the new administration’s expansionary fiscal policies and dovish monetary policy bias should continue to weigh on the currency, while verbal interventions so far indicate that any eventual action may still be steps away. In addition, the JPY may face further selling pressures due to its correlation to the JGB term premia, particularly if Takaichi decides to call for an early snap election that strengthens her political mandate to pursue more expansionary economic policies (see the JPY part of the overview). On the global front, US exceptionalism is a triple whammy for the JPY: 1) the decline in global equity risk premia has reduced safe-haven demand for the JPY, especially since 2023; 2) capital flows from Japan to the US equity persist, including retail flows under the New NISA tax exemption scheme; and 3) " digital deficits" continue to grow. records.text: M Idea 6 It is easy to remark that at time of sudden innovation in the information set positioning can matter as much as the perceived changed in fundamentals. 1 What is interesting to us is how markets developed as time passed in 2022. Oil stabilized fairly quickly whereas by the end of our cut off period the natural gas price had risen sharply. Inflation swaps did not reprice significantly higher, but nominal yields climbed steadily as central banks were forced to increase interest rates and the long end was hurt by rising term premia as bond-equity correlation flipped. 2022 serves a warning about the difficulty in gauging the eventual economic impact of geopolitical events. Exhibit 6 shows that revisions to inflation and growth were significant. We however caveat that the conditions that led to outsized central bank tightening are not present right now. Back then the energy supply shock interacted with post-Covid bottlenecks, central banks started from highly expansionary monetary policy and fiscal support was used freely. 1. These households are already struggling, so further erosion of their real spending power from surging energy prices could cause another leg up in delinquencies (particularly credit cards and autos). In turn, this could have a lasting impact on their ability to spend, if it constrains their access to credit. Third, higher energy prices could become a bottleneck for AI capex. The hyperscalers – Amazon, Microsoft and Google – have announced massive data center investment plans for this year. Our GDP forecast incorporates a continued tailwind from AI-related investment. Delays in investment because of an energy price shock could be a major headwind for 2026 growth. It is difficult to assess exactly how large and persistent the oil price shock would have to be for these effects to kick in. But in our view, a sustained period of oil prices above $100/bbl (~60% increase) would probably take more than 60bp off GDP growth. And a doubling in oil prices, unlikely as it seems, could cause a recession.

As of early 2025, the region’s female labor force participation rate stood at 52.6%, compared to 74.9% for men—a 22%-pts gap that is virtually unchanged from 2024 (ILO, 2025). The female employment rate reached 48.9% versus 71.4% for men, and the unemployment rate for women was 7.0%, still higher than the 4.8% observed for men. While the overall regional employment rate rose to 60% and informality declined slightly to 46.7%, disparities remain substantial, especially among young women and those from lower-income households. Persistent gaps in participation, employment, wages, and job quality underscore the need for further action and reflect the region’s multi-faceted challenges. LAC continues to have the second-highest adolescent fertility rate globally, and research shows that motherhood remains a key driver of gender gaps: after the birth of a first child, women’s labor force participation drops by over 20% and earnings by more than 40% in Latin America, with no comparable effect for men. We drilled down on the auto loan-level dataset to analyze the observed recovery lag. We denoted the month in which the charge-off amount first occurred at T and then looked at the total recovery rate as well as how fast recoveries came in the months after the default (T+m). For example, the recovery rate on auto loans charge-off across ABS pools in June 2025 was 37%, with 41% of the recoveries occurring in the same month as the charge-off, followed by 25%, 15% and 8% in subsequent months (Figure 4R e c o v e r y l a g f o r a g g r e g a t e a u t o l o a n A B S p o o l s ). In comparison, the recovery rate for auto loans charged off in June 2019 was roughly 50%, with 47% recovered in the same month as the chargeoff, and 18%, 9% and 5% in each of the following three months. Loans charged off at the peak of used car prices in December 2021 saw the highest recovery in recent years at 63%, but experienced a rela- tively longer lag as well, with only 28% of the recovery collected at month T, 20% at T+1m, 13% in T+2m and 10% in T+3m. records.text: 0 0 5Y 10Y 15Y 20Y 25Y 30Y Source: J.P. Morgan. Volatility It took months to forget volatility; it took a weekend to remember why it matters! Euro area rates volatility jumped this week as the US/Israel war versus Iran continues and concerns around energy prices remain at the forefront. Implied volatility curve flattened across tails as markets started to price more than 25bp of ECB hikes by end-2026 - around 35bp at the time of writing (Figure 18I m p l i e d v o l a t i l i t y e x p l o d e d t h i s w e e k w i t h a n a g g r e s s i v e f l a t t e n i n g o f t h e v o l a t i l i t y c u r v e a c r o s s t a i l s ). The implied volatility curve (3M expiry) has now inverted with 3Mx5Y being the peak of the surface. The 1W change in front-end implieds was one of the largest seen over the past few years (Figure 19T h e 1 W c h a n g e i n 3 M x 2 Y i m p l i e d s w a s o n e o f t h e l a r g e s t s e e n s i n c e t h e s t a r t o f t h e t i g h t e n i n g c y c l e ). 1M delivered volatility also jumped sharply higher, with that for 2Y and 10Y swaps rising around 3.2 and 1.5bp/day over the week. Anecdotal evidence suggests some unwinding of pre-existing short volatility positions and also covering of short OTM put positions which were initiated as part of the bullish struc- tures over the past few weeks.
