That being said, it was not all bad news. The U -6 measure of underemployment fell by two tenths to 7.9%, while our proxy for aggregate nominal wage growth remained healthy at 4.45% , supported by steady hours at the top of their range over the last almost two years (34.3) and continued solid wage gains (+0.4% vs. +0.4%). Indeed, there was a noticeable increase in hours worked and wage growth for production and nonsupervisory workers in the construction sector, suggesting that employers can adapt to the low -hiring/low-firing equilibrium by increasing labor demand on the intensive margin if they are unable to hire. In addition, some of the decline in the labor force can be attributed to the change in population controls and also seems to be focused among older workers; the prime -age participation rate remains near recent multi-decade highs. As some of the weakness ( -31k) was a function of workers at a large healthcare company going on strike, our preferred interpretation of February payrolls is to add back in that temporary strike -related decline and then average that with January’s stronger -than-expected gains. China, once a major recipient of FDI that fueled its rapid rise as a manufacturing powerhouse, has now emerged as a significant global FDI investor. Unlike US FDI, which often supports integrated supply chains and knowledge-intensive industries, Chinese outward investment has been shaped by different priorities. Early Chinese FDI was largely driven by state-owned enterprises and characterized by strategic, large-scale transactions aligned with the country’s broader global ambitions, most notably those outlined in the BRI. The BRI aims to enhance China’s global connectivity, expand export markets, and secure access to energy and natural resources. Over the past two decades, the destinations and sectors for Chinese FDI have diverged sharply from those favored by US investors. Chinese FDI has become increasingly relevant worldwide, but its greatest influence remains in developing countries, where it has accumulated an estimated US$1.2 trillion in flows since 2005. The main reason is the exceptionally favorable operating environment that the semiconductor companies are experiencing. Record supply shortfall in both DRAM and NAND relative to strong demand growth driven by hyperscaler investment is resulting in sharply increasing memory prices which flow to outsized bottom line gains for memory producers given the industry’s high operating leverage. TrendForce have raised their DRAM and NAND ASP forecasts again and Korea’s memory exports reached a record high in February. Moreover, our earnings revision lead indicator (ERLI), which maps high frequency monthly macro and industry data onto forecasts of sellside analyst forecast revisions in the next two months, is most positive on Korea and the tech sector. EM Strategy: Reduce EM local markets further, from OW to MW A considerable amount of uncertainty remains for EM six days into the conflict between the US/Israel and Iran and we are using yesterday’s rally back to reduce our remaining small OW EM FX and Local Rates positions to now MW both. We reduced our OW EM FX and OW EM Rates positions in half on Monday (see here) given what we felt was only a small market reaction in EM at the time against what was a much worse scenario of attacks on Iran that resulted in an effective shutting of the Straits of Hormuz and retaliatory strikes by Iran against GCC countries. Since then, markets had a day of panic on Tuesday but a rally back since then, while we are seeing the uncertainty as remaining and potentially growing through time. The uncertainty around how this conflict de-escalates in a way that allows energy supplies to freely flow again and energy prices to quickly decline is high and if there are still active hostilities in 3-4 weeks – which are timelines the US and Israel have outlined – then EM markets will likely need to rethink current levels given the potential impact on growth and inflation globally. records.text: 17 06 March 2026 According to McKinsey’s annual Women in the Workplace 2025 survey, women hold 29% of C-suite roles, unchanged from 2024. The “broken rung” begins at entry- level as women are less likely to be promoted within entry level (30% vs. 43% for men). McKinsey reports that only 31% of entry-level women have a sponsor vs. 45% of men. Employees with sponsors are nearly twice as likely to have been promoted (65% vs. 35%). Only about half of companies prioritize women’s advancement in 2025 as programs beneficial to women (e.g., remote/flexible work, formal sponsorship) have been scaled back. Political leadership: Paradoxes persist alongside widest gender gap While the World Economic Forum reports that the greatest progress towards gender parity has been observed in the area of Political Empowerment, it still has the largest remaining gap to close. The World Economic Forum’s Global Gender Gap Report 2025 measures gender parity across four key subindex categories. In the area of Health and Survival, the gender gap closed by 96.2% and the Educational Attainment gap by 95.1%, but the Economic Participation and Opportunity gap and the Political Empowerment gap remain large and have closed by only 61% and 23.4%, respectively. Despite the wide gap between men and women, political empowerment has seen by far the most improvement, with the gap narrowing by 9%-pts, from 14.3% in 2006 to 23.4 % in 2025. Morgan Securities plc Global Markets Strategy Global Fixed Income Markets Weekly (Advance version) 06 March 2026 J P M O R G A N • DM rate markets have repriced significantly following last weekend’s strikes on Iran: yield curves bear flattened 10-20bp over the past week with a 25-50bp sell-off in 1Yx1Y rates, with European rates’ underperformance driven by the energy price spike and liquidations of crowded positions. Relative to previous similar events, the response of DM rate markets to this week's Middle East tensions differs substantially from previous comparable events such as the outbreak of the Russia- Ukriane conflict in 2022. The magnitude of this week’s market moves and anecdot- al evidence suggest that unwinds of crowded positions has played an important role in exacerbating market moves, particularly in Europe. We think that the situation in the Middle East remains fluid, with the duration and scale of the oil and gas supply disruptions remaining key to determining the impact on inflation and growth over the coming months. We therefore remain cautious on outright fading the move in the Euro area duration but enter OW 5Y Germany vs. US as low-beta way to fade the cheapening and enter bullish proxies via options. Morgan Securities LLC Global Markets Strategy U.S. Fixed Income Markets Weekly 06 March 2026 J P M O R G A N Credit Strategy Update Addressing the default landscape for leveraged credit in the aftermath (or midst) of AI disruption When we published our 2026 outlook in November here, we established a preliminary 2027 par-weighted high-yield bond and leveraged loan default forecast of 2.0% and 3.5%, respec- tively, which was 25bp and 50bp above our 2026 default forecasts of 1.75% (HY) and 3.00% (LL). Following a 2026 calendar year which resembles what transpired in 2025 for default activity, our rationale for the inflection higher in default rates was a large maturity wall in 2028 ($488bn) that included a sizeable attribution to lower-rated loans. Fast forward, and concerns about disruption from AI in select segments of the leveraged credit universe have led to a rapid build in the distressed universe without a coinciding collapse in fundamentals. This has mostly included Software and some pockets of Services and Healthcare (insurance brokers are far from stressed), pockets which account for a much larger proportion of the leveraged loan universe. For example, Software accounts for 4.7% of High-Yield (par), 14.5% of Leveraged Loans (par), and 20.8% of Direct Lending (count). While there are only $21bn of Software loans

Unfortunately, the next comprehensive NZ labour force survey is not due until early May. This lack of a trigger links to a common topic in client discussions: the difficult carry set-up to play NZ policy normalization. NZD 1s/2s is steep, and the RBNZ is likely to normalize, but doesn’t show urgency to start. The relative underreaction of NZ assets to the survey and growth data is then partially justified in the sense that excess capacity buys the RBNZ time, pushing policy normalization into the forwards, which are now close to fair value (Figure 8N Z D 1 Y x 1 Y i s a b o u t f a i r i n o u t r i g h t t e r m s g i v e n m a c r o i n p u t s a s t h e y s t a n d ). The precise timing of the coming unemployment rate decline in a sense summarizes the carry headwind, as an imminent tightening of the labour market would overcome negative carry concerns. In our models, every 1%-pt lower on unemployment flattens 2s/10s swap by 40bp, and 6m forward 2s/10s is about 15bp below spot. A roughly 0.3-0.4%-pt fall in unemployment in the next six months is then needed to beat the forwards. If current curve shape is preserved, we look to re-enter NZD flattening trades closer to the 1Q labour data. At the risk of oversimplifying, the US exports economic shocks, but it doesn’t import them. Will this time be different? Focus on oil prices To the extent that geopolitical events (particularly those in the Middle East) do affect the US economy, the biggest concern would be oil prices. Energy goods and services account for less than 4% of US consumer spending. About half of that is gasoline. Accounting for the pass-through from crude oil to energy and other inflation components, we estimate that a 10% increase in crude oil prices would raise PCE inflation by nearly 10bp in the near term. This effect would fade over the course of a year, as higher oil prices would weigh on demand for other goods and services. We estimate that the headwind to consumer spending would be like the upside to inflation: about 10bp. What about other components of GDP? Input-output data suggest that petroleum and coal products make up about 1% of total value added across industries. Putting everything together, we estimate that a 10% increase in energy prices would weigh on US GDP by no more than 10bp. This figure might seem small but recall that the US is now a net exporter of oil and gas. records.text: e economic outlook: Until recently, downside risk scenarios in European equities were relatively subdued and not materially priced in. This week marked a sharp repricing of that tail. The longer the current dynamic persists, the higher the probability that a bear case begins to materialise. The mix of rising uncertainty, deteriorating sentiment and shifting risk distributions has forced investors (and us) to revisit base case assumptions and in turn our overweight exposure to equities, particularly for Europe. Vulnerabilities in the base case: Our outlook for a European economic recovery, and by extension revived corporate earnings growth, rested on a key pillar of a manufacturing pickup that now faces incremental headwinds. Germany’s fiscal impulse from infrastructure and defence programmes was expected to provide a demand tailwind. However, both sectors are notably energy-intensive and Europe remains a net importer of energy. Any spike in energy prices or supply disruption would amplify cost burdens for companies, creating a potential drag on the anticipated multiplier effect. One reason is that China aims to increase its near-term presence in the destination country, before gaining a clearer understanding of the local business, policy, and political environment. The key difference from greenfield FDI or M&A is that, overseas contracted projects are usually short/mid-term and project-based, with no ownership change, with focus on project completion. Official data from China’s Ministry of Commerce show that accumulated ODI to BRI-related economies amounted to US$336 billion by 2024. Meanwhile, Chinese enterprises have managed to secure steady contracted construction projects in BRI countries, followed by a jump in the past two years. Between 2014 and 2022, the value of contracts newly signed amounted to US$1.14 trillion in total, with completed value at US$748 billion. In 2023 and 2024, the value of contracts newly signed averaged US$230 billion, with completed value picking up to US$135 billion per year. Not uniform: The impact on individual member states depends on a number of factors, including the energy intensity of GDP as well as the energy mix and the extent to which energy is imported versus produced domestically (see Figure 2). In short, and unsurprisingly, Germany appears particularly vulnerable, given the weight of industry, the energy intensity of output and the fossil-fuel-based nature of its energy supply. By contrast, France looks more insulated, as renewables account for more than half of its energy mix. Italy looks more sensitive to gas prices than to oil, and Spain vice versa (Figures 18 and 19). While the UK benefits from lower energy intensity, its energy mix is relatively unfavourable. Overall, as economies suffer a terms-of-trade shock, the impact on GDP will be determined not only by energy intensity and mix but also by factors such as import dependence and substitution effects. Claudia Goldin, the 2023 Nobel laureate in economics, Professor of Economics at Harvard University and Co-Director of the Gender in the Economy group at the National Bureau of Economic Research, identifies greater female autonomy as producing lower birth rates. She notes that over the past 50 years, birth rates have declined in virtually every country. One of the great demographic surprises of the modern era is a negative relationship between per capita income levels and fertility. Higher-income households have fewer children than their lower-income counterparts. The greater agency that women have gained as they obtain more education and pursue a career has led to lower birth rates. Her modeling shows that the faster the per capita economic growth, the more the level of births desired by men relative to the level desired by women will diverge. records.text: US Credit Alpha Overview Yields remain the driving force in credit. Despite geopolitical and AI-driven risks, index-level spreads continue to track their typical relationships with yields. Macro data have been surprising to the upside, leading the market to price in fewer Fed cuts and at later dates. The power of yield Yields remain the dominant force shaping US credit. Despite the developments in the Middle East, secondary credit markets have for the most part maintained a "business-as-usual" attitude (see Investor repositioning in US IG amid geopolitical risk). In addition, index-level spreads ignored recent concerns about software/private credit and followed Treasuries' lead. With the 10y falling to 3.94%, investment grade spreads sold off, hitting wides of 84bp, but as rates reversed course (trading at 4.13% as of Thursday afternoon), so did spreads, rallying to 80bp (as of Wednesday close). The recent episode supports the view that rates continue to anchor demand in this environment, with the rates-spread beta roughly in line with what we discussed recently in All About the Yield Correlation. Within credit, spread recovery has been most pronounced in areas that had cheapened the most. BDCs have retraced 12bp of their widening since mid-February (20-25% retracement), and life insurers have recovered about 6bp (~25-30% retracement), helped by short covering as well. records.text: Global FX Strategy 08 March 2026 Citi Research 2 We remain USD bulls into summer; however, we do not want to get too excited about recent dollar strength. This USD rally was driven by geopolitical events rather than cyclical outperformance, which makes it susceptible to a reversal on US-Iran de-escalation. While timing there remains uncertain, a scenario is possible where Iran drone capability is degraded quickly. Citi Commodities see $80-90/bbl Brent for at least the next 1-2 weeks, before seeing prices moderate in 2Q. This reflects heavily disrupted flows for the next 1-2 weeks before flows gradually return in the latter part of March (Global Commodities - Energy market outlook: Strait of Hormuz closure - when a wildcard becomes the reality). In that context, the amount of Iranian drone launches needs to be watched. While the US and Israel have largely degraded Iran’s missile capabilities, its drones remain a threat (WSJ March 5, 2026). This is reflected in daily UAE data on such launches (Figure 1), which show missile attacks have fallen sharply while drone launches have plateaued. Secretary Hegseth and General Caine noted in a recent briefing that they are taking greater control of airspace, and will be accelerating the pace of attacks as well as the method, from “stand-off munitions to stand-in munitions” (Department of War). records.text: E M – L O C A L E YE S FO R A G L O B A L V IE W The UK would have to navigate a potential energy price shock with a similar fragmented political backdrop as its European peers but the added challenge of already subdued economic growth. Although the economy is less directly exposed than the eurozone, due to its lower energy intensity (Figure 2) and a relatively small manufacturing sector, the inflationary shock could dampen consumer sentiment and spending. A persistent but moderate energy price shock would not fundamentally change our UK outlook, but it would complicate an already delicate situation. A sustained and escalatory shock would require a complete reassessment of our ‘muddling through’ outlook. Transmission considerations: The transmission of a surge in oil and gas prices to fuel prices is broadly similar across countries; however, some idiosyncrasies affect UK households’ energy prices. First, the UK’s structurally low levels of gas storage (Figure 5) leave it more vulnerable to large price spikes. Second, the Ofgem price cap mechanically slows down the speed of transmission to household energy prices by one or two quarters. This contributes to the dynamics seen in 2022, when UK energy price shocks were of a similar size as in the eurozone but peaked slightly later (Figure 6). We have argued in the past that much of this statistical relationship is at least partially attributable to the fact that over longer periods, oil prices have covaried positively with growth expectations. How- ever, our analysis has also shown that 5Yx5Y inflation swaps have not tended to exhibit reduced sensitivity to supply-driven oil price increases (see TIPS Strategy, 10/25/24). In fact, while longer-run forwards initially lagged the move higher alongside the rally in oil prices in February 2022 following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, the move higher in inflation expectations was more parallel in nature as the conflict continued to escalate. Thus, if prior experience serves as a guide, we could see longer-run forwards creep higher over com- ing days (Figure 5. . . b u t h a v e b e e n r e m a r k a b l y s t a b l e o v e r t h e p a s t w e e k , t r a d i n g n e a r t h e i r l o w e s t l e v e l s s i n c e l a s t s p r i n g ).

Unfortunately, the next comprehensive NZ labour force survey is not due until early May. This lack of a trigger links to a common topic in client discussions: the difficult carry set-up to play NZ policy normalization. NZD 1s/2s is steep, and the RBNZ is likely to normalize, but doesn’t show urgency to start. The relative underreaction of NZ assets to the survey and growth data is then partially justified in the sense that excess capacity buys the RBNZ time, pushing policy normalization into the forwards, which are now close to fair value (Figure 8N Z D 1 Y x 1 Y i s a b o u t f a i r i n o u t r i g h t t e r m s g i v e n m a c r o i n p u t s a s t h e y s t a n d ). The precise timing of the coming unemployment rate decline in a sense summarizes the carry headwind, as an imminent tightening of the labour market would overcome negative carry concerns. In our models, every 1%-pt lower on unemployment flattens 2s/10s swap by 40bp, and 6m forward 2s/10s is about 15bp below spot. A roughly 0.3-0.4%-pt fall in unemployment in the next six months is then needed to beat the forwards. If current curve shape is preserved, we look to re-enter NZD flattening trades closer to the 1Q labour data. The ECB board members, while acknowledging that inflationary impact of the rising energy prices, are still highlighting patience. The duration and depth of the energy shock will ulti- mately shape inflation, growth, and sentiment—and thus the ECB’s reaction. Accordingly, we think a further material rise in energy prices would be required for the ECB to tighten, with any response calibrated to the growth/sentiment impact and to fiscal or other policy measures. Indeed, recent ECB commentary has been along similar lines (Figure 4E C B c o m m e n t a r y h i g h l i g h t s p a t i e n c e ; d u r a t i o n a n d d e p t h o f o n g o i n g c r i s i s w i l l d e t e r m i n e f u t u r e c o u r s e o f a c t i o n a s t h e E C B r e m a i n s i n a g o o d p l a c e ). That said, while we see the recent repricing of tightening expectations as excessive, linger- ing geopolitical headline risk and positioning/liquidity technicals argue for elevated market volatility. Trade Fraud: According to the IMF, discrepancies could also result from trade fraud, where firms may undervalue imports in order to evade import tariffs and non-tariff trade measures, or undervalue exports to avoid taxes. 4. Reporting Quality: Reporting quality can vary not only between countries but also within a country across imports and exports. For a given country, imports are usually recorded with more accuracy than exports because imports generally generate tariff revenues while exports do not. Further, reporting quality can vary across products within the same country. Meaningful trade discrepancies exist in US-China trade data, as we discussed in Global Trade Monitor: Staying Subdued. The flow of goods from China to the US is captured by the US CENSUS's data on US imports from China as well as by China GACC's data on Chinese Exports to the US. Prior to 2018, there had been a large and persistent gap between these two dataseries, with the US consistently reporting about US$100 billion worth of trade more than China. EUR Anti-dollar gains run against the energy shock The roughly 2% decline in EUR/USD since the start of the Middle East crisis is well within our estimated response of both the broad dollar to oil price spikes and the euro's own sensitivity to European natural gas prices. This development has partially offset the reemergence of US risk premia since the Greenland spat, which boosted the euro as the main "anti-dollar" at the start of the year. These two factors are likely to remain dominant for the path of EUR/USD in coming weeks and months, with energy prices likely the prime driver until a path to a more-stable geopolitical equilibrium emerges. The sharp hawkish repricing of the ECB in a world of energy supply shocks is unlikely to be too helpful, as the EUR tends to weaken during times of sharply deteriorating European competitiveness per the Ukraine war precedent. JPY Renewed weakness with higher oil prices Japan relies on the Middle East for about 90% of its crude oil imports. If transport disruptions were to be prolonged, there is a possibility that oil reserves – said to meet 254 days of demand – could be released to ensure the stability of domestic supplies. OPEC+ supply increases: OPEC+ announced last on 1 March its intention to increase production by 206kbd in April. The current (final) production unwind allows for another 1mbd. In addition, according to data from Energy Aspects, OPEC+ spare capacity would be 3mbd after this unwind is finished. There are two key caveats, though. First, given OPEC+ production levels, we expect at best 50% of any announced supply increase to be reflected in actual barrels to market. This implies the April increase should generate ~100kbd delivered, or 0.7% of the shortfall (we estimate 1mbd on paper means 500kbd delivered or 3.5% of the shortfall). Second, as most of the OPEC+ barrels would need to traverse the Strait of Hormuz, an ongoing disruption would require the avoidance pipelines we discussed above, implying upside is limited. Chinese crude stocks: China has built its crude stocks up to around 1.1bn barrels. We don’t expect a large SPR release, however. With 110 days of demand coverage, we anticipate Chinese offtakers will not feel an urgent need (or incentive) to immediately backfill Iranian barrels they might lose; they could take the barrels from storage instead. records.text: mple replacement will hold a key. Negative real wage growth again if oil exceeds $80/bbl A more important question is whether the positive growth in real wages can be sustained. The key determinant will be crude oil prices (see Escalation in the Middle East: Macro implications for Japan 02 March). For nominal wages, we expect the base pay increase in the FY26 Shunto wage negotiations to be around +3.7% YoY (see Shunto update: Union demands point to around 3.7% base-up 05 March), which should support underlying macro wage growth of around 2.5–3%. On inflation, under our current oil price assumption of around $60/bbl, we expect CPI to stay below 2% for the time being before gradually moving back toward 2%. Based on this, we have projected that real wages will remain positive throughout 2026 (Exhibit 5). However, the recent sharp increases in crude oil and LNG prices will push up the energy CPI, weighing on real wage growth. According to our simulations using several crude oil price scenarios1, if crude oil stays at or above $80/bbl, real wages will fall back into negative territory from April–June onward (Exhibit 6). Globalization and its discontent As China and other emerging markets (EMs) matured, supply chain relocation expanded and shifted toward higher-tech industries. At the same time, fueled by strong export profits, emerging market firms began expanding globally, making FDI flows increasingly two-way. However, the increasing globalization of production and investments also began to create fractures in the developed world. As supply chains relocated, the share of profits in national income grew while labor’s share declined, shifting more of the economic gains to firms rather than workers. Social and political discontent with globalization gathered steam in the West and intensified after the 2008 financial crisis recession. Demand led increases in oil prices typically coincide with stronger global activity and broad-based inflation across goods and services, which mechanically overstates the direct inflationary effect of oil itself. By contrast, pure oil supply shocks— such as those triggered by geopolitical disruptions—raise oil prices while weighing on global activity, generating stagflationary dynamics. Properly identifying these supply-side shocks is therefore essential to isolating the causal impact of oil prices on inflation. Our results indicate that while oil supply shocks do raise energy inflation, their effect on core inflation is modest once demand-driven forces are stripped out. In particular, we find no evidence of meaningful second-round spillovers. Quantitatively, a 10% increase in oil prices is associated with a roughly 35bp boost to headline inflation, with relatively rapid pass-through: most of the impact materializes within three months. The effect on core inflation is far more muted, at just about 3bp after three months. Finally, the limited impact on core inflation is not only small but also narrow in scope. Unfortunately, the next comprehensive NZ labour force survey is not due until early May. This lack of a trigger links to a common topic in client discussions: the difficult carry set-up to play NZ policy normalization. NZD 1s/2s is steep, and the RBNZ is likely to normalize, but doesn’t show urgency to start. The relative underreaction of NZ assets to the survey and growth data is then partially justified in the sense that excess capacity buys the RBNZ time, pushing policy normalization into the forwards, which are now close to fair value (Figure 8N Z D 1 Y x 1 Y i s a b o u t f a i r i n o u t r i g h t t e r m s g i v e n m a c r o i n p u t s a s t h e y s t a n d ). The precise timing of the coming unemployment rate decline in a sense summarizes the carry headwind, as an imminent tightening of the labour market would overcome negative carry concerns. In our models, every 1%-pt lower on unemployment flattens 2s/10s swap by 40bp, and 6m forward 2s/10s is about 15bp below spot. A roughly 0.3-0.4%-pt fall in unemployment in the next six months is then needed to beat the forwards. If current curve shape is preserved, we look to re-enter NZD flattening trades closer to the 1Q labour data. records.text: Asia Economic Weekly | 06 March 2026 7 Taiwan in Focus Xiaoqing Pi Merrill Lynch (Hong Kong) Helen Qiao Merrill Lynch (Hong Kong) See report: Taiwan Watch: Taiwan’s energy vulnerability amid Middle East tensions Taiwan is sensitive to a protracted conflict in Middle East The US–Israel military operation in Iran has raised the risk of higher energy prices and disrupted shipping around the Strait of Hormuz, a chokepoint that normally carries about one‑fifth of global LNG trade. While a protracted conflict is not our base case, if a de‑facto blockade were to persist, Taiwan would likely come under stress earlier than many Asian peers given its gas‑heavy power system and relatively thin on‑island LNG inventories. High dependence, thin buffers and power-hungry factories The island is vulnerable to any prolonged blockade to the Strait of Hormuz, for several reasons: Heavy dependence on imported LNG: Natural gas generated 48% of Taiwan’s power in 2025, as nuclear units were retired, and nearly all gas is imported as LNG. Hormuz accounts for a third of supply: Taiwan imported 34% of its LNG by volume from Qatar last year, and Qatari cargoes must transit the Strait of Hormuz. Qatar has halted its LNG production since March 2. Semiconductor-making is power intensive: Industry is the largest electricity consumer, using over half of Taiwan’s power. This is largely driven by a later-than-usual Lunar New Year holiday. Headline PPI inflation rose to -0.9% yoy in February from -1.4% yoy in January, mainly due to elevated nonferrous metal prices. Under the revised path, year-over-year PPI inflation is likely to turn positive as early as the start of Q2 2026. records.text: orrelation between oil prices and inflation at any given point in time. This is hardly surprising. Many other factors influence inflation, and in many cases the observed co-movement can signal common factors driving both oil prices changes and inflation and not necessarily implying any causality from the first into the second. For example, oil prices and inflation are quite correlated around the Global Financial Crisis, but the main mechanism is arguably the economic slowdown leading oil prices down. Similarly, after the initial lockdowns, the COVID reopening led to a boost in demand, though that was then compounded with a textbook supply shock with the war in Ukraine. Still, we find that only large and persistent spikes in oil prices, which we can usually track to a supply shock, seem to be a leading indicator for a persistent increase in inflation. records.text: e progress in closing gender pay gap The female working-age population (ages 15-64) labor force participation rate in Japan has been rising steadily, reaching over 77% in 2025—a high level even by international standards (Figure 5J a p a n ’ s f e m a l e l a b o r p a r t i c i p a t i o n r a t i o a n d g e n d e r p a y ). However, progress in closing the wage gap has stalled in recent years. While rising inflation and a tight labor market since 2022 have led to significant increases in nominal wages, companies have not used this opportunity to close the gender pay gap. The gender pay gap remained largely unchanged from 2022 to 2024, with women earning only 75.8% of men’s wages in 2024. In 2025, the ratio of female executives at listed companies rose by 1.5%-pts to 14%. To address these issues, the government made it mandatory in July 2022 for companies with more than 301 employees to disclose gender pay gaps. Furthermore, from April 2026, this requirement will be expanded to companies with more than 101 employees. Going forward, a key question will be whether mandatory disclosure of pay gaps and action plans will drive corporate change through market pressure. While direct economic spillovers from conflict in the Middle East are likely limited for now, the indirect impact via commodity prices has the potential to materially alter the THB’s trajectory. Energy prices are the most obvious channel, with a disruption of shipping lanes via the Strait of Hormuz the well flagged risk and Thailand running one of the largest energy deficits in the region at 7.4% of GDP. A secondary impact may also come from freight pricing, with Thailand structurally having the worst freight balance in the region - though we expect disruptions to be more manageable than during the 2021 spike. A tertiary effect of the conflict is likely to be higher gold prices, to the degree it escalates geopolitical risks and heightens safe haven demand. records.text: 6 March 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Deutsche Bank AG Page 3 Bond Market Strategy EUR Rates: Excess flattening in 2s30s The EUR 2s30s curve has flattened by over 35bps this week, as events in the Middle East shook out two popular trades in the Euro rates. The sharp rise in European energy prices in particular has led to a stark reassessment of the risks to policy rates. The market has pivoted from partially pricing a cut, to now pricing more than 25bps of hikes by year end. It is highly likely that this is in part driven by positioning. Front end carry trades have been popular, as the ECB was widely expected to remain on hold this year, combined with the perceived risks of policy easing given the undershoot in inflation, and growing private credit/AI concerns. Euribor and SFI futures volumes saw an exceptional 10 standard deviation move this week, which is indicative of unwinds. Current market pricing appears excessive in relation to the revaluation in inflation forecasts. The rise in natural gas prices in particular will have a large impact on HICP as our inflation strategists have highlighted. However, given the deeply inverted oil curve, the impact on medium-term inflation has been relatively limited. The upgrades to the inflation forecasts due to energy developments have primarily removed the downside risks to the target so far. records.text: Data Science: Update on companies' hiring for AI Renate Marold(v) BCI, US | David (Xinyuan) Liu(v) BCI, US This section is a Special Report that is not an equity or a debt research report under U.S. FINRA Rules 2241-2242. Previously, we provided insights into which companies might be at risk of falling behind in the AI race by analyzing those that have low hiring for "expert AI skills" and are also low on the sales-to-employees metric. In our view, a company hiring for very specific AI-related skills might be further along the curve of using AI to complement or replace commonplace work practices than a company hiring solely for general AI skills. Moreover, if a firm is positioned closer to the bottom of sales per employee, it is already at a disadvantage relative to peers that are able to generate more sales for each employee. To capture companies' AI hiring, we leverage our job openings data database. We label a job posting as an AI postings if it contains any AI-related keywords. We look for "general AI" skills, matching on keywords such as "AI, " "machine learning, " or "data scientist. " Furthermore, we classify a job posting as an expert AI skill job posting if it contains keywords reflective of niche AI skills, such as "pytorch" or "deep learning. " In our dataset of job postings, we also have company identifiers for the job posting, the creation and deletion dates of the posting, and the company's GIC sector. records.text: PLN: The NBP surprised the market by cutting the policy rate by 25bp. The governor highlighted that the decision did not factor in recent developments in commodity markets and was mainly driven by the new inflation projection and soft labour-market data. However, the governor stated that the outlook is very uncertain, suggesting that the NBP will remain on hold for the foreseeable future. Our PLN FRA 9x12 payer reached its target, so we close our recommendation, marking a hypothetical profit of 25bp. We now turn neutral, as we do not expect the NBP to hike rates any time soon. Polish back-end rates sold off, in line with peers. We do not expect the CPI print this week to have a material impact on PLN rates. ILS: Israeli assets — both FX and rates — outperformed their peers in the past week, as the market seems to be recalibrating to the new geopolitical landscape in the Middle East with reduced Israeli premia. We agree with the view that in the long term the current developments might offer a safer region for Israel, but the path to it is highly non-linear. Consequently, we remain cautious, and we expect Israeli assets to be volatile in the near term. ZAR: The global risk sell-off has weighed on the ZAR and SAGBs, in particular, due to the fact that both were heavily positioned before the war. records.text: ing the February deceleration. Average hourly earnings, +0.4% m/m and 3.8% y/y, along with a steady workweek, resulted in a rise in payroll incomes despite the fall in payrolls. Aggregate payroll incomes increased 0.3% m/m have risen at a 5.1% annual rate so far in 1Q—close to last year's pace. Now, however, tariffs are likely reducing real purchasing power more than they were. We think that the heavy snowfall and a swing toward colder weather temporarily depressed February payrolls, by around 30k. Construction payrolls, typically the most sensitive, fell 10k vs a +5k trend. Other industries too were likely weakened. This drag will reverse. Health care payrolls were lowered by a strike: 31k on strike in California and Hawaii. Also, they had risen 116k in January, around 50k above trend; their 19k decline in February probably reflected some combination of unwind of the January surge plus the strikers. The strike ended February 24, and health payrolls likely rebound in March. Federal payrolls fell 10k. We thought there might be some stabilization in federal government employment after last year’s rapid cuts, but today's report suggests that austerity will extend for longer. Apart from these one offs, payrolls showed broad slowing: professional and business services swinging from +18k to -5k; leisure from -12k to -27k; manufacturing +5k to -12k; and private education +13k to -16k. Some of these swings likely included weather effects, but this was still a broad slowing.

records.text: l volatility Despite heightened market volatility stemming from Middle East tensions, equity flows have remained resilient, marking a fifth consecutive week of inflows. This week’s activity was largely driven by RoW, offsetting sharp outflows from the US. EM equities, global funds, and Japan continued to attract solid interest. Europe ex-UK markets saw steady inflows, while the UK registered outflows Globally, sector allocations were heavily influenced by the geopolitical backdrop. Energy and Materials featured prominently among the top beneficiaries, with Industrials also seeing strong demand—likely supported by aerospace and defense. In contrast, Healthcare and Consumer Discretionary witnessed notable outflows. Within Europe, inflows were concentrated in Industrials, Energy and Utilities, with the rest of the sectors experiencing outflows. Fixed income flows remain anchored around the ~$20bn weekly run rate. Inflows were broad-based, led by safe-haven assets such as US treasuries and European government bonds. IG credit in both the US and Europe saw inflows, while HY was mixed - US HY marginally positive but Europe recording outflows. Money market funds posted $6bn of inflows, well below the year-to-date average of more than $30bn. Year-to-date, money market funds have accumulated roughly $275bn, while equities and fixed income are tracking closely at around $180bn each. 6 March 2026 5 Barclays | Equity Market Review

records.text: M Global Foundation 20 Navigating the Nuances and Quirks of Global Trade Data While the UN Comtrade data provides valuable insights, there are certain asymmetries in global trade that users should keep in mind. In an ideal world, the exports from country A to country B would equal imports by country B from country A. In practice, these figures rarely match, for a variety of reasons. These discrepancies are well documented and researched (WITS- World Bank and IMF), but reconciling them is not easy. Some reasons for the discrepancies include: 1. Differences in Valuation Methods: There are two ways to report trade — CIF (cost, insurance and freight), and FOB (free on board). Under CIF contracts, the seller assumes responsibility for costs and liabilities until the goods are loaded onto the vessel at the port of origin. Under FOB contracts, the buyer is responsible for shipping and other costs as well as insurance beginning when the goods are loaded onto the vessel and during the voyage. FOB contracts are generally more cost-effective because buyers have more control over shipping and insurance. In UN Comtrade, imports are recorded CIF while exports are FOB. This may result in a 10-20% difference. 2. Transshipment and Re-Exports: The re-routing of products through third countries often leads to a mismatch in the recorded country of origin, and additional transport and insurance costs incurred can further distort trade figures. 3. records.text: Europe Economic Weekly | 06 March 2026 9 Scenario 2: Brent at £60/barrel and gas prices at 140pence/therm in March-April and then a return to normal (in 2/3rd, 1/3rd steps) If gas prices are higher through March- April, it would still likely mean a rise in the July energy price cap. But a return to normal thereafter can imply a fall in the October cap.
